docs.title: Ashwagandha: What It Actually Does vs What People Think
docs.text:
The rare supplement whose popular use — a mild cortisol, stress and sleep lever — is genuinely supported, just modestly and at low certainty, while nearly everything above that core is oversold, and the flagship belief that "natural means safe" is false.

Independent research, 4 September 2026. 64 cited sources (62 PubMed-verified — every PMID title-matched against PubMed, 0 wrong). Not medical advice.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Bottom line

Ashwagandha is the rare supplement whose popular use is genuinely supported, but only modestly: it reliably lowers the cortisol biomarker and gives a small short-term sleep and stress benefit, on a short, small, manufacturer-funded evidence base with no long-term data. It is not a testosterone booster for a healthy man, "adaptogen" is a marketing word, and the flagship belief that "natural means safe" is false: it causes real, confirmed liver injury, with deaths and a transplant on record, plus a thyroid and transplant-rejection risk, and it is banned in Denmark.

Myths vs. reality

The claim you've heard What the evidence actually shows "Ashwagandha crushes your stress and cortisol" It reliably lowers the cortisol biomarker, but the best independent meta-analysis found cortisol falls while perceived stress does not, and the stress-scale effect is low-certainty, inflated by small manufacturer-funded trials "It's a natural testosterone booster" A modest men-only ~+57 ng/dL, carried by stressed, overweight and subfertile men and tracking the cortisol drop; the newest clean trial in healthy men was null, and no trial isolates a rise in a healthy non-stressed man "It fixes sleep better than melatonin" A real but small sleep benefit (best in diagnosed insomnia); in the one head-to-head, melatonin 3 mg slightly out-performed it, and there is zero polysomnography evidence "It's a safe adaptogen you can take forever" "Adaptogen" is a marketing term (EMA-rejected); no trial runs beyond ~12 weeks, and it causes confirmed liver injury (deaths, a transplant), raises thyroid hormones, and is banned in Denmark "It boosts your immune system" Only tiny marker studies — and the same immunostimulation caused a documented organ-transplant rejection "Ayurvedic means it's pure and natural" About 1 in 5 Ayurvedic products carry lead, mercury or arsenic above limits; safety depends on third-party testing, not the word "natural" "It protects your brain / prevents dementia" Zero human trials — the brain-protection data is entirely rodent and cell-line

What you actually learn

  • The popular use is real, but modest and low-certainty. Cortisol drops reliably, sleep improves a little (best in insomnia), stress scores improve short-term — but the effect sizes are inflated by small, 8-week, manufacturer-funded trials, and one independent meta found the feeling of stress didn't move even as cortisol did.
  • The testosterone story is stress-correction, not androgen-boosting. The +57 ng/dL rides on stressed, overweight and subfertile men; in healthy men the newest clean trial is null.
  • "Safe because natural" is the flagship myth. Ashwagandha causes confirmed drug-induced liver injury — with deaths and a transplant — plus a thyroid-hormone and transplant-rejection risk, and Denmark has banned it in supplements.
  • The whole evidence base is short, small, and sponsor-funded, with no Cochrane review; the most independent appraisals are the most cautious.
  • "Adaptogen" is a marketing word, not a validated drug class.

What this means for you

  • If you take it for stress or sleep, that's the one defensible reason — but expect a mild, short-term effect, not a cure, and know it doesn't beat melatonin for sleep.
  • Don't take it as a testosterone booster if you're a healthy, lean, low-stress man — the evidence there is null.
  • Treat "natural" as no safety guarantee. Avoid it, or use it only with monitoring, if you have liver, thyroid, or autoimmune disease, or take thyroid medication; never if pregnant, trying to conceive, or breastfeeding; and never as a transplant recipient or on immunosuppressants. Stop immediately and check your liver if you get jaundice or dark urine.
  • If you use it: a standardized root extract (KSM-66-type), 300-600 mg a day, third-party-tested for heavy metals, in a defined block (8-12 weeks) matched to a stress or sleep goal — not a permanent daily tonic.
  • Expect additive effects with alcohol and sedatives, and with blood-pressure or diabetes medication.

TL;DR

Ashwagandha is the unusual case where the popular use is not a fabrication — but it is modest, short-term, and low-certainty. Its one reproducible human effect is lowering cortisol15, and it probably produces small short-term reductions in perceived stress, anxiety scores and, best-evidenced, sleep (the sleep meta pools SMD -0.59, strongest in diagnosed insomnia at 600+ mg for 8+ weeks)14. The honest ceiling: the large "SMD ~-1.5" stress headline is inflated by small, 8-week, manufacturer-funded Indian trials at LOW-certainty evidence with heterogeneity up to 94%, and the one independent meta found cortisol falls while perceived stress does not86. Testosterone is a modest, men-only ~+57 ng/dL meta effect5 carried by stressed, overweight and subfertile men and tracking the cortisol drop — and the newest clean trial in healthy men is null36. "Adaptogen" is a Soviet-era marketing term, EMA-rejected57. And "safe because natural" is the flagship myth: ashwagandha causes RUCAM-confirmed drug-induced liver injury with deaths and a transplant on record19202122, raises thyroid hormones28, triggered a documented transplant rejection47, and has been banned in Denmark26. The popular use is real but oversold; the harmless-natural-tonic framing is not.

The picture, ranked by how strongly the evidence agrees

Tier 1 (settled): cortisol-lowering is the one reproducible human biomarker (but a surrogate) · perceived-stress/anxiety scores improve short-term at LOW certainty · cortisol can fall while perceived stress does not · sleep is the best-evidenced benefit (SMD -0.59, best in insomnia) · zero polysomnography exists · "safe because natural" is refuted by real liver injury · the whole base is short, small, Indian, manufacturer-funded, no Cochrane review · it raises thyroid hormones · physical performance is the best-meta'd benefit (but training-confounded). Tier 2 (real but modest / population-specific): testosterone rises modestly, but only in stressed/overweight/subfertile men, tracking cortisol · the newest healthy-men trial is null · fertility gains are real only in subfertile men · no testosterone effect in women · strength gains are training-driven and testosterone-neutral · depression is very weak · cognition rests on single trials · the immunostimulation is a real transplant/autoimmune hazard. Tier 3 (weak/preclinical): the calming mechanisms (GABA, serotonin) are rodent-only · withaferin A is a cytotoxicity story, not the stress mechanism · the sleep molecule is from mouse leaf, the products are root · human pharmacokinetics is sparse · the brand/form changes everything · dementia is a myth in humans. Tier 4 (myths): "adaptogen" is a marketing term · "T booster for anyone" · "boosts immunity" · "beats melatonin" · "a safe forever tonic" · "Ayurvedic means pure."

docs.title: What this review covered
docs.text: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is the best-selling "adaptogen" on the market, sold for stress, sleep, testosterone, immunity and general vitality. A seven-cluster evidence sweep — pharmacology and forms, stress/cortisol/anxiety, testosterone and fertility, sleep, cognition/performance/thyroid, safety and hepatotoxicity, and the marketing myths — tested each claim against the peer-reviewed literature: the randomized trials, the meta-analyses, the case-report and pharmacovigilance record, and the regulatory positions. Every PubMed citation was title-matched against PubMed before use (0 wrong), and three citation conflicts were resolved by hand. Unlike most supplements in this series, its popular use turns out to have a genuine signal — the honest work is separating that modest, low-certainty core from everything the marketing piles on top, including the false idea that "natural" means "safe."

docs.title: Tier 1 — The strongest, settled evidence
docs.text:
Cortisol-lowering is the one reproducible human biomarker — but cortisol is a surrogate. Multiple randomized trials show a ~20-28% serum-cortisol drop versus placebo1234, and the hormone meta pools a large cortisol effect5. This HPA-axis lowering is the best human-anchored mechanism ashwagandha has. But cortisol is diurnally noisy, assay-dependent, and a surrogate — a lower number is not the same as a better outcome, and the decisive independent finding is that cortisol can fall while perceived stress does not (one independent meta found no significant pooled effect on perceived stress, and the independent US trial was null between groups even as cortisol dropped)67. The biomarker moves more reliably than the feeling — the reverse of the marketing.

Perceived-stress and anxiety scores improve short-term — but at low certainty. The meta-analyses report large pooled reductions (anxiety and stress standardized effects around -1.5 to -1.8)89, but on heterogeneity up to 94%, GRADE certainty rated LOW, trials mostly 8 weeks or less, samples of 40-130, overwhelmingly Indian and manufacturer-linked108111213. The direction is probably real; the size and certainty are overstated. Depression is the weakest endpoint — no adequately powered standalone trial, very-low certainty, with publication bias detected13.

Sleep is the best-evidenced benefit, with a clear ceiling. The dedicated sleep meta pools a significant SMD -0.59, larger in diagnosed insomnia and at higher dose and longer duration14; real-world magnitude is modest (sleep onset shaved ~12-16 minutes, efficiency up ~7-8 points)1516. But there is zero polysomnography — the objective evidence is wrist-actigraphy in only two trials, and everything else is self-report1718; "objectively fixes sleep architecture" is unproven.

"Safe because natural" is refuted — this is the most important finding. NIH LiverTox scores ashwagandha "B" — a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury — cataloguing ~23 RUCAM-assessed cases of cholestatic or mixed hepatocellular injury with jaundice19. The DILIN case series established the signal20, an Indian series reported three deaths in patients with pre-existing liver disease21, and a US case required a liver transplant2223. It is idiosyncratic, and short efficacy trials are structurally too small to detect a roughly one-in-thousands harm — so "no serious events in the trials" is not evidence against it.

The whole evidence base is short, small, single-country and manufacturer-funded. Almost every pivotal trial is 12 weeks or less, n 40-130, Indian single-center, and supplied or funded by the extract's maker (KSM-66/Ixoreal, Sensoril/Natreon, Shoden/Arjuna); publication bias has been detected, there is no Cochrane review, and the most independent appraisals are the most cautious81324252627. Ashwagandha also measurably raises thyroid hormones (T3, T4 up; TSH down)28 — a narrow benefit in subclinical hypothyroidism, and a hazard for everyone else. Physical performance is the best-meta'd benefit (large pooled effects on VO2max and strength)29303132, but the inputs are small, industry-linked, and paired with training programs that drive much of the gain.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Real but modest, and population-specific
docs.text:
Testosterone is the modest, population-dependent exception. The hormone meta pools a men-only ~+57 ng/dL (women's change is non-significant; no estradiol effect either sex)5, but the average is carried by stressed, overweight and subfertile men, and the coherent through-line is the parallel cortisol drop — this reads as stress- and deficiency-correction, not a direct androgenic action. The most-cited trial is confounded by a resistance-training program plus fat loss3334; the Sensoril strength trial was even testosterone-neutral35; and the newest clean trial in healthy men found no significant testosterone rise36. No trial isolates a testosterone increase in a healthy, non-stressed, non-training man3736. Male fertility gains (sperm count, motility) are real but only in oligospermic or infertile men — correction of a suppressed axis38394041. In women, ashwagandha does not raise testosterone, and the female sexual-function signal is subjective54243.

Cognition and the immune claim. Cognition rests on single small trials each — MCI memory, bipolar cognition, a reaction-time crossover — none replicated444546. The immunostimulant action is real enough to be a hazard: a documented kidney-transplant rejection followed ashwagandha use, so it warrants caution in transplant, autoimmune and immunosuppressed users47.

docs.title: Tier 3 — Weak or preclinical: mechanism outruns the data
docs.text: The calming mechanisms are rodent-only. The GABAergic and serotonergic effects invoked to explain the anxiolysis are shown in mouse neurons, not humans, and are attributed to withanolide glycosides, not the marquee compounds4849; the human evidence stops at the cortisol biomarker. Withaferin A — the most-assayed withanolide — is mainly a cytotoxicity story (a reactive electrophile), not the reason a stress capsule works, and higher-withaferin leaf extracts are arguably a liability for daily use5051. Even the sleep mechanism does not line up: the proposed sleep molecule (triethylene glycol) is from mouse leaf extract, while the tested products are withanolide-standardized root52. Human pharmacokinetics is sparse (about four studies, low ng/mL, no dose-response link)5354, so in-vitro withaferin-A pharmacology does not translate to a swallowed capsule. "Ashwagandha 600 mg" is nearly meaningless — KSM-66, Sensoril, Shoden and generic powder differ by plant part and standardization and are not bioequivalent55. And for dementia or Alzheimer's there are zero human trials — only rodent and cell-line data56; in humans this is a myth.

docs.title: Tier 4 — Myths and refuted claims
docs.text: "Adaptogen" is a Soviet-era (1947) marketing construct with unfalsifiable criteria; the EMA rejects it for marketing authorization and no regulator recognizes it as a drug class5726. "A natural testosterone booster for anyone" is a myth for the general man — the signal is extract-, population- and industry-specific, and the newest healthy-men trial is null53658. "Boosts immunity" rests on tiny marker studies and is double-edged (the same immunostimulation caused a transplant rejection)47. "Beats melatonin" is a myth — in the one head-to-head, melatonin 3 mg slightly out-performed ashwagandha14. "A safe daily tonic you can take forever" is a myth — no trial runs beyond ~12 weeks, and regulators (Denmark's ban, an EU procedure, Dutch liver warnings) do not treat the file as settled265960, and it is a precautionary contraindication in pregnancy6162. And "Ayurvedic means pure" is false — about one in five Ayurvedic products carry lead, mercury or arsenic above limits6364, so real-world safety depends on third-party testing, not on the word "natural."

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text: Ashwagandha is a rare case where the popular use — a mild, short-term cortisol, stress and sleep lever — is genuinely supported, just modestly and at low certainty, on a manufacturer-funded evidence base with no long-term data. Everything above that core — a general testosterone boost, immune boosting, a validated "adaptogen" identity, a consequence-free daily tonic — is oversold, and the flagship consumer belief that "natural" means "safe" is contradicted by a real, RUCAM-confirmed liver-injury signal with deaths and a transplant. Used sensibly — a standardized root extract, 300-600 mg a day, third-party-tested for heavy metals, in a time-limited block matched to a stress or sleep goal — it is a reasonable tool. Taken as a permanent daily tonic, as a testosterone booster, or trusted because it is "natural," it is not what it is sold as.

docs.title: The full findings — all 35
docs.text:
Every conclusion this review reached, grouped by how strongly the evidence backs it. Each finding is distilled from the fully-cited evidence above.

Tier 1 — Settled: strongest, cleanest, multi-study evidence (9 findings)

1. Ashwagandha's one reproducible human biomarker effect is lowering cortisol — but cortisol is a noisy surrogate, not a clinical outcome.

Multiple RCTs show a ~20-28% serum-cortisol drop vs placebo (Chandrasekhar −27.9%), and the hormone meta pools a large cortisol effect (SMD −1.18). This HPA-axis lowering is the single best human-anchored mechanism the herb has. But cortisol is diurnally noisy, assay-dependent, and a surrogate — a lower number is not the same as a better outcome.

2. Perceived-stress and anxiety SCORES improve short-term vs placebo — but at LOW-certainty evidence with extreme heterogeneity and inflated effect sizes.

Meta-analyses report large pooled reductions (anxiety SMD −1.55, stress −1.75), but on I² ≈ 83-94% heterogeneity, GRADE certainty rated LOW, trials mostly ≤8 weeks, n 40-130, overwhelmingly Indian and manufacturer-linked. The direction is probably real; the "SMD ≈ −1.5" headline is inflated by small, short, sponsored trials.

3. The decisive independent nuance: cortisol can fall while perceived stress does NOT — the biomarker moves more reliably than the feeling.

The one independent meta focused on this found a real cortisol drop but no significant pooled effect on perceived stress (SMD −0.36, p=0.40), and the independent US trial (Remenapp) was null between groups on mood/stress even as cortisol fell. This is the reverse of the marketing, and it is the honest ceiling on the stress claim.

4. Sleep is the best-evidenced benefit — a small-to-moderate real effect, concentrated in diagnosed insomnia at higher dose and longer duration.

The dedicated sleep meta pooled SMD −0.59 (5 RCTs, n=400), larger in the insomnia subgroup (−0.84), at ≥600 mg/day (−0.69), and ≥8 weeks (−0.68); it is weak-to-null in healthy sleepers. Real-world magnitude is modest — sleep onset shaved ~12-16 min, efficiency +7-8 points.

5. There is ZERO polysomnography evidence — every sleep trial is subjective questionnaires plus actigraphy in only two, so "objectively fixes sleep architecture" is unproven.

No human RCT has used the gold-standard PSG; objective data is wrist-actigraphy (a movement proxy) in just Langade 2021 and Deshpande 2020, and everything else is self-report (PSQI, diaries) — the most placebo-sensitive instrument. There is no data on sleep stages, REM, or slow-wave sleep.

6. "Safe because it's natural" is false — ashwagandha causes RUCAM-confirmed drug-induced liver injury, with deaths and a transplant.

NIH LiverTox scores it "B" (a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury) with ~23 published cases; the DILIN case series (Björnsson) and RUCAM-"probable" reports document cholestatic/mixed hepatocellular injury with jaundice, one series reported 3 deaths in patients with pre-existing liver disease, and another an acute liver failure requiring transplant. It is idiosyncratic (variable latency, not tight dose-response), and short RCTs are structurally too small to detect it.

7. The whole evidence base is short, small, single-country and manufacturer-funded, with no Cochrane review — so confidence should be downgraded, not upgraded.

Almost every pivotal RCT is ≤12 weeks, n 40-130, Indian single-center, and supplied/funded by the extract maker (KSM-66/Ixoreal, Sensoril/Natreon, Shoden/Arjuna); publication bias has been detected, no Cochrane systematic review exists, and the most independent appraisals are the most cautious. Certainty drops as independence rises — itself a tell.

8. Ashwagandha measurably raises thyroid hormones — a narrow benefit in subclinical hypothyroidism and a real hazard for everyone else.

In the subclinical-hypothyroid RCT it raised T3 +41.5% and T4 +19.6% and lowered TSH −17.4% over 8 weeks. The same pharmacodynamic push can move a euthyroid or hyperthyroid person out of range (documented thyrotoxicosis) and can potentiate levothyroxine — so it is beneficial only in that narrow group and a monitored-caution elsewhere.

9. Physical performance is the best-meta'd benefit — but the large effects come from small, industry-linked, training-confounded trials.

The Bayesian meta reports large pooled effects on VO₂max (d≈1.85), strength/power (d≈0.68) and recovery, but the inputs are small, mostly Indian, several manufacturer-funded, and paired with a supervised training program that itself drives much of the gain. Read it as "large signal, low-quality inputs."

Tier 2 — Probable / population-dependent (9 findings)

10. The modest testosterone rise is real on average but population-dependent — it tracks cortisol-drop, fat-loss and sleep, not a direct androgenic action.

The hormone meta pools a men-only +57.43 ng/dL (women +5.09, non-significant; no estradiol effect either sex), but the average is carried by stressed, overweight and subfertile men, and the coherent through-line is the parallel cortisol drop (SMD −1.18). This reads as stress- and deficiency-correction, not testicular stimulation.

11. The newest clean trial in HEALTHY men found no significant testosterone rise — undercutting the "T booster for anyone" claim.

Khanna 2026 (KSM-66, 76 healthy men, 8 weeks) reported no significant between-group difference in testosterone; sexual-desire and erectile scores improved, but the hormone did not. The strongest recent, cleanest-population data point moves against the general-male booster story.

12. No trial isolates a testosterone increase in a healthy, non-stressed, eugonadal, weight-stable, non-training man.

Every positive testosterone trial is confounded by a stressed/overweight population, a resistance-training program, low-desire selection, or subfertility. The specific claim that ashwagandha raises T in an already-healthy man, by itself, has never been demonstrated.

13. Male fertility improvements are real but only in subfertile/infertile/stressed men — deficiency-axis correction, not a booster effect.

In oligospermic men, ashwagandha raised sperm count ~167% and improved motility/volume, and in infertile men it normalized a suppressed hormone axis (T↑, LH↑, FSH↓). The effect is correction of a dysregulated baseline, and does not generalize to a fertile, healthy man.

14. In women, ashwagandha does not raise testosterone and changes no estradiol — the female sexual-function signal is subjective, not hormone-mediated.

The hormone meta found no significant testosterone change in women and no estradiol effect in either sex; the one female-sexual-function pilot improved subjective FSFI scores without demonstrating a hormonal mechanism.

15. Strength and body-composition gains are real WITH a training program — but the STAR trial was testosterone-neutral, so the muscle effect does not run through a T rise.

Wankhede showed greater strength, muscle size and fat loss under resistance training, and the Sensoril STAR trial showed strength/recovery gains with no significant testosterone difference. The performance benefit is real in trained contexts but is not a testosterone story.

16. Depression is the weakest endpoint — secondary subscales only, very-low certainty, with publication bias detected.

There is no adequately powered standalone depression RCT; the signal appears only as DASS/secondary subscales, the mental-disorders meta rated depression very-low GRADE (SMD −1.28, wide CI) and detected publication bias for anxiety. The anti-anxiety signal does not transfer to a clean depression claim.

17. Cognition and memory rest on single small RCTs each, with no independent replication.

The MCI-memory trial (Choudhary), the bipolar-cognition trial (3 of ~12 tasks positive), and the healthy-men reaction-time crossover (n=20) are each one small, mostly KSM-66/Sensoril study. Direction is favorable but the evidence is thin and unreplicated.

18. Immunostimulant activity is real enough to be a hazard — a documented kidney-transplant rejection followed ashwagandha use.

A kidney-transplant recipient developed acute T-cell-mediated rejection and lost the graft after taking ashwagandha, consistent with its Th1-activating/immunostimulant action. It therefore warrants active caution in transplant recipients, autoimmune disease, and anyone on immunosuppressants.

Tier 3 — Weak / preclinical / mechanism (6 findings)

19. The calming mechanisms people cite (GABAergic, serotonergic) are rodent/in-vitro only — the sole human-anchored mechanism is cortisol lowering.

Direct GABA_A/ρ-receptor activity and serotonergic effects are shown in mouse neurons and oocytes, not humans, and are attributed to withanolide glycosides, not the marquee compounds. The human evidence stops at the cortisol biomarker.

20. Withaferin A — the most-studied, most-assayed withanolide — is mainly a cytotoxicity story, not the reason a stress/sleep capsule works.

Withaferin A is a reactive electrophile that covalently modifies many proteins, making it potently cytotoxic to normal as well as cancer cells; its pharmacology is an anticancer/in-vitro story, and higher-withaferin leaf extracts are arguably a liability for daily use. The compounds plausibly behind the calming effect are the harder-to-measure glycosides.

21. The proposed sleep molecule (triethylene glycol) is from mouse LEAF extract, but the tested products are withanolide-standardized ROOT — the mechanism and the product don't line up.

Triethylene glycol induced NREM sleep in mice while the withanolide-rich alcoholic extract did not, yet the human sleep trials use withanolide-standardized root products. The clinical benefit and the proposed molecule come from different plant fractions.

22. Human pharmacokinetics is real but sparse — low ng/mL plasma, only ~4 studies, and no PK/PD link.

Withanolides are absorbed to only single-digit-to-tens-of-ng/mL levels, from just four human PK studies, with no data linking a plasma concentration to a clinical effect. In-vitro withaferin-A pharmacology runs at micromolar concentrations far above what an oral capsule achieves — so straight-line extrapolation from the bench is unjustified.

23. "Ashwagandha 600 mg" is nearly meaningless — the brand, plant part and standardization determine everything.

KSM-66 (root, low-withaferin) ≠ Sensoril (root+leaf) ≠ Shoden (≥35% glycosides) ≠ generic powder, and at equal total withanolide dose two products are not bioequivalent. Pooling different brands, or extrapolating a branded trial to generic powder, is not valid.

24. Dementia and Alzheimer's: zero human RCTs — the "brain-protective" claim is rodent and cell-line only.

There are no human trials for dementia or slowing cognitive decline; the Aβ-plaque and neurite-regeneration findings are from the 5xFAD mouse and cell lines (withanolide A). In humans this is a myth, not a proven neuroprotectant.

Tier 4 — Myths (6 findings)

25. "Adaptogen" is a Soviet-era marketing/heritage construct, not a validated pharmacological or regulatory class.

The term was coined by Lazarev in 1947 for a synthetic compound and its criteria ("non-specific resistance," "normalizing") are essentially unfalsifiable; the EMA rejects it for marketing authorization and it has never been adopted as a class by the FDA or EMA. Ashwagandha's specific effects stand or fall on trial data, not on the adaptogen label.

26. "Natural testosterone booster for anyone" is a myth for the general man — the signal is confined to specific extracts, stressed/overweight/subfertile populations, and industry trials.

Positive testosterone data is extract- and population-specific and manufacturer-linked, and the newest clean trial in healthy men is null between groups. For a healthy, non-stressed man it is not a demonstrated booster.

27. "Boosts immunity" is overstated — only tiny mechanistic RCTs exist, and the immunostimulation is itself a transplant/autoimmune hazard.

Immune claims rest on small marker studies (NK-cell/WBC counts) with no hard clinical immune outcomes, and the very same Th1 activation caused a documented transplant rejection. "Boosts immunity" is both under-evidenced and double-edged.

28. "Beats melatonin for sleep" is a myth — in the one head-to-head, melatonin 3 mg slightly out-performed it on every metric.

In a 4-arm insomnia trial, melatonin 3 mg edged ashwagandha 600 mg on PSQI, sleep-onset latency and efficiency, and the combination was best. At best a tie, at worst a slight loss — not the superior natural hypnotic it is sold as.

29. "A safe daily tonic you can take forever" is a myth — there is no RCT beyond ~12 weeks, so long-term efficacy and safety are unknown.

Every trial is ≤12 weeks, reviewers explicitly flag the absence of >180-day data, and regulators (Denmark's outright restriction, an EU Article 8 procedure, RIVM/Lareb liver warnings) do not treat the file as settled. Indefinite daily use is unstudied and shadowed by the liver and thyroid signals.

30. "Ayurvedic means pure and clean" is a myth — about 1 in 5 Ayurvedic products carry lead, mercury or arsenic above limits.

JAMA surveys found ~20% of Ayurvedic products (US stores and online) exceeded regulatory metal limits at recommended dosing. Real-world safety depends on third-party testing, not on the "natural" label.

Practical — what to actually do (5 findings)

31. Contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation — on precaution, though the strength of the abortifacient evidence is itself disputed.

Traditional abortifacient use plus the cytotoxic withaferin A and the absence of adequate reproductive-toxicity data support a precautionary contraindication; recent ethnobotanical reviews argue the abortifacient literature is inflated and inconclusive, but the precaution stands. Do not use if pregnant, trying to conceive, or breastfeeding.

32. Avoid or use only with monitoring if you have liver, thyroid, autoimmune disease, or are a transplant recipient — and stop immediately if jaundice or dark urine appear.

The liver-injury, thyroid-hormone and immunostimulant signals converge on a clear caution list: pre-existing liver disease, hyper/hypothyroidism or thyroid meds, autoimmune disease, transplant/immunosuppression. Any jaundice, dark urine, or right-upper-quadrant pain warrants stopping and checking liver enzymes.

33. If you use it, the sensible form is a standardized ROOT extract (KSM-66-type), 300-600 mg/day, third-party-tested, for a defined block matched to a goal — not indefinitely.

The trials that work use standardized root extracts at 300-600 mg/day for 8-12 weeks; low-dose MK-4-style claims aside, root beats leaf for daily-use safety (less withaferin A), and heavy-metal testing matters more than the "natural" label. Match a defined course to a goal (stress or sleep) rather than taking it as a permanent tonic.

34. Expect additive drug effects — sedation with alcohol/benzodiazepines, and possible additive glucose- and blood-pressure-lowering.

Its GABA-mimetic action can add to CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines), and its modest glucose- and BP-lowering can add to antidiabetic and antihypertensive drugs. These are mostly theoretical/mechanistic but worth flagging for anyone on those medications.

35. For Patryk's stack (ashwagandha before sleep, for cortisol/sleep support), it is the one item with a defensible mechanism for the goal — but it is not a T booster for him, not risk-free, and should be time-limited and third-party-tested.

This is the single supplement in the stack with real (if modest, low-certainty) evidence for what it is taken for — a cortisol/sleep lever — unlike vitamin D, zinc or magnesium whose "T-boost" rationale is deficiency-only. But it does not raise testosterone in a healthy man, it carries a real liver + thyroid risk, and it should be cycled and heavy-metal-tested, not taken as a permanent daily tonic.

docs.title: Test yourself
docs.text:
Twelve questions drawn at random from the findings above. Pick an answer, see why, and learn. Replayable, and your best score is remembered on this device.

  1. Chandrasekhar K et al. 2012, Indian J Psychol Med. PMID 23439798. Landmark RCT (n=64, KSM-66 600 mg, 60 d): cortisol −27.9%, large stress-scale reductions vs placebo. ↩↩

  2. Salve J et al. 2019, Cureus. PMID 32021735. 3-arm dose-response RCT (250 vs 600 mg): dose-dependent cortisol and perceived-stress reductions. ↩

  3. Lopresti AL et al. 2019, Medicine (Baltimore). PMID 31517876. RCT (n=60, Shoden 240 mg, 60 d): HAM-A down (p=.04), morning cortisol down (p<.001), DHEA-S down; DASS-21 only near-significant. ↩

  4. Gopukumar K et al. 2021, Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. PMID 34858513. Largest/longest stress+cognition RCT (n=130, 90 d): PSS and cortisol down, sleep and well-being improved. ↩

  5. Fornalik M et al. 2026, Planta Med. PMID 41740946. Hormone meta (23 RCTs, n=1,706): men testosterone +57.43 ng/dL; women +5.09 (non-significant); no estradiol effect either sex; cortisol SMD −1.18. ↩↩↩↩↩↩

  6. Albalawi AA et al. 2025, Nutr Health. PMID 40746175. Independent meta titled 'Dual impact: Significant cortisol reduction but NO effects on perceived stress' (cortisol −1.16 µg/dL; PSS SMD −0.36, p=0.40). ↩↩

  7. Remenapp A et al. 2022, J Ayurveda Integr Med. PMID 34838432. Independent US RCT (n=60, NooGandha): NULL between-group on anxiety/depression/PSS (both arms improved over time); cognition favored ashwagandha. ↩

  8. Akhgarjand C et al. 2022, Phytother Res. PMID 36017529. Meta (12 RCTs, n=1,002): anxiety SMD −1.55, stress −1.75, but I² 83-94% and GRADE certainty LOW. ↩↩↩↩

  9. Explore (NY) 2024 (Arumugam-type) meta. PMID 39348746. Meta (9 RCTs, n=558): PSS −4.72, HAM-A −2.19, cortisol −2.58 µg/dL, all significant, CIs near zero. ↩

  10. Fuladi S et al. 2021, Curr Rev Clin Exp Pharmacol. PMID 32282308. The one clinical-population, non-industry RCT (n=40 diagnosed GAD, WS 1 g/day adjunct to SSRI, 6 wk): HAM-A fell more than placebo. ↩

  11. Della Porta M et al. 2023, Nutrients. PMID 38140274. Systematic review of cortisol trials, WS decreases cortisol; no long-term/adrenal-function data. ↩

  12. Pratte MA et al. 2014, J Altern Complement Med. PMID 25405876. Earliest systematic review, could NOT pool: all 5 studies unclear/high risk of bias. ↩

  13. Marchi M et al. 2025, BJPsych Open. PMID 41140145. Meta (14 RCTs, n=713) in people with mental disorders: depression SMD −1.28 (very-low GRADE), stress/sleep low GRADE; publication bias detected for anxiety. ↩↩↩

  14. Cheah KL et al. 2021, PLoS One. PMID 34559859. Dedicated sleep meta (5 RCTs, n=400): sleep SMD −0.59; larger in insomnia (−0.84), ≥600 mg (−0.69), ≥8 wk (−0.68); QoL no significant effect. ↩↩↩

  15. Langade D et al. 2019, Cureus. PMID 31728244. Insomnia+anxiety RCT (KSM-66 600 mg, 10 wk): sleep-onset latency, sleep efficiency and PSQI improved vs placebo (mostly subjective). ↩

  16. Kelgane SB et al. 2020, Cureus. PMID 32226684. Elderly (65-80 y, KSM-66 600 mg, 12 wk): improved sleep quality, QoL, mental alertness, subjective only. ↩

  17. Langade D et al. 2021, J Ethnopharmacol. PMID 32818573. The only actigraphy trial (n=80, healthy+insomnia, 8 wk): significant SOL/SE/TST/WASO gains, larger in insomnia; healthy-subgroup HAM-A/alertness NOT significant. ↩

  18. Deshpande A et al. 2020, Sleep Med. PMID 32540634. Healthy adults with non-restorative sleep (Shoden 120 mg, 6 wk): sleep quality +72% vs +29%; actigraphy improvements. ↩

  19. NIH LiverTox, 'Ashwagandha'. LiverTox NBK548536. Authoritative DILI monograph: likelihood score 'B' (a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury), ~23 cases, cholestatic/mixed, latency 2-12 wk, rare ALF/transplant/death. ↩↩

  20. Björnsson HK et al. 2020, Liver Int. PMID 31991029. Index DILI case series from Iceland + the US DILIN network (n=5): cholestatic/mixed injury, jaundice, positive dechallenge, DILIN-structured causality. ↩↩

  21. Philips CA et al. 2023, Hepatol Commun. PMID 37756041. India case series (n=23): 3 patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure DIED, establishes ashwagandha DILI can be fatal in pre-existing liver disease. ↩↩

  22. Suryawanshi G et al. 2023, Am J Ther. PMID 36321995. Acute liver failure (hepatocellular, R>5) requiring liver transplantation, the severe tail. ↩↩

  23. Bokan G et al. 2023, Pharmaceuticals (Basel). PMID 37631044. Updated-RUCAM causality assessment scoring ashwagandha hepatotoxicity 'probable', 'an emerging cause' (Björnsson ES is a co-author). ↩

  24. Vollmer G et al. 2026, Phytother Res. PMID 41454558. Independent evaluation of ashwagandha's potential hormonal activities (Brendler-team appraisal series). ↩

  25. Williamson EM et al. 2026, Phytother Res, 'Is It Safe? Part 2: Preclinical'. PMID 40968393. Preclinical safety evidence review (Brendler-team series). ↩

  26. Brendler T et al. 2026, Phytother Res, 'Is It Safe? Part 1: Regulatory Review'. PMID 41420287. Regulatory review, notes the EU Article 8 procedure that could ban ashwagandha as a food-supplement ingredient, and national actions. ↩↩↩↩

  27. Coope OC et al. 2026, Pharmaceuticals (Basel), 'Back to the Roots'. PMID 42198398. Safety/tolerability systematic review of standardized root extract, notes 16 of 23 included studies used KSM-66, and limited >180-day data. ↩

  28. Sharma AK et al. 2018, J Altern Complement Med. PMID 28829155. Subclinical-hypothyroid RCT (n=50, 600 mg, 8 wk): TSH −17.4%, T4 +19.6%, T3 +41.5%, narrow benefit AND the safety-signal source. ↩↩

  29. Bonilla DA et al. 2021, J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. PMID 33670194. Bayesian meta of physical performance (13 studies): VO₂max d≈1.85, strength/power d≈0.68, fatigue/recovery d≈−1.18. ↩

  30. Choudhary B et al. 2015, Ayu. PMID 26730141. Cardiorespiratory endurance (KSM-66, 12 wk): VO₂max +5.67 vs +1.86 mL/kg/min. ↩

  31. Shenoy S et al. 2012, J Ayurveda Integr Med. PMID 23326093. Elite Indian cyclists (n=40, 8 wk): VO₂max, METS and time-to-exhaustion improved. ↩

  32. Sandhu JS et al. 2010, Int J Ayurveda Res. PMID 21170205. Healthy young adults (multi-arm): ashwagandha increased muscular velocity, power and VO₂max. ↩

  33. Wankhede S et al. 2015, J Int Soc Sports Nutr. PMID 26609282. Young untrained men on a resistance program (KSM-66): testosterone +96.2 vs +18.0 ng/dL, body-fat −3.5%, but confounded by training + fat loss. ↩

  34. Chauhan S et al. 2022, Health Sci Rep. PMID 35873404. Men with LOW sexual desire (n=50): testosterone ~+66 ng/dL, selected population. ↩

  35. Ziegenfuss TN et al. 2018, Nutrients (STAR trial). PMID 30463324. Recreationally-active men, 12-wk resistance program (Sensoril): strength/body-comp gains with NO significant testosterone difference, undercuts 'works via testosterone'. ↩

  36. Khanna A et al. 2026, Front Reprod Health. PMID 41766918. NEWEST clean trial in healthy men (n=76, KSM-66, 8 wk): no significant between-group testosterone rise; sexual-desire/erectile scores improved. ↩↩↩↩

  37. Lopresti AL et al. 2019, Am J Mens Health. PMID 30854916. Crossover in aging/overweight fatigued men (Shoden): +14.7% salivary testosterone, +18% DHEA-S, but no improvement in fatigue/vigor/sexual well-being. ↩

  38. Ambiye VR et al. 2013, Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. PMID 24371462. Oligospermic men (n=46, 90 d): sperm count +167%, motility +57%, volume +53%. ↩

  39. Ahmad MK / Mahdi AA et al. 2010, Fertil Steril. PMID 19501822. Infertile men: improved semen quality, reduced seminal oxidative stress, T↑ LH↑ FSH↓ (correction of a suppressed axis). ↩

  40. Mahdi AA et al. 2011, Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. PMID 19789214. Stress-related male infertility (5 g/day, 3 mo): reduced stress markers, improved semen quality; 14% partner pregnancy. ↩

  41. Nasimi Doost Azgomi R et al. 2018, Biomed Res Int. PMID 29670898. Systematic review of reproductive effects, improves semen/reproductive hormones predominantly in subfertile/infertile men; small heterogeneous evidence. ↩

  42. Dongre S et al. 2015, Biomed Res Int. PMID 26504795. Female sexual-function pilot (n=50): improved subjective FSFI/arousal/lubrication/orgasm, subjective, not hormone-mediated. ↩

  43. Phytother Res 2026, reproductive-health systematic review. PMID 41249015. Sex-specific hormonal and fertility outcomes review, 'promising natural adjunct, more study needed'; not a settled testosterone booster. ↩

  44. Choudhary D et al. 2017, J Diet Suppl. PMID 28471731. MCI memory RCT (n=50, KSM-66, 8 wk): improved Wechsler Memory Scale indices, executive function, attention. ↩

  45. Chengappa KNR et al. 2013, J Clin Psychiatry. PMID 24330893. Bipolar cognition adjunctive RCT (Sensoril): significant on only 3 of ~12 tasks (digit-span backward, a Flanker RT, social cognition). ↩

  46. Pingali U et al. 2014, Pharmacognosy Res. PMID 24497737. Healthy young men (n=20, crossover, 14 d): faster reaction times on multiple psychomotor tasks. ↩

  47. Sriperumbuduri S et al. 2020, Kidney Int Rep. PMID 33305135. Kidney-transplant recipient developed acute T-cell-mediated rejection and lost the graft after ashwagandha, the immunostimulation hazard, documented. DOI 10.1016/j.ekir.2020.09.024 (hand-corrected). ↩↩↩

  48. Candelario M et al. 2015, J Ethnopharmacol. PMID 26068424. Direct electrophysiological evidence the extract activates ionotropic GABA_A and GABA_ρ receptors (picrotoxin-blocked), the GABAergic mechanism, rodent/oocyte level. ↩

  49. Am J Chin Med 2013 (GABA-mimetic study, PMID 24117067). PMID 24117067. GABA-mimetic action on substantia gelatinosa (trigeminal) neurons in mice, corroborating GABAergic mechanism, preclinical. ↩

  50. Bashir A et al. 2023, Front Pharmacol. PMID 37063285. Updated phytochemistry/molecular-targets review of Withania somnifera, the withanolide catalogue and the root-vs-leaf distinction. ↩

  51. Vaishnavi K et al. 2012, PLoS One. PMID 22973447. Withaferin A is strongly cytotoxic to normal AND cancer cells (reactive electrophile), whereas withanone spares normal cells, withaferin A is a toxicity story, not the stress mechanism. ↩

  52. Kaushik MK et al. 2017, PLoS One. PMID 28207892. Triethylene glycol (leaf-derived) induced NREM sleep in mice while the withanolide-rich alcoholic extract did not, the proposed sleep molecule, from leaf, not the tested root products. ↩

  53. Speers AB et al. 2024, Nutrients. PMID 39599622. Systematic review of human withanolide plasma pharmacokinetics, notes only ~4 human PK studies exist, low ng/mL, rapid absorption, no PK/PD link. ↩

  54. Patil D et al. 2013, J Pharm Biomed Anal. PMID 23584079. Mouse plasma PK of withaferin A / withanolide A, low oral bioavailability of withaferin A from crude extract. ↩

  55. Kim S-K et al. 2023, Heliyon. PMID 38144272. Double-blind crossover PK/bioequivalence in healthy adults, a 35% extract was far more bioavailable than a 2.5% one at equal withanolide dose; the two are NOT bioequivalent. ↩

  56. Kuboyama T et al. 2005, Br J Pharmacol. PMID 15711595. Withanolide A induces neurite regeneration and synaptic reconstruction, the cholinergic/neuro-regeneration mechanism, rodent/cell level. ↩

  57. Panossian A 2017, Ann N Y Acad Sci. PMID 28640972. Pharmacology of 'adaptogens', argues a molecular basis (HPA/stress-mediator modulation) while conceding classic single-target dose-response cannot capture it. ↩↩

  58. Smith SJ et al. 2021, Adv Nutr. PMID 33150931. Systematic review of herbs on testosterone in men, ashwagandha/fenugreek 'positive', but the review team runs industry-funded ashwagandha trials. ↩

  59. Fatima N et al. 2024, Hum Psychopharmacol. PMID 39083548. Systematic review for anxiety and insomnia, effective short-term; 'further information required for long-term safety'. ↩

  60. Regulatory record, Denmark DTU / Fødevarestyrelsen; RIVM (NL) 2024-0029; EMA-HMPC. RIVM 2024-0029 / DTU National Food Institute. Denmark restricted/banned ashwagandha in food supplements (could not set a safe limit); RIVM concluded products 'may lead to liver injury, thyrotoxicosis and adrenal suppression in sensitive people'; EMA does not recognize 'adaptogen'. ↩

  61. Tallon N et al. 2026, Phytother Res. PMID 40887707. Systematic ethnobotanical review of teratogenic/abortifacient potential, argues the abortifacient literature is inflated and inconclusive. ↩

  62. Brendler T et al. 2026, Phytother Res, 'Is Ashwagandha an Abortifacient?'. PMID 41454549. Independent appraisal of the abortifacient claim (Brendler-team series). ↩

  63. Saper RB et al. 2004, JAMA. PMID 15598918. ~20% (14/70) of Boston-area Ayurvedic products contained lead/mercury/arsenic above limits at recommended dosing. ↩

  64. Saper RB et al. 2008, JAMA. PMID 18728265. ~20.7% of online-sold Ayurvedic medicines contained detectable lead/mercury/arsenic; 40% of rasa-shastra products. ↩

docs.title: BPA in Thermal Receipts and Human Health
docs.text:
How bisphenol A from till and credit-card receipts gets into the body, what it does to human health, and how real and how large the risk is — for the average person versus cashiers. This is the whole picture, ranked by how strongly the evidence holds — settled exposure facts first, the genuinely-contested disease-causation question last.

Complete · Published 25 June 2026 · Rebuilt 14 July 2026 — every cited study re-read from source and re-verified · 29 cited studies & official assessments · Confidence: High on exposure · Moderate on harm magnitude.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Bottom line

A paper receipt coats your fingers in loose, hormone-active BPA that your skin absorbs more dangerously than your gut does, trivial for the occasional shopper but a real daily dose for cashiers and pregnant women, and free to skip by declining the paper.

Myths vs. reality

What most people believe What the evidence actually shows Plastic bottles are the big BPA worry, receipts are nothing One receipt carries thousands of times more loose, rub-off BPA than a plastic bottle leaks, roughly 1 to 2 percent of the paper's weight (about 19.6 mg per gram) sitting on the surface. Swallowing BPA is worse than just touching it Skin is worse per microgram. It skips the liver's first-pass cleanup, so more reaches your blood in the active form and lingers up to a week, versus 24 hours for swallowed BPA. "BPA-free" receipts are the safe choice "BPA-free" almost always means BPS or BPF, about as hormonally active as BPA, and BPS resists your metabolism so more stays active. Only genuinely bisphenol-free paper is a real fix. Receipts are my main source of BPA For the average person, canned and packaged food dominates (canned tuna up to about 105 micrograms per kg, worse when heated). A stray receipt is a small add-on. Cashiers are the exception. A quick touch is harmless Sanitizer or lotion first can raise absorption up to about 185 times. One "sanitize, hold receipt, eat fries by hand" event pushed a person to the whole US population's 95th percentile in 90 minutes. Regulators agree BPA is basically fine They do not. In 2023 the EU cut the safe daily dose about 20,000-fold, while the US FDA still calls it safe and does not regulate receipts at all. Same molecule, roughly 1,000x disagreement. If it were dangerous, there would be proof it causes disease The exposure is proven and measured, but whether the receipt fraction causes a specific disease is genuinely unproven and expert-contested. The reason to avoid it is that avoiding it is free. Gloves would not really change anything Gloves abolish the exposure entirely. In two separate studies the urinary BPA rise disappears with nitrile gloves, which is the clean proof it is the skin.

What you actually learn

  • A receipt is coated in loose BPA, about 1 to 2 percent of its weight, that rubs onto your fingers in seconds, thousands of times more free BPA than a plastic bottle leaks. In one US survey, 44 percent of 50 receipts carried high BPA.
  • BPA through skin is more dangerous than BPA in food: it dodges the liver, so more of it stays in the active form and is still detectable up to a week later (9 days in one person), versus 24 hours for food BPA.
  • Gloves make the exposure vanish. Bare hands raised cashiers' urinary BPA roughly 2 to 3 times over a shift; nitrile gloves gave zero rise. Two independent studies.
  • Cashiers run about 2 to 3 times elevated, and roughly 70 percent of their BPA comes through the skin. It tracks with a DNA-damage marker (8-OHdG) and higher insulin resistance.
  • Hand sanitizer or lotion turns a minor touch into a big dose, up to about 185 times more absorbed. One combined event pushed someone to the US 95th percentile in 90 minutes.
  • The scary "20,000 times over the limit" figure exists because the EU moved the line, not because receipts got worse. The same exposure was "42 times under the limit" on the 2015 rule and about 4,850 times over on the strict 2023 rule. The receipt never changed.
  • "BPA-free" is mostly marketing: it means BPS or BPF, about as hormone-active as BPA, and more free BPS survives through the skin than BPA (6.9 percent versus 2.7 percent). Only bisphenol-free paper like Pergafast 201 is a genuine fix.
  • For the average person your BPA mostly comes from canned and packaged food (worse when heated), not receipts, so a stray receipt is a small add-on, not your main source.
  • No study has proven a receipt causes a specific disease, and two respected agencies disagree by roughly 1,000 times on how risky BPA even is. The strongest signal is on sperm count and male hormones (an 18-study meta), plus prenatal hyperactivity as a "presumed hazard."

What this means for you

  • Decline paper receipts and pick digital (email or app) when offered. It costs nothing and removes a real bioactive exposure.
  • Never handle a receipt right after hand sanitizer or lotion, that is the up-to-185x amplifier. Wash your hands before eating if you have handled receipts, and do not eat finger food while holding one.
  • If you are a cashier or pregnant, treat it seriously: wear nitrile gloves (proven to zero out the exposure), keep receipts away from kids, and push your employer toward bisphenol-free paper.
  • Do not bother "upgrading" to BPA-free receipts, that is usually BPS or BPF and no safer. The only real fixes are digital or genuinely bisphenol-free paper.
  • Keep it in proportion: for an occasional shopper the risk is small and unproven, so do not stress one receipt. Take the free win by declining it, and if you actually want to cut BPA, target the bigger source, canned and packaged food, worse when heated.

TL;DR

Thermal receipts are coated in free, rub-off BPA (≈19.6 mg/g, in 44% of receipts) that absorbs through the skin — a route that bypasses liver detox, so more reaches the blood in its active form and lingers for days. Hand sanitizer amplifies absorption up to 185×. Diet is still the average person's main BPA source, so a stray receipt is a small, easily-avoided add-on — but for cashiers it's a real occupational exposure (~2–3× higher urinary BPA, with DNA-oxidative-damage and insulin-resistance correlates). "BPA-free" receipts are usually BPS/BPF — no safer. EFSA (2023) cut the safe dose ~20,000× and says background diet already exceeds it; the US FDA still calls it safe and doesn't regulate receipts at all. Verdict: avoidance is cheap and rational — strongly so for cashiers and pregnant women.

The picture, ranked by how strongly the evidence holds

  • Tier 1 — settled (multi-study + agency): receipts carry mg-level free rub-off BPA;1 gloves abolish the exposure (proof it's the skin);23 the dermal route is more bioactive + slower-clearing than diet;4 cashiers run ~2–3× elevated across three cohorts;563 "BPA-free" = BPS/BPF, as hormonally active as BPA;7 EFSA cut the safe dose ~20,000× and diet already exceeds it.10
  • Tier 2 — well-supported: hand-sanitizer amplifies absorption (~up to 185×);1 one worst-case event ≈ the population 95th percentile;1 BPA lowers sperm + bioactive androgen (18-study meta);12 diet/canned food dominates for the average person (so a stray receipt is a small add-on);1413 the EU restricts receipts, the US does not.1618
  • Tier 3 — consistent but observational: low-dose organ effects (CLARITY academic);19 prenatal hyperactivity (presumed hazard);20 a modest CVD signal;21 BPS/BPF obesity/diabetes epidemiology;24 placental cytotoxicity in vitro.26
  • Tier 4 — genuinely contested: whether the receipt fraction causes a specific disease turns on the unresolved EFSA-vs-FDA/BfR dispute.27 Verdict: real exposure, contested harm, cheap avoidance — precaution is rational, strongly for cashiers and pregnant women.

docs.title: Tier 1 — Settled: the exposure is real
docs.text:
Bisphenol A (BPA) is a high-volume industrial chemical and a confirmed endocrine disruptor — it binds estrogen receptors and acts as a weak exogenous estrogen, with additional anti-androgenic and metabolic activity. In thermal receipt paper it is not a bound polymer (as in polycarbonate plastic or epoxy can-linings) but a free, powdery colour developer coating the surface — so it rubs off onto skin on contact.

Receipts carry milligram quantities of free BPA. In a US survey of 50 thermal receipts, 22 (44%) carried high BPA at 19.6 ± 1.0 mg per gram of paper (≈1–2% of the paper's weight) — thousands of times more free BPA than migrates from a plastic bottle; BPS, the main substitute, was found in 52% of receipts.1

Gloves abolish the exposure — the cleanest proof it's the skin. Holding receipts for 2 hours without gloves raised volunteers' urinary BPA from 1.8 → 5.8 µg/L (peak 11.1 at 8 h); nitrile gloves abolished the rise entirely,2 and a separate cashier intervention found the ~2× post-shift rise vanished with gloves.3

The skin route bypasses first-pass detoxification — more bioactive, slower-clearing. Dermal BPA shows prolonged kinetics: after a single contact, urinary excretion rose linearly for ~2 days, was still detectable in half of participants after 1 week (up to 9 days in one), with a higher unconjugated (bioactive) fraction than diet — whereas swallowed BPA clears within 24 h.4

Cashiers absorb most of their BPA dermally, and run ~2–3× elevated. In cashiers, dermal contact contributed 51.9–84% (geometric mean 70.9%) of total urinary BPA;5 French cashiers had median total urinary BPA 8.92 µg/L vs 3.54 µg/L in controls,6 and Korean female cashiers showed ~2× higher post-shift urinary BPA.3 A documented occupational exposure across three independent cohorts.

"BPA-free" usually means BPS/BPF — not safer. A systematic review (1,370 studies screened) found BPS and BPF are "as hormonally active as BPA," with estrogenic, anti-estrogenic, androgenic and anti-androgenic activity (mean estrogenic potency relative to BPA: BPF 1.07, BPS 0.32).7 Worse for the dermal route, more free (unmetabolized) BPS than BPA survives in urine after handling receipts (6.9% vs 2.7%) because BPS resists metabolism.8 Only genuinely bisphenol-free paper (e.g. Pergafast 201) is a real fix — proven feasible when Switzerland mandated it (BPA-developed receipts fell 82.2% → 10.8%).9

EFSA cut the safe daily dose ~20,000× — and diet already exceeds it. In 2023 EFSA set a tolerable daily intake of 0.2 ng/kg body weight/day — ~20,000× below its 2015 temporary 4 µg/kg — on immune-system (Th17) evidence, concluding mean and high dietary exposure in all age groups exceed the new TDI by two-to-three orders of magnitude.10 Receipts add a dermal, bioactive increment on top of an already-exceeded background.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Well-supported (amplifiers, magnitude, hormones, diet, regulation)
docs.text:
Hand sanitizer and greasy hands are powerful amplifiers. Penetration enhancers in sanitizers/lotions open the skin barrier: after sanitizer use, up to 185× more BPA transferred from a receipt to a wet hand than a dry hand.1 In the worst-case protocol (sanitizer → hold receipt → eat finger-food), unconjugated serum BPA peaked at ~7 ng/mL and urinary total BPA hit ~20 µg/g creatinine within 90 min — pushing a person to roughly the NHANES 95th percentile (~11 µg/g) of the whole US population from a single event.1

Putting the 20,000× in receipts. Worst-case occupational handling (~10 h/day) models to a dermal BPA dose of ~71 µg/day (≈0.97 µg/kg bw/day).11 Hold that exposure fixed and only move the regulatory line: it is ~0.24× the 2015 temporary TDI — Biedermann's 2010 paper literally called it "42× below" the limit of its day — but ~4,850× the 2023 TDI.10 The receipt didn't change; EFSA's ~20,000× cut did. (Illustrative order-of-magnitude; the absorbed fraction is smaller.)

BPA lowers sperm count and bioactive androgen. A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 18 studies found urinary BPA inversely associated with sperm concentration (β −0.03) and total count (β −0.05), alongside higher SHBG, higher estradiol, and lower bioactive androgen — a coherent estrogenic/anti-androgenic signature (the below-reference sperm-quality link was "not robust").12

Diet dominates for the average person — and it's well-quantified. BPA is essentially absent from unprocessed food; it migrates out of epoxy can-linings and plastic, rising sharply with heat, sunlight and storage.13 Canned tuna reached up to ~105 µg/kg (highest after retort at 121 °C; the lining shed up to 646 µg/kg into a fatty simulant);14 canned sardines carried 5.2–48.7 µg/kg, migration +437% with temperature.15 So for the general public a stray receipt is a smaller add-on to the dietary baseline — it's cashiers where the dermal route dominates.

The EU restricts receipt BPA; the US does not. Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2235 banned BPA in thermal paper above 0.02% from 2 January 2020,16 ECHA lists BPA as an endocrine-disruptor SVHC,17 and the EU banned BPA in all food-contact materials in 2024;18 the US FDA does not regulate thermal receipts at all, so there is no US receipt limit and US exposure is ~1,000× EFSA's new safe level.18

docs.title: Tier 3 — Consistent but observational (disease associations)
docs.text:
Important caveat

Almost all human disease epidemiology measures total urinary BPA (mostly dietary), not receipt-specific BPA. These studies establish what BPA at population exposure is associated with; receipts are one contributor. Causal attribution of a specific disease to receipt-borne BPA specifically is not established, and most associations are cross-sectional.

Low-dose organ effects (CLARITY-BPA academic arm). The academic laboratories reported consistent low-dose effects at 2.5 / 25 / 250 µg/kg/day across brain, heart, prostate, ovary, mammary and immune tissue, "at doses relevant to human exposures," with non-monotonic dose–response — why "no effect at high dose" does not guarantee safety at realistic low doses.19

Prenatal / childhood — the precautionary core. A systematic review (29 rodent + 3 human studies) concluded "early life BPA exposure is a presumed human hazard for the development of hyperactivity," urging precautionary reduction in pregnant women, infants and children.20

Cardiovascular — a modest, consistent-direction signal. The prospective EPIC-Norfolk study found incident coronary artery disease OR 1.13 (95% CI 1.02–1.24) per SD urinary BPA, attenuating to borderline after full adjustment; earlier NHANES cross-sectional data linked BPA to CVD (OR 1.39) and diabetes.21 The type-2-diabetes signal is present but inconsistent — positive in a prospective Nurses' Health analysis (OR up to 2.08 in middle-aged women) and an overall-positive meta-analysis, but null in older women.2223

BPS/BPF now carry disease-outcome signals + cell toxicity. Human biomonitoring ties urinary BPS/BPF to obesity and type-2 diabetes (BPS the most impactful), though the epidemiology is younger and mostly cross-sectional;2425 and in human placental (JEG-Tox) cells, BPA and BPF triggered more inflammasome/apoptosis caspase activity than BPS, with BPF uniquely activating caspase-8 — direct cytotoxicity in a pregnancy-relevant tissue.26 Cashier BPA also correlated with the DNA-oxidative-damage marker 8-OHdG and with insulin resistance.53

docs.title: Tier 4 — Genuinely contested (disease causation)
docs.text: Whether the receipt fraction causes a specific disease is unproven and expert-contested. EFSA's 20,000× cut rests on an immune (Th17) endpoint that Germany's BfR and a group of regulatory toxicologists argue is not a demonstrated adverse effect — BfR derived a TDI ~1,000× higher;27 the FDA still reads the CLARITY Core study as "no clear adverse effects."1918 Two respected agencies disagree by ~1,000× on how dangerous BPA is at all. This is genuine expert disagreement, not a settled harm.

docs.title: The scorecard
docs.text: Claim Verdict Confidence Receipts carry large amounts of free BPA that transfers to skin True High Dermal route yields more bioactive, longer-lasting BPA than diet True High Hand sanitizer / lotion massively amplifies absorption True High Cashiers have measurably elevated BPA (≈2–3×); gloves prevent it True High Receipts are the main BPA source for the average person False (diet dominates) High "BPA-free" receipts are safer Not established (usually BPS/BPF) High BPA at population exposure harms human health Associated & plausible, mostly cross-sectional & contested Moderate Receipt-borne BPA specifically causes a named disease Unproven Low–Moderate Is avoiding receipts worth it? Yes High (decision)

docs.title: What this rebuild changed
docs.text: This page was rebuilt on 14 July 2026 by re-reading every PMID-bearing study from its source abstract and re-verifying every identifier against PubMed. That process confirmed the entire report and required no corrections — all 15 PMID-bearing sources title-matched (0 wrong PMIDs), and the agency documents (EFSA, FDA, ECHA, EU regulations) are verifiable by DOI/URL. The exposure facts, the "regrettable substitution," and the 20,000× regulatory shift all held on a fresh read. The findings are now presented ranked by how strongly the evidence backs them.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
Receipt-borne BPA is one of the most easily avoided exposures, and the interventions are evidence-backed (gloves abolished the urinary rise in two independent studies23).

General public: decline the paper receipt / choose digital receipts (the exact tool Dr. Shanna Swan recommends28); don't handle receipts right after hand sanitizer or lotion (the 185× amplifier1); don't let children hold receipts;20 wash hands before eating.1

Cashiers / retail workers (highest exposure): wear (nitrile) gloves — the single most effective, proven control;23 minimize skin time; avoid hand cream/sanitizer immediately before handling; employers should switch to bisphenol-free thermal paper (e.g. Pergafast 201).9

The honest bottom line: the exposure is real and quantified; the disease consequence is plausible but unproven for receipts specifically; avoidance is cheap. Therefore precaution is rational — strongly for cashiers and pregnant women, mildly for everyone else. The case rests on asymmetry of risk (cheap to avoid, plausibly harmful), not on a demonstrated receipt-to-disease causal chain.

Every source below is real and verifiable by its DOI / PMID / URL. Grades: agency = official risk assessment / regulation · SR/MA = systematic review / meta-analysis · primary = human biomonitoring / controlled exposure · secondary = review / commentary.

docs.title: The full findings — all 22
docs.text:
Every conclusion this review reached, grouped by how strongly the evidence backs it. Each finding is distilled from the fully-cited evidence above.

Tier 1 — Settled: the exposure is real (multi-study + agency-backed) (6 findings)

1. Receipts carry milligram quantities of free, rub-off BPA

In 50 US thermal receipts, 44% had high BPA at 19.6 mg per gram of paper (~1–2% of the paper's weight); the canonical transfer study found 8–17 g/kg in 11 of 13 papers — thousands of times more free BPA than migrates from a plastic bottle.

2. Gloves abolish the exposure — the cleanest proof it's the skin

Two hours of bare-handed receipt handling raised urinary BPA 1.8 → 5.8 µg/L (peak 11.1 at 8 h); wearing nitrile gloves produced no rise, and a separate cashier intervention found the ~2× post-shift rise vanished with gloves. Two independent causal demonstrations.

3. The skin route bypasses the liver's first-pass detox — more bioactive, slower-clearing

Dermal BPA reaches blood with a higher unconjugated (bioactive) fraction (0.71–8.3%) than diet (0.29–1.4%) and clears slowly — urinary excretion rises ~2 days and is detectable up to 1 week (9 days in one person), versus 24 h for swallowed BPA. This is why a receipt's BPA matters more per microgram than dietary BPA.

4. Cashiers absorb most of their BPA through the skin, and run ~2–3× elevated

In cashiers, dermal contact contributed 51.9–84% (GM 70.9%) of urinary BPA; French cashiers had median total urinary BPA 8.92 µg/L vs 3.54 µg/L in controls, and Korean female cashiers showed ~2× post-shift BPA. A documented occupational exposure across three independent cohorts.

5. "BPA-free" usually means BPS/BPF — not safer

A 1,370-study systematic review found BPS and BPF are "as hormonally active as BPA" (estrogenic potency BPF 1.07, BPS 0.32 relative to BPA), with estrogenic/anti-androgenic activity — the classic "regrettable substitution". Only bisphenol-free paper (e.g. Pergafast 201) is a real fix — proven feasible when Switzerland mandated it (BPA-developed receipts fell 82% → 11%).

6. EFSA cut the safe daily dose ~20,000× — diet alone already exceeds it

In 2023 EFSA set a tolerable daily intake of 0.2 ng/kg bw/day (immune/Th17 endpoint), ~20,000× below its 2015 value; mean and high dietary exposure in all age groups exceed it by 2–3 orders of magnitude. Receipts add a dermal, bioactive increment on top of an already-exceeded background.

Tier 2 — Well-supported: amplifiers, magnitude, hormones, regulation (7 findings)

7. Hand sanitizer / lotion is a massive amplifier (up to ~185×)

Skin penetration enhancers in sanitizers and lotions open the barrier — the study reported penetration enhancers can raise dermal absorption of lipophilic compounds "up to 100-fold," and measured receipt-to-sanitized-hand transfer up to ~185× higher than to a dry hand. Never handle receipts right after sanitizer.

8. One worst-case event ≈ the population's 95th percentile

Sanitizer → hold receipt → eat finger-food pushed unconjugated serum BPA to ~7 ng/mL and urinary BPA to ~20 µg/g creatinine in 90 min — roughly the NHANES 95th percentile for the entire US population, from a single event.

9. The same receipt exposure went from "42× under the limit" to ~5,000× over it — because EFSA moved the line, not the receipt

Worst-case occupational receipt handling (~10 h/day) models to ~71 µg/day (≈0.97 µg/kg bw/day) of dermal BPA — about 0.24× the 2015 temporary TDI (Biedermann's 2010 paper called it "42× below" the TDI of its day) but ~4,850× the 2023 TDI of 0.2 ng/kg/day. One dry-hand 5-second hold puts ~1 µg on the skin (up to ~10 µg wet/greasy); an illustrative order-of-magnitude, absorbed fraction smaller.

10. BPA lowers sperm count and bioactive androgen (the HPG-axis link)

Meta-analysis of 18 studies: urinary BPA inversely associated with sperm concentration (β −0.03) and total count (β −0.05), with higher SHBG and estradiol and lower bioactive androgen — the same estrogenic/anti-androgenic pathway VL6 names for bisphenols. (The below-reference sperm-quality link was "not robust.")

11. Canned/packaged food is the quantified "diet" that dominates for the average person — and heat makes it worse

BPA is absent from raw food and migrates out of epoxy can-linings and plastic, rising with heat, sunlight and storage: canned tuna up to ~105 µg/kg (max after 121 °C / 90 min retort; lining shed up to 646 µg/kg); canned sardines 5.2–48.7 µg/kg, migration +437% with temperature/concentration. So a stray receipt is a small add-on to the dietary baseline for the average person — it's cashiers where the dermal route dominates.

12. The EU restricts receipt BPA; the US does not

The EU banned BPA in thermal paper above 0.02% from Jan 2020 (Reg (EU) 2016/2235) and lists BPA as an endocrine-disruptor SVHC; the US FDA still calls BPA safe at current levels, does not regulate receipts at all, and US exposure is ~1,000× EFSA's limit.

13. Mitigation is cheap and proven

Decline paper receipts / go digital; don't handle them after sanitizer or lotion; keep them from children; wash hands before eating; cashiers should wear gloves (the proven control) and employers should switch to bisphenol-free paper.

Tier 3 — Consistent but observational (disease associations) (7 findings)

14. Low-dose effects are real at human-relevant doses (CLARITY-BPA academic arm)

The CLARITY-BPA academic laboratories found consistent effects at 2.5 / 25 / 250 µg/kg/day across brain, heart, prostate, ovary, mammary and immune tissue — doses relevant to human exposure — contradicting the assumption that low doses are harmless. (The Core-study "no clear adverse effects" reading is the counter-position — see Tier 4.)

15. Prenatal BPA is a "presumed human hazard" for hyperactivity

A systematic review (29 rodent + 3 human studies) concluded early-life BPA exposure is a presumed hazard for childhood hyperactivity, urging precautionary reduction in pregnant women, infants and children. Pregnancy/childhood is the priority population, though the human arm is only three studies.

16. Modest but consistent cardiovascular signal

Prospective EPIC-Norfolk: incident coronary artery disease OR 1.13 (95% CI 1.02–1.24) per SD urinary BPA (borderline after full adjustment, OR 1.11, p=0.058), echoing earlier NHANES cross-sectional links to CVD (OR 1.39) and diabetes.

17. Cashier BPA tracks a DNA-damage marker and insulin resistance

Cashier urinary BPA correlated with the oxidative-DNA-damage marker 8-OHdG (R²=0.237, p<0.001), and higher cashier BPA tracked with higher fasting insulin / insulin resistance — biological correlates of the occupational exposure, though cross-sectional.

18. "BPA-free" BPS/BPF now carries human disease-outcome signals, not just in-vitro activity

Beyond estrogenic potency, human biomonitoring ties urinary BPS/BPF to obesity (NHANES: higher in obese adults; BPS↔general+abdominal obesity in 6–19-year-olds) and type-2 diabetes (BPS/BPAF positive even after BMI adjustment); two 2022–2023 reviews conclude BPS/BPF "could promote obesity and diabetes," BPS most — though this epidemiology is younger, thinner and mostly cross-sectional.

19. Dermal BPS may be worse than BPA — it resists metabolism

After handling receipts, more free (unmetabolized) BPS (6.9%) than BPA (2.7%) reached urine, and only the free form binds estrogen receptors — so switching to "BPA-free" thermal paper does not remove the dermal-absorption risk.

20. "BPA-free" BPS/BPF are directly cytotoxic to human placental cells, not just hormonally active

In JEG-Tox placental cells, BPA and BPF induced more caspase-1/-9/-3 (inflammasome + apoptosis) than BPS, and BPF uniquely activated caspase-8 — substitute-bisphenol toxicity in a pregnancy-relevant tissue, reinforcing that "BPA-free" is not automatically safe, especially prenatally (in-vitro).

Tier 4 — Genuinely contested (disease causation + the verdict) (2 findings)

21. Whether receipt BPA causes a specific disease is unproven and expert-contested

The disease-causation question turns on the unresolved EFSA-vs-FDA/BfR dispute: EFSA's 20,000× cut rests on an immune (Th17) endpoint that regulatory toxicologists and Germany's BfR argue is not a demonstrated adverse effect (BfR derived a TDI ~1,000× higher), and the FDA still reads the CLARITY Core study as "no clear adverse effects". This is genuine expert disagreement, not a settled harm.

22. Verdict — real exposure, contested harm, cheap avoidance

Receipt BPA is a documented, avoidable dermal/occupational exposure (high confidence); whether it causes a specific disease is unproven for the receipt fraction specifically (low–moderate confidence) and depends on the EFSA-vs-FDA dispute above. Because avoidance costs ~nothing, precaution is rational — strongly for cashiers and pregnant women. Independently corroborated inside the knowledge base by Huberman Lab EP-236 (Dr. Shanna Swan), who gives a dedicated "avoid thermal-receipt BPA/BPS skin absorption" tool.
