docs.text: Almost every downstream "wellness" effect can be explained by supplying glycine + proline and by collagen being a cheap, glycine-dense protein — not a unique peptide mechanism proven in humans. A 15 g collagen dose delivers only ~3.5 g glycine, exactly the dose used in the glycine sleep trials.3 Where a benefit exists, the parsimonious reading is glycine, delivered expensively — and free glycine is several-fold cheaper per gram.4

docs.title: Collagen does NOT build muscle
docs.text: Two independent tracer trials show that collagen cannot raise muscle protein synthesis: whey (and even pea) stimulate it while collagen does not, because collagen is leucine-poor and incomplete.25 "Fat-free mass" on a body-scan includes connective tissue and water, so a body-comp signal can be real yet not be muscle. For muscle or sarcopenia, a complete protein beats collagen — it should not displace it.

docs.title: The skin benefit collapses under bias control
docs.text: Pooled meta-analyses look positive, but the single independent, bias-stratified review is decisive: in non-industry-funded trials and in high-quality trials the benefit disappears (Myung & Park 2025, 23 RCTs / 1,474 — "no clinical evidence to support collagen supplements to prevent or treat skin aging").6 A newer independent umbrella review (Ravindran 2026) reports the opposite, but it pools mostly low-quality reviews and inherits their bias — two independent reviews disagreeing is itself a sign the primary trials are too weak to settle it.7 Crucially, no skin RCT uses an equal-protein comparator — every one compares collagen to inert placebo, never to isonitrogenous whey — so a general protein effect cannot be ruled out. Verdict: unproven, not disproven. (Nail evidence is one single-arm, open-label, no-placebo study; hair evidence is scarce and industry-adjacent — and nail/hair are keratin, not collagen.)

docs.title: Funding bias is the dominant confound
docs.text: Nearly every positive collagen trial has a collagen manufacturer among the authors (Rousselot, GELITA/VERISOL, Nitta, Jellice, Nippi, Newtree); the benefit disappears in the independent, high-quality subgroups.63 This one pattern explains most of the gap between the marketing and the evidence.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Real but modest (joints, sleep, glucose, glutathione, bone, tendon)
Joints / osteoarthritis — the strongest case
docs.text: A trial-sequential meta-analysis (35 RCTs / 3,165 patients) finds collagen reduces OA pain (SMD −0.35) and improves function (SMD −0.31), and the analysis reached its required information size.8 The catch: effects sit near the minimal-clinically-important line, the trial base is heavily manufacturer-funded, and a manufacturer-independent RCT (N=68) found no benefit over placebo.9 Undenatured type-II collagen (UC-II, 40 mg) is a different product with an oral-tolerance mechanism and its own positive trial — but "beating glucosamine + chondroitin" is a low bar, because that comparator is itself at/near placebo in the large independent GAIT trial, and UC-II's evidence is almost entirely from its maker.1011 No human trial shows cartilage regeneration; every benefit is a symptom score.

docs.title: Sleep — a modest glycine effect, primaries null
docs.text: The whole collagen-sleep case is one small (n=13), manufacturer-funded RCT whose primary sleep outcomes were null; only a secondary "fewer awakenings" (21.3 vs 29.3, p=0.028) and a near-ceiling cognition score improved.3 A decisive flaw compounds this: the comparator was an inert taste-matched drink, not protein-matched, so even "fewer awakenings" can't be pinned on collagen over any bedtime protein. The glycine sleep literature it leans on is real but small and high-risk-of-bias: ~3 g glycine before bed shortens sleep-onset latency via a core-temperature drop.1213

docs.title: The one collagen-peptide-specific signal: post-meal glucose
docs.text: A specific hydrolysate cut the post-meal glucose rise ~40–53% — genuinely collagen-peptide-specific — but every human trial shares one funder (Rousselot), it has not been independently replicated, its GLP-1/gastric-emptying mechanism was measured in mice only, and it is mechanistically a general protein-preload effect that whey shares.1415

docs.title: Glutathione, bone, tendon
docs.text: Glutathione needs GlyNAC — glycine plus N-acetylcysteine — used in aged/diseased people, from a single lab, mostly open-label; collagen supplies no cysteine, so it cannot reproduce it, and the mainstream view is that cysteine, not glycine, is the rate-limiting precursor in the first place.16 Bone: König 2018 (postmenopausal women, 5 g/day, 12 months) found significant spine and femoral-neck density gains — Gelita-funded, a surrogate endpoint (density, not fractures), heterogeneous when pooled.17 Tendon — loading does the work: 5 g specific collagen peptides during 14 weeks of heavy training increased tendon cross-sectional area, but stiffness, strength and performance rose equally in both groups; a 2026 review grades this formally — GRADE A that size/stiffness rise with training, GRADE A against an added strength effect.1819 Muscle gains are real only as generic added protein (small fat-free-mass effect, SMD 0.48, with training), not as a muscle-builder.20

docs.title: Tier 3 — Weak, single-study, or conditional
docs.text:
Gut, inflammation. Gut-barrier "leaky gut" repair is in-vitro/animal only (one mouse study found collagen worsened colitis, and a glutamine gut-permeability meta-analysis is null); anti-inflammatory benefit is confined to diseased cohorts, and the collagen trial's own inflammation markers were null.3 A collagen serving delivers ~3.5 g glycine — roughly 4× below the ~15 g/day that moved markers in the glycine trials.

Wound healing. In clinical nutrition, collagen peptides speed pressure-ulcer healing — a dose-response trial (a high-dipeptide formula beating a low-dipeptide one at equal protein) is the cleanest evidence a benefit is peptide-specific, and an independent RCT found ~2× faster healing.2122 But this is enteral nutrition in malnourished patients, and much of the "collagen heals wounds" evidence people cite is actually topical collagen dressings — a physical scaffold device, a different route.

Nocturia has a direct human signal, but for glycine, not collagen (~6 g/day in overactive-bladder patients), via a bladder/spinal reflex — not antidiuretic hormone and not "deeper sleep".23 Liver "detox" is a real conjugation pathway but not a proven human outcome (and the rodent bile-acid arm doesn't transfer — mouse bile acids are taurine-conjugated). Arteries: human data are small, manufacturer-linked, and surrogate-only.

docs.title: Tier 4 — Myths and misconceptions
docs.text:
Anxiety. No human trial has tested collagen against an anxiety endpoint. The claim extrapolates from 30–60 g isolated glycine in psychiatric trials (mixed-to-null; the largest, CONSIST, was negative) — doses 7–20× the glycine in a collagen serving.24 At food doses this is a misconception.

"Rebuilds arteries." The glycine→heart-disease causal link fails the best genetic and mouse tests (pleiotropy-robust Mendelian randomization and ApoE-knockout feeding, both null);25 digestion does not route dietary collagen to arterial tissue.

"Less urine at night." No trial measured urine volume or ADH, so the "collagen makes you produce less urine at night" claim is a misconception — the real (weak) signal is bladder-signaling, not reduced urine output.23

Product type is everything. UC-II (40 mg, immune tolerance) ≠ hydrolyzed peptides (grams, substrate/signalling) ≠ gelatin + vitamin C (synthesis cofactor) ≠ topical dressings (a device). A trial on one form is not evidence for another — and a widely-circulated "2025 N=48 glycine sleep RCT" does not exist in PubMed; don't cite it.

docs.title: The scorecard
docs.text: Claim Verdict Tier Collagen "is protein" / builds muscle Myth — incomplete protein, can't raise MPS<sup>2</sup><sup>5</sup> 1 Wellness benefits are collagen-specific Mostly a glycine effect (delivered expensively)<sup>4</sup> 1 Skin (hydration/elasticity/wrinkles) Unproven (null in independent + high-quality trials)<sup>6</sup> 1 Joints / osteoarthritis Real but modest (SMD −0.35; funding-limited, independent null)<sup>8</sup><sup>9</sup> 2 Deepens sleep Modest, glycine-driven (collagen primaries null)<sup>12</sup><sup>3</sup> 2 Blunts post-meal glucose Promising (peptide-specific, but single-funder, mouse mechanism)<sup>14</sup> 2 Boosts glutathione Needs GlyNAC — collagen has no cysteine<sup>16</sup> 2 Bone density / tendon size Promising surrogate (funded; structure, not function)<sup>17</sup><sup>18</sup> 2 Gut "leaky gut" / anti-inflammatory Weak/unproven (in-vitro/animal; disease-only)<sup>3</sup> 3 Wound healing Real in patients (clinical nutrition / topical dressings)<sup>21</sup> 3 Nails / hair Weak (one open-label study; keratin, not collagen) 3 Calms anxiety Myth (dose-impossible extrapolation)<sup>24</sup> 4 "Rebuilds arteries" Myth (causal test null)<sup>25</sup> 4 "Less urine at night" (via ADH) Misconception (no urine-volume/ADH data)<sup>23</sup> 4

docs.title: What this rebuild changed
docs.text: This page was rebuilt on 14 July 2026 by re-reading all cited studies from their source abstracts and re-verifying every PMID against PubMed. That process confirmed the entire verdict — the skin-null, glycine-vehicle, doesn't-build-muscle and funding-bias conclusions all held on a fresh read — and corrected only attribution details: all 48 PMID-bearing sources title-matched, 0 wrong PMIDs (the prior verification held), and five first-author names were fixed. The findings are now presented ranked by how strongly the evidence backs them.

docs.title: Dose, cost, and safety
docs.text:
• Cost: if the goal is the glycine benefits, plain glycine (~3 g) is several-fold cheaper per gram of glycine than collagen.4
  • Heavy metals: brand-variable — testing found ~47% of protein powders exceeded a conservative safety threshold. Buy third-party-tested (NSF/USP).26
  • Kidney stones — hydroxyproline-specific. Hydroxyproline (unique to collagen/gelatin) is metabolized to oxalate; gelatin raised urinary oxalate 43% vs whey at 5–10 g, while glycine itself contributes under 5% of urinary oxalate — so the caution applies to collagen, and plain glycine dodges it. A flag for recurrent calcium-oxalate stone-formers, negligible for others with good hydration.27
  • Allergen / pregnancy: marine collagen is a fish allergen (rare anaphylaxis; a serious skin-reaction case report exists); bovine carries a theoretical, undocumented prion caveat; pregnancy safety data are limited — treat as insufficient, not "proven safe".

docs.title: The honest bottom line
docs.text:
Collagen is, first, a glycine/proline-rich incomplete protein. Its most-marketed benefit (skin) is unproven once funding and quality are controlled; its "wellness" benefits are mostly glycine mechanisms extrapolated past the human evidence, and glycine is cheaper bought directly. Its genuinely best-evidenced uses are musculoskeletal — joint/OA pain, bone density, tendon size, and wound healing in patients — all modest, product-specific, and manufacturer-entangled, and it is an inferior protein for muscle. The evidence-based reason to take collagen, if any, is joint or connective-tissue support alongside training — not the wellness claims it is mostly sold on.

This is an independent research summary, evidence-graded and funding-flagged. It is not medical advice. Every claim is footnoted to a primary study or systematic review with a DOI/PMID.

docs.title: The full findings — all 54
docs.text:
Every conclusion this review reached, grouped by how strongly the evidence backs it. Each finding is distilled from the fully-cited evidence above.

Tier 1 — Strongest, settled (composition + the load-bearing crux) (10 findings)

1. Collagen is ~1/3 glycine and an INCOMPLETE protein

Collagen's Gly-X-Y triple helix puts glycine at every third residue (~33% by count, ~19% by weight) plus proline/hydroxyproline; tryptophan is absent, so its protein-quality score (PDCAAS/DIAAS) is near-zero and it should NOT be counted 1:1 as dietary protein.

2. The crux: most "actual" benefits are glycine effects, not collagen-specific

Almost every downstream benefit traces to supplying glycine + proline (collagen is a glycine-dense delivery vehicle); a 15 g collagen dose carries only ~3.5 g glycine — the exact glycine sleep dose — and the authors of the anchor sleep trial cannot separate a glycine from a collagen effect.

3. Collagen is expensive glycine

A 15 g collagen serving delivers only ~3.5-5 g glycine, so hitting a 3 g sleep dose or the ~10 g "gap-filling" dose via collagen costs several times more than plain glycine powder per gram of glycine.

4. Collagen does NOT build muscle — it can't raise muscle protein synthesis

Collagen is a leucine-poor, tryptophan-free incomplete protein; two independent tracer RCTs show it does not raise muscle protein synthesis above baseline, while whey (and even pea) do — so for muscle/sarcopenia a complete high-leucine protein beats collagen and collagen should not displace it.

5. Collagen is leucine-poor by the numbers — the quantified reason it can't build muscle

A collagen serving carries ~0.9 g leucine vs ~4.3 g in whey, below the ~2.5-3 g needed to trigger mTORC1/muscle protein synthesis; its protein-quality score is ≈ 0 — the concrete crux of "don't count collagen as protein for muscle".

6. The skin benefit collapses under bias control

The independent meta-analysis (Myung & Park 2025, 23 RCTs / 1,474) found the skin benefit exists only in industry-funded and low-quality trials and is null in independent, high-quality ones: "no clinical evidence to support collagen for skin aging" — though industry flags data-extraction errors, so the honest read is unproven, not disproven.

7. Skin, updated: two independent 2025-26 reviews openly contradict

Myung & Park 2025 (bias-controlled subgroups null) and the Ravindran 2026 umbrella review (high-GRADE positive, SMD 0.71-1.01) are both non-industry-funded yet reach opposite conclusions; the umbrella pools mostly AMSTAR-2 "critically low" reviews and inherits their bias, so the skeptical "unproven" verdict stands with an explicitly-flagged dissent.

8. No collagen SKIN RCT uses an equal-protein comparator

Every skin trial compares collagen against an inert placebo (maltodextrin/silica), never against isonitrogenous whey/casein, so even the pooled-positive signal cannot be separated from a generic protein/glycine effect — and the one place collagen WAS tested against equal protein (muscle,) it lost.

9. Funding bias is the dominant confound across the whole literature

Nearly every positive collagen trial has a collagen manufacturer among the authors (Rousselot, GELITA/VERISOL, Nitta, Jellice, Nippi, Newtree); the benefit disappears in the independent, high-quality subgroups.

10. Oral collagen does not reach skin "as collagen" — detection is not efficacy

Ingested collagen is digested to free amino acids plus small peptides (Pro-Hyp, Hyp-Gly) that appear in blood and stimulate fibroblasts in vitro, but plasma levels are micromolar/transient while the cell-culture effects use far higher concentrations, so absorption does not prove a clinical outcome.

Tier 2 — Well-supported, real but modest (joints, sleep, glucose, GlyNAC, bone, tendon, muscle-FFM) (19 findings)

11. Joints/osteoarthritis is collagen's single best-evidenced use — a real but modest, funding-limited effect

A trial-sequential meta-analysis (35 RCTs / 3,165) found collagen derivatives reduce OA pain (SMD −0.35) and improve function (SMD −0.31, high certainty), effects near the minimal-clinically-important line, but the trial base is heavily manufacturer-funded and a manufacturer-independent RCT (N=68) found no benefit over placebo.

12. "Collagen for joints" is two different products that don't transfer

Hydrolyzed peptides (8-12 g, a substrate/signalling effect) and undenatured type-II collagen (UC-II, 40 mg, an oral-immune-tolerance mechanism) are mechanistically distinct; UC-II's positive trials are almost entirely manufacturer-generated, and evidence for one product does not transfer to the other.

13. No human evidence collagen regenerates cartilage

Every positive OA result is on symptom scales (WOMAC/VAS), which are patient-reported surrogates; no RCT shows cartilage regrowth on validated imaging, and symptom relief is not structural repair.

14. UC-II "beats glucosamine+chondroitin" is beating a placebo-level comparator

UC-II's headline superiority is hollow: glucosamine+chondroitin is at/near placebo in the independent GAIT trial (N=1,583), UC-II's own positive evidence is manufacturer-generated, and a 2023 limited meta-analysis flags its thin independent replication.

15. The seed collagen-sleep trial missed its primary endpoints

Thomas 2023 (PMC10799148), a Rousselot-funded n=13 RCT, found NO change in the primary sleep outcomes (onset latency, efficiency, quantity); only a secondary "fewer awakenings" improved (PSG 21.3±9.7 vs 29.3±13.8, P=0.028), and inflammation + core temperature were null.

16. Even the seed sleep trial had no protein-matched control

The one objective positive — fewer awakenings — cannot be attributed to collagen: the comparator was an inert taste-matched drink, NOT isonitrogenous, so the result can't be separated from any bedtime protein, and every primary sleep endpoint was still null.

17. Sleep is a modest glycine effect

~3 g glycine before bed shortens latency to sleep onset and slow-wave sleep and improves next-day fatigue (Yamadera 2007; Bannai 2012), but an independent review grades the glycine-sleep evidence as small-sample/high-risk-of-bias, and several trials are manufacturer-linked.

18. Glycine's sleep mechanism is a core-temperature drop — but it was null in humans

Glycine acts on NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus to trigger peripheral vasodilation and a core-temperature fall (rat mechanism); the one human study that measured core temperature (the collagen RCT) found no temperature effect.

19. The one reproducible glucose signal is glucose-blunting — and it IS collagen-peptide-specific

A specific screened hydrolysate (H80/Nextida GC) 5-10 g pre-meal cut the post-meal glucose rise ~40-43% overall and ~48-53% in prediabetics (Grasset 2024, n=16) — but manufacturer-only, acute, and its GLP-1/gastric-emptying mechanism was measured in MICE, not the human arm.

20. The glucose-blunting effect is still NOT independently replicated

Both human collagen glucose/GLP-1 trials (Grasset 2024, Reynolds 2025) come from the same Rousselot-funded network, and the effect is mechanistically a general protein-preload/GLP-1 effect (whey does the same) with no equal-protein comparator — real in those trials but single-funder and not shown collagen-specific.

21. Glutathione needs GlyNAC — collagen has no cysteine

The strong human GSH data use glycine PLUS N-acetylcysteine in aged/diseased people (Kumar 2023; Sekhar 2011); collagen supplies no cysteine, so it cannot reproduce the GlyNAC effect, and in healthy young adults glycine is unlikely to be the limiting precursor.

22. Cysteine, not glycine, is the classical rate-limiting glutathione precursor

The "glycine is rate-limiting for glutathione" claim is a McCarty/DiNicolantonio advocacy-review hypothesis; mainstream biochemistry holds cysteine as the limiting precursor — and collagen supplies neither cysteine nor (reliably) the glycine dose that matters, so the collagen→glutathione story is doubly weak.

23. The whole GlyNAC evidence base is one lab, mostly open-label, largest RCT n=24

Every positive GlyNAC study is from the single Sekhar/Baylor group — Kumar 2020 (HIV, n=8, open-label), 2021 (n=16, open-label), 2023 (n=24 RCT, isonitrogenous-alanine control) — all small, disease-specific cohorts with pre-existing glutathione deficiency; not a broad, replicated, healthy-population result, and it needs NAC collagen lacks.

24. Bone: a real BMD signal in postmenopausal women, but surrogate and funded

König 2018 (N=131, 5 g/day, 12 months) found significant spine + femoral-neck BMD gains with favourable bone-turnover markers, but it is Gelita-funded, the endpoint is BMD (not fractures), and the pooled bone effect is highly heterogeneous (I²~80%).

25. Tendon: collagen + heavy training grows tendon size but not its function

5 g specific collagen peptides during 14 weeks of resistance training increased patellar-tendon cross-sectional area vs placebo, but stiffness, strength and performance rose equally in both groups — the loading is the driver, the CSA trials are one manufacturer's product (TENDOFORTE), and ~96% of participants are men.

26. For tendon, loading is the proven driver; collagen is at most an adjunct

A 2026 systematic review grades GRADE A that tendon cross-sectional area/stiffness rise WITH training and GRADE A AGAINST an added strength effect; no factorial trial isolates gelatin/vitamin-C/loading — so the training does the work and collagen adds a modest structural increment at most.

27. Muscle: small fat-free-mass gains only WITH resistance training, from one funded group

Collagen peptides + resistance training give a real pooled fat-free-mass effect (meta SMD 0.48, moderate certainty) but a small, low-certainty strength effect (SMD 0.19); every arm trained, and the positive trials are dominated by one German group using one Gelita product.

28. "Fat-free mass" gains are not the same as contractile muscle

DXA/BIA fat-free mass includes connective tissue, tendon, fascia and water; collagen demonstrably stimulates collagenous-tissue synthesis, and proteomics (Oertzen-Hagemann 2019) shows collagen + training upregulates contractile + Z-disk proteins while muscle protein synthesis still does not rise — so an FFM signal can be real yet not be muscle-fibre hypertrophy.

29. Body-composition gains without training are tested by one funded trial

The "only WITH resistance training" pattern is near-universal but not absolute — Zdzieblik 2021 (untrained middle-aged men, 15 g/day, no structured RT, Gelita-funded) is the single test of the no-training case, so the training-dependence rests on that one caveat.

Tier 3 — Weak, single-study, or conditional (gut, anti-inflammatory, wound, recovery, nail/hair, nocturia, liver, arterial) (13 findings)

30. Gut-barrier / "leaky gut" repair is unproven in humans

Collagen barrier data are in-vitro/animal only, a glutamine gut-permeability meta-analysis is null, and one mouse study found collagen peptide WORSENED colitis — so the direction of effect is not even settled preclinically.

31. Anti-inflammatory effect is disease-restricted, and null in the collagen trial

The glycine-gated chloride channel is a real anti-inflammatory mechanism, but human benefit appears only in diseased cohorts (one glycine RCT in T2D at 15 g/day), an independent review finds no effect in healthy people, and the manufacturer's own collagen trial found IL-6/CRP null.

32. Collagen can't even reach the glycine dose that moved inflammation markers

The glycine-alone trials that lowered oxidative-stress/cytokine markers used 15 g/day (Cruz, Díaz-Flores); a 15 g collagen serving delivers only ~3.5 g glycine — roughly 4× under-dosed — so even granting the glycine mechanism, a collagen serving is below the effective dose.

33. Wound healing: real in clinical nutrition, and the cleanest peptide-specific signal — but for sick patients

Collagen peptides speed pressure-ulcer healing, and a dose-response trial where a high-dipeptide formula beat a low-dipeptide one at equal protein (Sugihara, N=112) is the best evidence a collagen benefit is bioactive-peptide-specific — but this is enteral nutrition in malnourished ulcer patients (with an independent, non-Nitta ~2× corroboration), not evidence a healthy person's supplement heals faster.

34. The "collagen heals wounds" evidence people cite is largely topical dressings

Holmes 2022 (11 RCTs) shows collagen wound dressings/matrices help chronic wounds — but that is a physical scaffold device, not the oral supplement; no adequately-powered oral post-surgical-recovery RCT in healthy people exists.

35. Recovery/DOMS: one small manufacturer trial, inconsistent across the field

A fish-collagen crossover (Kuwaba, N=18, Nippi employees) reported less post-exercise soreness, but systematic reviews find DOMS results inconsistent and a general protein-recovery effect is not excluded.

36. Nail evidence is one open-label, no-placebo study

The only nail trial (Hexsel 2017, single-arm, open-label, no control, n=25) reported +12% growth / −42% breaks, but the design cannot rule out regression/placebo, and the nail plate is keratin, not collagen.

37. Hair evidence is genuinely scarce and industry-only

There is no placebo-controlled meta-analysis for hair; the hair shaft is keratin, giving no collagen-specific rationale, and marketed density percentages could not be independently verified (confirm).

38. Nocturia: a real but weak glycine signal, via a bladder reflex — not ADH

The only direct nocturia evidence is for glycine (~6 g/day in overactive-bladder patients, Sugaya 2021), the design is weak (no parallel control; placebo also improved), and the mechanism is a spinal glycinergic bladder reflex, NOT antidiuretic hormone and NOT "deeper sleep".

39. Liver "detox" is a pathway, not a proven outcome

Glycine conjugates benzoate/bile acids and protects the liver in rodent alcoholic/NAFLD models via the Kupffer-cell glycine-gated chloride channel, but no human trial shows collagen or glycine improves liver function or xenobiotic clearance — mechanism is not benefit.

40. The liver "detox" bile-acid arm is rodent-only and species-specific

Glycine protects rodent liver (e.g. 83% vs 0% survival in a rat IR+LPS model), but mouse bile acids are almost entirely taurine-conjugated, so the glycine-bile-conjugation "detox" mechanism does not transfer to humans.

41. Arterial evidence is small, manufacturer-linked, and surrogate-only

Human collagen cardiovascular data cover only stiffness/BP/LDL (no MI/stroke/death); the top trial is open-label with no placebo (Tomosugi, Jellice), and a 12-RCT meta shows SBP −5/LDL −4 but with I²≈99% and the BP effect vanishing at 12 weeks.

42. The tendon biomarker story is weak — PINP is a bone marker

Gelatin + vitamin C raised serum PINP +153% (Shaw, N=8), but PINP overwhelmingly reflects bone turnover (not tendon), and the effect failed to replicate (Lis & Baar, non-significant) — so a blood-PINP rise does not prove tendon collagen was made.

Tier 4 — Myths, misconceptions, and discredited single sources (8 findings)

43. Anxiety: no human trial exists; the claim is dose-impossible extrapolation

No study tested collagen against an anxiety endpoint; the evidence is receptor pharmacology from 30-60 g isolated glycine in schizophrenia/OCD (mixed-to-null; the largest trial, CONSIST, was negative), doses 7-20× the glycine in a collagen serving, so it does not scale to food doses.

44. The collagen sleep trial found no shift in stress physiology

The seed RCT specifically measured and found NO change in cortisol, sympathetic normetanephrine, or inflammatory markers — evidence against a nervous-system-calming effect, not for it.

45. The only collagen "cognition" signal is a ceiling-effect Stroop result

The manufacturer trial's single positive cognitive endpoint was Stroop accuracy 1.00±0.00 vs 0.97±0.05 (P=0.009) — a 0.03 near-ceiling difference on 1 of 4 cognitive tests (the others null), multiplicity-prone, and possibly sleep-independent; not evidence collagen sharpens next-day cognition.

46. The "less urine at night" (ADH) story is a misconception

No trial in this literature measured ADH/vasopressin or nocturnal urine volume for collagen or glycine, so the claim that collagen cuts urine production at night is unsupported; the real signal (if any) is bladder-signaling, not reduced urine output.

47. "Collagen rebuilds arteries" fails the best causal tests

Pleiotropy-robust Mendelian randomization and an ApoE-knockout mouse feeding study were both null for atherosclerosis (Hazen lab, 2023-24); "collagen rebuilds artery walls" is a misconception because digestion does not route collagen to arterial tissue.

48. No isolated-collagen ligament/ACL trial with a hard endpoint exists

Every human ligament-graft trial bundles collagen with hyaluronic acid + chondroitin + plasma proteins + vitamin C, so collagen's independent contribution is unmeasurable, and UC-II has zero tendon/ligament outcome data — the connective-tissue-injury claims rest on cocktails, not isolated collagen.

49. Product type is everything — the evidence does not transfer across collagen forms

UC-II (40 mg, immune tolerance) ≠ hydrolyzed peptides (grams, substrate/signalling) ≠ gelatin + vitamin C (synthesis cofactor) ≠ topical collagen dressings (a physical wound scaffold, a device not a supplement); marketing blurs these, but a trial on one form is not evidence for another.

50. Guard-rail: the "2025 N=48 3 g glycine PSG RCT" is a fabricated citation

A widely-blog-cited "2025 randomized double-blind N=48 3 g glycine polysomnography RCT" does not exist in PubMed — it appears only on supplement blogs and looks like a re-description of Bannai & Kawai 2012; do not cite it.

Safety (cross-cutting) (4 findings)

51. Kidney-stone caution: hydroxyproline becomes oxalate

Ingested hydroxyproline (unique to collagen/gelatin) is metabolized to oxalate; gelatin raised urinary oxalate +43% AND glycolate 5.3× vs whey at 5-10 g (Knight 2006), null at 1-2 g — a real caution for recurrent calcium-oxalate stone-formers / hyperoxaluria, likely negligible for others with good hydration.

52. The kidney-stone risk is hydroxyproline-specific — plain glycine dodges it

The oxalate load comes from hydroxyproline, not glycine (glycine contributes <5% of urinary oxalate), so the stone caution belongs to collagen/gelatin, not to the cheaper glycine alternative.

53. Heavy-metal contamination is real but brand-variable

Clean Label Project testing found ~47% of protein powders exceeded a conservative Prop-65 metal threshold (organic and plant-based averaged higher lead/cadmium); "non-detect" is achievable, so choose third-party-tested (NSF/USP/Clean Label) products.

54. Safety beyond metals/stones: mostly mild-GI, but real edge cases

Hydrolyzed collagen/gelatin is GRAS with mostly mild GI effects, but the honest safety tail includes marine (fish) collagen allergy/anaphylaxis, a Stevens-Johnson/TEN case report, a theoretical (undocumented) bovine prion caveat, and insufficient pregnancy/lactation data; for the glycine alternative, ≤15 g/day is well tolerated but a ~0.8 g/kg single bolus caused adverse effects.

docs.title: Test yourself
docs.text:
Twelve questions drawn at random from the findings above. Pick an answer, see why, and learn. Replayable, and your best score is remembered on this device.

  1. Collagen amino-acid composition (~⅓ glycine by residue; no tryptophan; leucine-poor). Structural biochemistry, DOI 10.1110/ps.062560107 · PMID 17189476. ↩↩↩

  2. Oikawa SY, et al. (2020) Am J Clin Nutr. Whey but not collagen raised muscle protein synthesis (equal-protein, n=22; independent). DOI 10.1093/ajcn/nqz332 · PMID 31919527. ↩↩↩↩

  3. Thomas C, et al. (2023) Eur J Nutr. Collagen peptides pre-sleep RCT (n=13; primary endpoints null; control not protein-matched; Rousselot-funded). DOI 10.1007/s00394-023-03267-w · PMID 37874350. ↩↩↩↩↩↩↩↩

  4. Meléndez-Hevia E, et al. (2009) J Biosci 34(6):853-872. Glycine ~10 g/day synthesis shortfall (conditionally essential). DOI 10.1007/s12038-009-0100-9. ↩↩↩↩

  5. McKendry J, et al. (2024) Am J Clin Nutr. Whey and pea raised myofibrillar synthesis; collagen did not (n=31). DOI 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2024.05.009 · PMID 38762187. ↩↩↩

  6. Myung SK, Park Y (2025) Am J Med 138(9):1264-1277. Systematic review/meta-analysis, 23 RCTs / 1,474; skin benefit null in independent + high-quality subgroups. DOI 10.1016/j.amjmed.2025.04.034 · PMID 40324552. ↩↩↩↩

  7. Ravindran S, Pizzol D, López-Gil JF, et al. (2026) Aesthetic Surg J Open Forum. Umbrella review (16 meta-analyses / 113 RCTs); high-GRADE positive for skin, but pools mostly low-quality reviews. DOI 10.1093/asjof/ojag018. ↩

  8. Liang CW, et al. (2024) Osteoarthritis Cartilage 32(5):574-584. Trial-sequential meta-analysis, 35 RCTs / 3,165; OA pain SMD −0.35, function SMD −0.31. DOI 10.1016/j.joca.2023.12.010 · PMID 38218227. ↩↩↩

  9. Yuenyongviwat V, et al. (2025) Sci Rep. Manufacturer-independent OA RCT, n=68; null vs placebo. DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-17505-0. ↩↩↩

  10. Lugo JP, Saiyed ZM, Lane NE (2016) Nutr J. Undenatured type-II collagen (UC-II, 40 mg) vs glucosamine+chondroitin vs placebo, n=191 (InterHealth-funded). DOI 10.1186/s12937-016-0130-8 · PMID 26822714. ↩

  11. Clegg DO, et al. (GAIT, 2006) N Engl J Med 354:795-808. Glucosamine/chondroitin at/near placebo (N=1,583) — the weak comparator UC-II "beats". DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa052771. ↩

  12. Yamadera W, et al. (2007) Sleep Biol Rhythms. 3 g glycine pre-bed shortens sleep-onset/slow-wave latency. DOI 10.1111/j.1479-8425.2007.00262.x. ↩↩↩

  13. Soh J, et al. (2023) GeroScience. Systematic review of glycine in humans (52 studies); sleep evidence small/high-risk-of-bias. DOI 10.1007/s11357-023-00970-8 · PMID 37851316. ↩

  14. Grasset E, et al. (2024) Food Sci Nutr. Collagen hydrolysate + post-meal glucose RCT (n=16; GLP-1/emptying mechanism measured in mice only; Rousselot-funded). DOI 10.1002/fsn3.4538. ↩↩↩

  15. Reynolds A, et al. (2025) Br J Nutr. Bovine collagen peptides + GLP-1/appetite, n=15 (Rousselot-linked; the glucose effect is still not independently replicated). DOI 10.1017/S0007114525103851. ↩

  16. Kumar P, et al. (2023) J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. GlyNAC (glycine + NAC) RCT, n=24 older adults; single-lab, needs cysteine collagen lacks. DOI 10.1093/gerona/glac135 · PMID 35975308. ↩↩↩

  17. König D, et al. (2018) Nutrients 10(1):97. Specific collagen peptides + bone mineral density in postmenopausal women, n=131, 12 mo (Gelita-funded). DOI 10.3390/nu10010097 · PMID 29337906. ↩↩↩

  18. Jerger S, et al. (2023) Eur J Sport Sci. 5 g collagen peptides + resistance training; tendon CSA increased, stiffness/strength did not (TENDOFORTE/GELITA). DOI 10.1080/17461391.2023.2232758. ↩↩↩

  19. Systematic review of collagen + tendon adaptation (2026) J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):130. GRADE A that CSA/stiffness rise with training; GRADE A against an added strength effect. DOI 10.3390/jfmk11010130. ↩

  20. Bischof K, et al. (2024) Sports Med. Collagen + resistance-training meta-analysis (19 RCTs / 768); fat-free-mass SMD 0.48, strength SMD 0.19. DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02079-0 · PMID 39060741. ↩

  21. Sugihara F, et al. (2018) Sci Rep. Collagen-dipeptide dose-response in pressure-ulcer healing, n=112 (Nitta-funded). DOI 10.1038/s41598-018-29831-7 · PMID 30061579. ↩↩

  22. Lee SK, et al. (2006) Adv Skin Wound Care 19(2). Independent pressure-ulcer RCT (n=71); ~2× faster healing vs control. DOI 10.1097/00129334-200603000-00011 · PMID 16557055. ↩

  23. Sugaya K, et al. (2021) J Complement Integr Med 18(3):617-620. Glycine ~6 g/day in overactive-bladder patients (bladder-reflex mechanism; no parallel control). DOI 10.1515/jcim-2020-0282. ↩↩↩↩↩

  24. Buchanan RW, et al. (CONSIST, 2007) Am J Psychiatry. Adjunctive high-dose glycine showed no benefit (largest trial). DOI 10.1176/appi.ajp.2007.06081358 · PMID 17898352. ↩↩↩

  25. Biswas S, Hilser JR, et al. (2023-24, Hazen lab) pleiotropy-robust Mendelian randomization + ApoE⁻/⁻ mouse feeding: no causal glycine→atherosclerosis effect. DOI 10.1101/2023.12.08.23299748 · PMID 38168321 (preprint). ↩↩↩

  26. Clean Label Project (2024) protein-powder heavy-metal report — ~47% exceeded a Prop-65 threshold; brand-variable. ↩↩

  27. Knight J, et al. (2006) Kidney Int 70(11). Hydroxyproline/gelatin raises urinary oxalate (+43% vs whey); glycine itself <5% of urinary oxalate. PMID 17021603. ↩↩

docs.title: Creatine: What It Actually Does vs What People Think
docs.text:
Creatine is the most-studied and best-selling sports supplement on earth — and the most myth-laden. It is blamed for kidney damage, hair loss, "being a steroid," permanent bloating and cramps, and sold in a dozen "advanced" forms. What does it actually do, which claims (good and bad) survive the peer-reviewed evidence, and how should a healthy person use it? This is the whole picture, ranked by how strongly the evidence backs each claim — settled consensus first, single-study and myth last.

Complete · Published 23 July 2026 · Every one of the 169 cited studies was title-matched against PubMed (0 wrong, 0 retracted) and the load-bearing ones read from source · expanded the same day with a second literature sweep (+50 sources) · 169 cited sources · Confidence: High on efficacy-with-training, the kidney-artifact, safety, and "not a steroid"; Moderate–High on the hair-loss myth; Moderate on the therapeutic claims (depression, glycemic, bone, long-COVID).

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Bottom line

Creatine monohydrate is the safest, best-proven supplement there is, but it only builds muscle when you're actually lifting, and almost every scary story about it is flat wrong.

Myths vs. reality

What most people believe What the evidence actually shows Creatine wrecks your kidneys It doesn't. It only nudges up the creatinine number labs use to estimate kidney function, with no real drop in filtration. The entire scare is 2 case reports in people who already had kidney disease. It causes hair loss and baldness The whole claim is one 2009 study of 20 rugby players that measured a hormone and never looked at a single hair. The first trial that actually measured hair (2025) found zero change. It's basically a steroid It's an amino acid found in steak and fish. It does not change testosterone at all and isn't banned anywhere. You have to "load" it and "cycle" off 3 to 5 g a day fully saturates you in 3 to 4 weeks with no loading, and you never need to cycle off. Fancy forms (HCl, buffered, ethyl ester) work better Plain monohydrate beats all of them. Ethyl ester was worse; the rest were no better and cost more. Creatine builds the muscle The training builds the muscle. Creatine adds about 1 kg on top. With no lifting it adds basically nothing (+0.03 kg). It makes you smarter Only if your brain is short on it: old, vegetarian, or sleep-deprived. In young rested people the biggest trial found almost nothing, and EFSA rejected the brain claim in 2024. The "bloat" is fat you can't lose The water sits inside the muscle cell, not under your skin, and it clears in about 4 weeks if you stop.

What you actually learn

  • Creatine works, but the barbell does most of the work. Training plus creatine adds about 1 kg of lean mass; creatine with no training adds 0.03 kg, which is nothing.
  • The kidney scare is a lab-reading artifact, not real damage. It's been used safely at up to 30 g/day for 5 years, and a safety review of 951 women found no serious adverse events.
  • The hair-loss panic rests on a single 2009 study that never measured hair. The only trial that actually looked (2025) found no change in DHT or hair density.
  • Vegetarians are the biggest winners, not the people who "don't need it." They start with low stores, so they gain the most, for both muscle and brain.
  • "Advanced" forms are marketing. Plain monohydrate is about 99% absorbed; the pricier versions are equal or worse.
  • No loading and no cycling. 3 to 5 g a day saturates you in a few weeks and you just keep taking it.
  • The brain hype outran the science. The big Parkinson's trial (1,741 people) and Huntington's trial (553 people) both failed, and EFSA rejected the cognition claim in 2024.
  • Gummies and pre-mixed drinks can quietly under-deliver, because dissolved creatine slowly turns into useless creatinine. Take it as fresh-mixed powder.
  • It won't do the glamorous stuff: no testosterone boost, no fat loss on its own, no cure for heart failure or cancer wasting.

What this means for you

  • Buy plain creatine monohydrate, third-party tested (Creapure or Informed-Sport). Skip HCl, buffered, ester, nitrate, and gummies, they cost more and do no more.
  • Take 3 to 5 g every day as fresh-mixed powder. Don't bother loading, don't bother cycling. Taking it with a carb or protein meal speeds saturation a bit.
  • Only expect the muscle benefit if you're actually lifting. Creatine is an amplifier, not a shortcut.
  • If you're healthy, ignore the kidney and hair scares completely. Check with a doctor first only if you have existing kidney disease, bipolar disorder (a small risk of triggering hypomania), or you're pregnant (no safety trial exists yet).
  • Don't buy it as a brain pill unless you're vegetarian, older, or chronically short on sleep. For a young, well-fed, rested person the cognitive payoff is close to zero.

TL;DR

Creatine monohydrate is the most-studied, best-evidenced and safest sports supplement, and almost every scary claim about it is wrong. Taken daily and paired with resistance training it genuinely builds strength and lean mass,12 though the fast early gain is partly intracellular water1312 and it does almost nothing for muscle without training.1 The "it wrecks your kidneys" fear is a measurement artifact — creatine raises serum creatinine without lowering true kidney filtration1416 — and the scare traces to two confounded case reports.2223 It does not cause dehydration or cramps (if anything, fewer),3032 it is not a steroid and does not change testosterone,34 and the hair-loss panic rests on one 2009 study that never measured hair36 — the only trial that did measure hair was null.38 You do not need to load or cycle it,39 and plain monohydrate beats every "advanced" form.41424344 Brain, mood and metabolic benefits are real but bounded — largest in older adults, vegetarians, the sleep-deprived, or as an antidepressant adjunct in women,464760 and small-to-null in young, rested people.51 The honest caveat cutting the other way: much of the enthusiastic literature is industry-funded — but the safety core is independently corroborated.14285161

The picture, ranked by how strongly the evidence agrees

  • Tier 1 — strongest consensus: creatine + resistance training builds strength and lean mass (nothing without training);12 it does not damage healthy kidneys (the raised creatinine is a metabolic artifact);1416 it is safe long-term across populations;2528 no dehydration or cramps;3032 it is not a steroid and does not change testosterone.34
  • Tier 2 — well-supported, with nuance: the hair-loss scare is one DHT study that never measured hair, and the direct hair trial was null;3638 no loading or cycling needed;39 monohydrate beats every "advanced" form;41 brain benefits are real but bounded to deficit/stress (aging, vegetarians, sleep loss).465147
  • Tier 3 — promising but preliminary: an antidepressant adjunct signal in women;60 glycemic control with exercise only;89 partial bone-geometry benefit;94 an early long-COVID-fatigue signal.92
  • Tier 4 — myths & marketing: "it's a steroid,"35 "wrecks your kidneys,"24 "permanent bloat you can't lose,"12 "you must cycle it,"39 "causes hair loss,"38 "bad for teenagers,"29 "vegetarians don't need it,"9 and the failed cardiac/cancer-cachexia cures.10461

docs.title: What this review covered
docs.text: An eight-part search swept the peer-reviewed literature across the ergogenic core, kidney safety, hormones and hair, brain and mood, women/aging/bone, mechanism and product forms, metabolic and therapeutic claims, and the specific influencer myths (steroid, cycling, bloating, teenagers, vegetarians, contamination). Every candidate PMID — 119 — was then independently title-matched against PubMed (0 wrong, 0 retracted), and the load-bearing abstracts (the efficacy meta-analyses, the kidney meta, the DHT and hair trials, the depression and glycemic RCTs, the metabolic-burden paper, the postmenopausal and cachexia trials) were read from source for their exact numbers. A recurring honesty note runs through it: much of the positive creatine research comes from the industry-linked International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN), which is flagged throughout — but the safety core is backed by independent groups.

docs.title: What the deeper search added
docs.text:
A second literature sweep (50 more sources, → 169) did not change the verdict — it hardened it and opened a clinical dimension the first pass only touched:

  • A real therapy versus a failed neuroprotectant. The one place creatine is genuinely disease-modifying is the rare inborn creatine-synthesis disorders — GAMT and AGAT deficiency respond to oral creatine,6263 while the creatine-transporter (SLC6A8) defect does not (the transport step itself is broken).64 Against that, creatine's biggest clinical hope — slowing common neurodegeneration — failed in the definitive independent trials: the NIH Parkinson's trial (NET-PD LS-1, N=1,741) and the Huntington's trial (CREST-E, N=553) were both stopped for futility,6566 and a review from within the field calls broad neuroprotection "end of story."67 In muscular dystrophy a Cochrane review does find a real symptomatic strength gain.68
  • The regulators and even the advocates are skeptical about cognition. Beyond the null largest trial, the European Food Safety Authority ruled in 2024 that a cause-and-effect relationship between creatine and improved cognition is not established,69 a 2024 review found the mechanism unsupported,70 and leading creatine researchers now warn the brain hype has "put the cart before the horse."71 The depression signal, by contrast, firmed up in a 2025 meta-analysis,72 while a bipolar trial stayed null on mood.73
  • Dose, timing and forms got concrete. Co-ingesting carbohydrate (or protein plus carbohydrate) raises muscle uptake by up to ~60% via insulin;74 high-dose loading adds nothing in already-trained athletes;75 monohydrate is near-completely absorbed (which sinks the "better-absorbed form" pitch);76 and creatine dissolved in liquid slowly degrades to inactive creatinine — the chemistry behind under-dosed gummies and pre-mixed drinks.77
  • Sleep, metabolic and bone claims were tempered. "Creatine lets you sleep less" is rats only;78 the human sleep and recovery signal is modest and mixed (subjective sleep and soreness improved, objective sleep architecture did not).79 The fatty-liver benefit is preclinical only (rats and cells, no human trial),80 creatine does not raise metabolic rate on its own,81 and it does not cause fat loss during a calorie deficit.82 Two 2-year bone trials found no bone-density benefit,8384 settling that creatine is not an osteoporosis therapy — and one reassurance for women: loading does not cause problematic bloating across the menstrual cycle.85

docs.title: Tier 1 — The strongest evidence (it works, and the safety scares are wrong)
It builds muscle and strength — but the training does most of the work
docs.text: This is the most-replicated result in sports supplementation. Meta-analyses agree that creatine combined with resistance training builds lean mass and strength: a 35-trial meta put the lean-mass gain at +1.10 kg with training (and a non-significant +0.03 kg without exercise),1 a 22-trial meta in older adults found +1.37 kg lean mass plus greater chest- and leg-press strength,23 and strength meta-analyses (upper and lower limb) agree.456 The load-bearing nuance is size and dependency: the pooled body-composition effect is "small-to-moderate,"7 and creatine is an amplifier of resistance training, not a substitute for it — with no training stimulus it does almost nothing.1

docs.title: It is real muscle — but the fast early gain is partly water
docs.text: The "it's just water weight" line is half true. Muscle-biopsy trials show creatine drives genuine growth: larger fiber cross-sectional area,89 more satellite cells and myonuclei (true remodeling),10 and an anabolic gene-expression signature.11 But the rapid first-week increase in scale weight is largely intracellular water drawn into the muscle cell,12 and a 2025 RCT with a supplement wash-in showed that once that water was accounted for, 5 g/day added no lean mass beyond training alone (a +0.51 kg wash-in bump, then no between-group difference).13 So the honest picture is real hypertrophy over months, with the "instant gains" of the first week being cell hydration.

docs.title: The kidney scare is a measurement artifact
docs.text: Creatine is metabolized to creatinine, so supplementing mildly raises serum creatinine — and therefore lowers estimated-GFR equations — without any true fall in kidney filtration.1415 Studies using measured GFR (⁵¹Cr-EDTA and clearance markers) find no renal impairment,1617 including in resistance-trained men on high-protein diets18 and in type-2 diabetics with elevated renal risk;19 three separate meta-analyses reach the same conclusion.142021 The entire "creatine destroys kidneys" narrative traces to two confounded single-patient case reports — both in people with pre-existing kidney disease and on other nephrotoxic drugs.2223 A 2023 review put it bluntly: it is time for a "requiem" for the creatine-kidney-failure myth.24

docs.title: It is safe long-term, across populations
docs.text: Up to 21 months of use left roughly 50 clinical health markers unchanged;25 the ISSN safe ceiling is 30 g/day for five years;26 and high doses were tolerated in months-long trials in ALS27 patients. A dedicated female-only adverse-event meta-analysis (29 studies / 951 women) recorded no deaths and no serious adverse events, and no difference versus placebo in total adverse events, gastrointestinal events, weight gain, or renal/hepatic markers.28 Youth are not a special-risk group either — a review of active adolescents found a strong safety profile and no evidence-based reason for a blanket ban.29

docs.title: No dehydration, no cramps — if anything, fewer
docs.text: The dehydration/cramp myth runs the opposite way to the evidence. A meta-analysis found no impairment of hydration or thermoregulation and no rise in heat-illness risk;30 subjects who exercised dehydrated in the heat were unharmed;31 and season-long football cohorts had fewer cramps, dehydration episodes and injuries on creatine.3233 The intracellular water creatine draws into muscle is, if anything, protective.

docs.title: It is not a steroid and does not raise testosterone
docs.text: Creatine is a naturally occurring amino-acid derivative found in meat and fish — not a hormone, and not a banned substance. Controlled trials show no change versus placebo in total testosterone, SHBG, free-androgen index, cortisol, growth hormone or IGF-1,34 and umbrella reviews of "testosterone boosters" place it outside the category of supplements that raise serum T.35

docs.title: Tier 2 — Well-supported, with real nuance (hair, dosing, forms, brain)
The hair-loss scare rests on one study that never measured hair
docs.text: The entire "creatine causes baldness" claim comes from a single 2009 study in 20 rugby players, in which DHT rose (+56% after loading, +40% after maintenance) and the DHT-to-testosterone ratio rose — but which never measured hair and was never replicated,36 and was formally critiqued at publication.37 In 2025 the first trial designed to look at hair directly — 12 weeks, 5 g/day, with Trichogram and FotoFinder imaging — found no change in DHT, in the DHT:T ratio, or in any hair-density, thickness or follicle-count measure versus placebo, and concluded it was "strong evidence against the claim that creatine contributes to hair loss."38 The mechanism is an unreplicated hypothesis; the only outcome data are null.

docs.title: You do not need to "load," and you do not need to "cycle"
docs.text: A loading phase (20 g/day for about six days) saturates muscle creatine quickly, but 3–5 g/day reaches the identical saturation in three to four weeks — loading only speeds arrival, it is not required.3940 There is likewise no cycling requirement: continuous 3–5 g/day simply maintains the elevated stores, and stopping lets them drift back to baseline over about a month.39

docs.title: Plain monohydrate is the gold standard — the "advanced" forms are marketing
docs.text: Creatine monohydrate is roughly 99% bioavailable and raises muscle stores 15–40%.41 Head-to-head trials show every marketed alternative fails to beat it: creatine ethyl ester was actually worse (lower muscle-creatine gain, more degradation),42 buffered "Kre-Alkalyn" was no better even at a lower dose,43 and creatine nitrate did not outperform equimolar monohydrate.44 Pay for monohydrate, ideally a tested brand.

docs.title: Brain benefits are real but concentrated in deficit and stress
docs.text: Creatine crosses the blood–brain barrier slowly — brain creatine rises only about 8% versus roughly 20% in muscle45 — so the cognitive effect is largest where the brain is short of it or under stress: memory in older adults,46 vegetarians (lower baseline stores),4748 and sleep deprivation.4950 In young, rested, meat-eating adults the largest trial to date (123 people) found only a small, borderline effect and no vegetarian advantage,51 and a balanced review confirms the benefit shrinks toward zero without a deficit.50 The "response" question is the same story from the muscle side: uptake is inversely related to your baseline, so low-store individuals — especially vegetarians — gain the most and already-saturated meat-eaters the least.5253

docs.title: Women benefit and it is safe
docs.text: Women carry roughly 70–80% lower endogenous creatine stores than men.54 The evidence in women is favorable: a 2026 meta-analysis of postmenopausal trials found +0.37 kg lean mass and +7.5 kg leg-press strength when at least 5 g/day is combined with resistance training,55 vulnerable older women improved lean mass and function with creatine plus training,56 and there is no evidence that creatine disrupts female sex hormones.57

docs.title: Tier 3 — Promising but preliminary, or conditional
docs.text:
• Depression — the strongest data are for augmentation: adding 5 g/day to an SSRI accelerated and deepened the response in women with major depression (greater symptom improvement from week 2),60 with a supporting brain-bioenergetics rationale86 and an association in a large dietary survey.87 But this is adjunct-to-medication in women, not a monotherapy, and an open-label study saw both bipolar patients switch into hypomania — a real safety flag.88
  • Blood sugar — creatine plus exercise cut HbA1c by 1.1% in type-2 diabetics and raised GLUT-4 translocation (the strongest human trial),89 but without an exercise co-intervention, meta-analyses find no glycemic effect.9091
  • Fatigue / long-COVID — small, mostly single-blind trials suggest 6 g/day reduces fatigue and raises grip strength;9293 promising, not established.
  • Bone — the best 12-month trial attenuated femoral-neck bone-density loss and improved hip bone geometry with resistance training,94 but overall bone density is unchanged in the meta-analysis55 and reviews decline to recommend creatine as an osteoporosis therapy.9596
  • Immune / inflammation — an acute blunting of post-exertion cytokines,97 but no chronic anti-inflammatory effect (a meta of double-blind trials was null for CRP, IL-6 and TNF).98
  • Brain injury — mechanistically promising, with one small pediatric study,99 but no adult concussion trial.50
  • Caffeine — the "caffeine cancels creatine" rule is a single 1996 study of nine people;100 later reviews find everyday co-use is fine.101102

docs.title: Tier 4 — Myths, misconceptions, and marketing
docs.text:
• "It's a steroid / a banned PED." No — it is an amino-acid derivative from meat and fish, not a hormone, and it is not on any banned list.3526
  • "It wrecks your kidneys." The higher creatinine reading is the metabolic artifact, not lost filtration; measured-GFR studies and meta-analyses show no decline even in kidney patients.1724
  • "Water bloat you can't lose." The water it retains is inside the muscle cell, not subcutaneous, so it does not read as a puffy look, and it reverses within about four weeks of stopping.1239
  • "You must cycle it." There is no physiological basis; continuous 3–5 g/day simply keeps stores saturated.39
  • "It causes hair loss." One DHT study, no hair endpoint, direct hair trial null (see Tier 2).3638
  • "Bad for teenagers." No evidence of harm in active youth.29
  • "Vegetarians don't need it." Backwards — they have lower baseline stores and respond the most.947
  • Cardiac and cancer-cachexia cures. Creatine improved skeletal-muscle endurance but not heart function in heart-failure trials,103 added nothing to cardiac rehabilitation,104 and a 263-patient cancer trial found no benefit for the anorexia/weight-loss syndrome.61 Not every promising clinical use panned out.

docs.title: What actually matters
docs.text:
For a healthy person who lifts, creatine is close to a free lunch: creatine monohydrate, 3–5 g every day, with no loading and no cycling,39 taken consistently and paired with resistance training for the muscle benefit,1 from a third-party-tested product (Informed-Sport / Creapure) because roughly 15% of loosely-regulated supplements have been found contaminated with undeclared substances.58 Expect modest, real strength and lean-mass gains over months (not a dramatic overnight change once the initial water settles), possible cognitive help if you are older, vegetarian or sleep-deprived, and none of the harms the myths promise. What it will not do is build muscle without training, boost testosterone, cure a disease, or wreck your kidneys or hairline.

One mechanistic footnote worth knowing: your body makes creatine from the amino acids glycine, arginine and methionine, and this synthesis consumes a striking ~40% of the body's methyl groups (from methionine/SAM) — which is part of why vegetarians, who must make nearly all their own creatine, respond the most to supplementation.59

Informational only, not medical advice. This page is a public link but is unlisted (noindex). Every citation points to a public, independently verifiable source (DOI / PMID). Use the language selector at the top right for English / Ελληνικά.

docs.title: The full findings — all 41
docs.text:
Every conclusion this review reached, grouped by how strongly the evidence backs it. Each finding is distilled from the fully-cited evidence above.

Tier 1 — Strongest, settled (it works, and the safety scares are wrong) (6 findings)

1. Creatine + resistance training reliably builds lean mass and strength — but modestly, and the training is what does most of the work

This is the most-replicated finding in sports supplementation. Meta-analyses agree: creatine + resistance training adds roughly +1.1 kg lean mass overall, +1.37 kg in older adults, and meaningfully more strength. The honest size: the effect is small-to-moderate (ES ~0.24), and it is training-dependent — creatine without exercise adds essentially nothing to lean mass (+0.03 kg, NS). Creatine is an amplifier of resistance training, not a substitute for it.

2. It is real muscle, not "just water" — but a chunk of the fast early gain genuinely is intracellular water

The "it's only water weight" claim is half-true and half-wrong. Biopsy studies show creatine drives true contractile-tissue growth — larger muscle-fiber cross-sectional area, more satellite cells and myonuclei, and an anabolic gene-expression response. But the rapid first-week scale gain is largely intracellular water drawn into muscle cells, and a 2025 RCT with a wash-in showed that once that water is accounted for, 5 g/day added no lean-mass beyond training alone (+0.51 kg wash-in bump, then no between-group difference, p=0.71). So: real hypertrophy over months, but the headline "instant gains" are partly water.

3. Creatine does not damage healthy kidneys — the "high creatinine" is a measurement artifact

Creatine is metabolized to creatinine, so supplementing mildly raises serum creatinine (and lowers estimated-GFR equations) without any true drop in kidney filtration. Studies using measured GFR (⁵¹Cr-EDTA, clearance markers) show no renal impairment, including in resistance-trained men on high-protein diets and even in type-2 diabetics; three meta-analyses agree. The scare traces to two confounded single-case reports in people with pre-existing kidney disease and other nephrotoxic drugs.

4. Long-term use is safe — up to 30 g/day for 5 years, across populations from youth to the elderly

Up to 21 months of use left ~50 clinical health markers unchanged; retrospective long-term-user cohorts agree; high doses were well tolerated in months-long trials in ALS and Parkinson's patients; and the ISSN position stand puts the safe ceiling at 30 g/day for 5 years. A dedicated female-only adverse-event meta-analysis (29 studies / 951 women) found no deaths or serious adverse events and no difference vs placebo in total AEs, GI events, weight gain, or renal/hepatic markers.

5. Creatine does not cause dehydration or cramps — if anything, fewer

The dehydration/cramp myth is contradicted by the controlled data: a meta-analysis found no impairment of hydration or thermoregulation and no rise in heat-illness risk, subjects exercising dehydrated in heat were unharmed, and season-long football cohorts had fewer cramps, dehydration episodes and injuries on creatine. The intracellular water it draws into muscle (#2) is, if anything, protective.

6. Creatine is not a steroid or a hormone — it does not meaningfully change testosterone

Creatine is an amino-acid derivative, not an androgen, and it is not a banned substance. Controlled trials show no change vs placebo in total testosterone, SHBG, free-androgen index, cortisol, growth hormone or IGF-1, no effect on testosterone/cortisol/sperm, and reviews of "testosterone boosters" place it outside the category of supplements that raise serum T.

Tier 2 — Well-supported, with real nuance (hair, dosing, forms, brain, women) (6 findings)

7. The hair-loss scare rests on ONE study that never measured hair — and the only direct hair trial was null

The entire "creatine causes baldness" claim comes from a single 2009 rugby study where DHT rose (+56% loading, +40% maintenance) and DHT:T ratio rose — but hair was never measured and the finding was never replicated (and was critiqued at publication). In 2025 the first RCT to measure hair directly (Trichogram + FotoFinder, 12 wk) found no change in DHT, DHT:T ratio, or any hair-density/thickness/follicle-count metric vs placebo. The mechanism is a hypothesis; the outcome data are null.

8. You do not need to "load," and you do not need to "cycle"

A loading phase (20 g/day for ~6 days) saturates muscle creatine fast, but 3–5 g/day reaches the exact same saturation in ~3–4 weeks — loading only speeds arrival, it is not required. And there is no cycling requirement: continuous 3–5 g/day simply maintains the elevated stores; stopping lets them decline back to baseline over ~4 weeks.

9. Plain monohydrate is the gold standard — the "advanced" forms are marketing

Creatine monohydrate is ~99% bioavailable and raises muscle stores 15–40%. Head-to-head trials show no marketed alternative beats it: creatine ethyl ester was worse (lower muscle-creatine gain, more degradation), buffered "Kre-Alkalyn" was no better even at lower dose, and creatine nitrate did not outperform equimolar monohydrate. Pay for monohydrate (ideally Creapure), not HCl/buffered/ester/nitrate.

10. Brain benefits are real but concentrated in deficit and stress states — not in young, rested, well-fed people

Creatine crosses the blood–brain barrier only slowly (~8% brain rise vs ~20% in muscle), so the cognitive effect is largest where the brain is under-supplied or stressed: memory in older adults, vegetarians (lower baseline), sleep deprivation and metabolic/oxygen stress. In young, rested, omnivorous adults the largest RCT (N=123) found only a small, borderline effect and no vegetarian advantage, and a broad review confirms benefits shrink to near-zero without a deficit. The viral "single 0.35 g/kg megadose before an all-nighter" comes from one N=15 study.

11. Whether you "respond" depends on your baseline — meat-eaters with full stores respond least

Muscle creatine uptake is inversely related to starting level: people with low baseline stores gain the most, those already saturated (regular red-meat/fish eaters) gain the least. Performance improvement scales with how much creatine the muscle actually takes up. This is why vegetarians and vegans are the biggest responders (diet-poor baseline).

12. Women benefit and it is safe — and they may be an under-served population

Women have ~70–80% lower endogenous creatine stores than men, and the evidence in women is favorable: a 2026 meta of postmenopausal RCTs found +0.37 kg lean mass and +7.5 kg leg-press 1RM when ≥5 g/day is combined with resistance training, vulnerable older women improved lean mass/function with creatine + RT, and the female-safety meta found no serious adverse events. There is no evidence creatine disrupts female sex hormones.

Tier 3 — Promising but preliminary, or conditional (7 findings)

13. Depression: an antidepressant adjunct signal in women — but not a standalone treatment, and a bipolar caution

The strongest data are for augmentation: adding 5 g/day creatine to an SSRI accelerated and deepened the response in women with major depression (greater HAM-D improvement from week 2), consistent with a brain-bioenergetics rationale and an inverse dietary-creatine/depression association in NHANES. But this is adjunct-to-medication in women, not a monotherapy, and an open-label study saw 2/2 bipolar patients switch into hypomania — a real safety flag.

14. Blood sugar: creatine helps glycemic control only WITH exercise, not on its own

The single strongest human trial found creatine + exercise cut HbA1c by 1.1% in type-2 diabetics (7.4→6.4 vs placebo 7.5→7.6) and raised GLUT-4 translocation — but the benefit is exercise-dependent: meta-analyses of creatine without an exercise co-intervention find no effect on fasting glucose, HbA1c or insulin resistance.

15. Fatigue / long-COVID: an early, promising but thin signal

Small trials suggest 6 g/day reduces fatigue and raises grip strength in post-COVID condition and that months of creatine raise tissue creatine while easing symptoms — but these are small (N=12–67), short, and mostly single-blind. Promising, not established.

16. Bone: a partial, geometry-level benefit with training — not an osteoporosis cure

The best bone trial (12 months, postmenopausal women + resistance training) found creatine attenuated femoral-neck BMD loss (−1.2% vs −3.9% placebo) and improved hip bone geometry (a bending-strength predictor), with a small regional effect in older men. But whole-body/lumbar BMD did not rise, the 2026 meta found bone density unchanged overall, a 1 g/day no-training trial was null, and reviews decline to recommend creatine as an osteoporosis therapy.

17. Immune/inflammation: an acute post-exertion blunting, but no chronic anti-inflammatory effect

Creatine loading before hard endurance events blunts the acute post-exercise rise in inflammatory cytokines, but a 2026 meta of double-blind RCTs found no significant reduction in resting CRP, IL-6 or TNF-α. It is not an anti-inflammatory supplement.

18. Brain injury: mechanistically promising, but the human evidence is one small pediatric study

An open-label pediatric TBI trial found faster recovery on creatine, and reviews call the neuroprotection direction promising, but there is no adult concussion/TBI RCT — this remains hypothesis-level.

19. The "caffeine cancels creatine" rule is one 1996 study — reviews say co-use is fine

The claim traces to a single N=9 crossover where caffeine abolished the performance gain; systematic reviews since find caffeine does not impair creatine loading, retention or benefit, and everyday pre-workout co-use is fine.

Tier 4 — Myths, misconceptions, and marketing (8 findings)

20. "Creatine is a steroid / a banned PED" — false

It is a naturally occurring amino-acid derivative found in meat and fish, not a hormone; it is not on any banned list[S6-context]. The only doping-adjacent concern is contamination of cheap products (#28), not creatine itself.

21. "Creatine wrecks your kidneys" — the serum-creatinine artifact, not real damage

A higher creatinine reading reflects creatine → creatinine conversion, not lost filtration; measured-GFR studies and meta-analyses show no renal decline in healthy people or even CKD patients.

22. "Water bloat you can't lose" — the water is inside the muscle, and it reverses

The water creatine retains is intracellular (in muscle cells), not subcutaneous edema, so it does not read as a "puffy" look, and stores (and the water) decline to baseline within ~4 weeks of stopping.

23. "You must cycle creatine" — no

There is no physiological basis for cycling; continuous 3–5 g/day simply keeps stores saturated.

24. "Creatine causes hair loss / baldness" — one DHT study, never measured hair, direct trial null

See #7: the scare is a single unreplicated DHT finding with no hair endpoint; the only trial that actually measured hair found nothing.

25. "Bad for teenagers" — no evidence of harm in active youth

A review of adolescent/youth data found a strong safety profile with no adverse renal/hepatic/health markers; a blanket prohibition is not evidence-based.

26. "Vegetarians don't need it" — backwards; they respond the MOST

Because dietary creatine comes almost entirely from meat and fish, vegetarians have lower baseline stores and are the biggest responders for both muscle and cognition.

27. Cardiac and cancer-cachexia claims failed in trials

Creatine improved skeletal-muscle endurance but not heart function in heart-failure trials, added nothing to cardiac rehab, and a 263-patient NCI trial found no benefit for cancer anorexia/weight-loss syndrome. Not every "promising" clinical use panned out.

Practical — what to actually do (3 findings)

28. What actually matters: 3–5 g/day monohydrate, daily, consistently, third-party tested — paired with training

The evidence-based protocol is simple and cheap: creatine monohydrate, 3–5 g every day (no loading or cycling needed — loading just speeds saturation), taken consistently, paired with resistance training for the muscle benefit. Buy a third-party-tested product (Informed-Sport / Creapure) because ~15% of loosely-regulated supplements have been found contaminated with undeclared substances and cheap creatine can carry impurities.

29. The mechanism links creatine to glycine and (mostly) to methylation

Creatine is synthesized in the body from glycine + arginine + methionine via AGAT/GAMT. The whole glycine molecule is consumed, but glycine is readily made, so the dominant metabolic cost of endogenous synthesis is methyl groups — about 40% of the body's SAM-derived labile methyl groups — plus 20–30% of arginine's amidino groups. Supplementing creatine spares this synthesis load (which is why vegetarians, who must make nearly all their own, respond most).

30. Honest COI framing: most pro-creatine research is industry/ISSN-linked — but the safety core is independently corroborated

A large share of positive creatine studies come from ISSN-affiliated, supplement-industry-funded labs, which is a real reason for caution on effect sizes and enthusiasm. But the load-bearing safety conclusions are backed by independent work — the kidney meta-analyses, the female-safety meta, the null cognition RCT, and the failed cachexia/cardiac trials — so "creatine is safe and works with training" does not rest on industry evidence alone.

Deepen pass (2026-07-23) — additional findings (11 findings)

31. Creatine is genuinely disease-modifying in the inborn creatine-synthesis disorders — but not the transporter defect, and not common neurodegeneration

The one setting where creatine is a real therapy, not a supplement, is the rare inborn errors of creatine metabolism: GAMT and AGAT deficiency respond to oral creatine (better the earlier it starts), while the creatine-transporter (SLC6A8) defect does NOT respond — the transport step itself is broken. This is the mechanistic bookend to the failed common-disease trials (#32).

32. The big neurodegenerative-disease hopes FAILED in large independent trials

Creatine's most-hyped clinical promise — slowing neurodegeneration — did not survive the definitive trials: the NIH NET-PD LS-1 Parkinson's RCT (N=1,741, 5 g/day) was stopped for futility, and CREST-E in Huntington's (N=553, up to 40 g/day) was halted for futility with numerically higher mortality on creatine; a PD meta-analysis and the ALS trials agree. A review from within the field calls broad neuroprotection "end of story".

33. In muscle-wasting disease it gives a real symptomatic strength gain — but only some kinds

A Cochrane review found creatine improves muscle strength in muscular dystrophies and inflammatory myopathy (symptomatic benefit, high-quality evidence) but not in metabolic myopathies (possible worsening), consistent with an older crossover trial across mixed neuromuscular disease. Symptomatic, not disease-modifying.

34. The authorities are skeptical about the brain-cognition claim

Against the popular "creatine sharpens your brain" narrative, EFSA ruled in 2024 that a cause-and-effect relationship with improved cognition is NOT established, a 2024 systematic review found the research "fails to support the theoretical basis" for a cognitive effect, and even leading creatine advocates now warn the brain hype has outrun the trials ("cart before the horse"). This sharpens finding #10: real only in deficit/stress states, unproven as a general cognitive enhancer.

35. The depression signal firmed up; the bipolar caution got an RCT

A 2025 meta-analysis found creatine reduced depressive symptoms across trials, and a 2026 systematic review confirms adjunctive depression is the strongest mental-health signal (anxiety/PTSD/others sparse) — but a bipolar RCT found creatine did not beat placebo on mood, reinforcing the bipolar mood-switch caution from #13.

36. Uptake is boosted by carbohydrate/protein co-ingestion; high-dose loading adds nothing in trained athletes

Co-ingesting ~90 g carbohydrate (or protein+carb) with creatine raises muscle uptake up to ~60% via insulin — a real timing lever if you want faster saturation. But dose is not magic: a GRADE dose-response meta found only a modest dose relationship (mostly with training), and 20 g/day loading gave no benefit in already-trained cyclists. A small pilot hints pre-workout timing edges out post.

37. The "poor absorption" premise behind premium forms is false — and dissolved creatine decays to creatinine

Monohydrate is near-completely bioavailable, so the marketing rationale for "better-absorbed" forms is empty (reinforces #9). A practical corollary: creatine dissolved in liquid degrades to inactive creatinine over time (faster in acid/heat) — the chemistry behind why some gummies and pre-mixed drinks under-deliver; take it as powder, mixed fresh.

38. Sleep and recovery: a modest, mixed signal — and "creatine lets you sleep less" is animal-only

Creatine may modestly increase sleep duration/subjective quality and lowers post-exercise creatine kinase, but objective sleep architecture was unchanged in the best-controlled human trial, a recovery RCT was null, and the direct HRV data are one trial. The striking "reduces sleep need" finding is rats only; the human sleep-deprivation benefit is cognitive resilience, not less sleep.

39. Metabolic/liver: fatty-liver benefit is preclinical only, and creatine is not a fat-loss or metabolic-rate aid on its own

The NAFLD story is entirely animal/cell (rats, hepatocytes) with the reviews themselves flagging no human trial (and it failed for alcoholic steatosis); in humans, creatine did not even raise GLUT-4. For fat: creatine + training shaves body-fat percentage slightly but not absolute fat mass, does not raise resting metabolic rate on its own, and does not cause fat loss during a calorie deficit.

40. Bone: the two 2-year RCTs were NULL — no osteoporosis-therapy claim; and no problematic bloating in women

The one positive bone result (12-month hip geometry, #16) is outweighed by two 2-year RCTs that found no BMD benefit — a 237-woman training trial and a 200-woman low-dose trial — so creatine is not an osteoporosis therapy (as #16 already flagged). Separately, a menstrual-phase RCT found loading shifts intracellular water without problematic redistribution, refuting the "creatine bloats women" fear.

41. Human pregnancy: a real observational signal, but no supplementation trial — hypothesis, not a recommendation

Human cohorts link lower maternal creatine to lower fetal growth, and the biology is plausible, but there is still no human pregnancy supplementation RCT — so maternal creatine is a promising research hypothesis, not a recommendation for pregnant women.

docs.title: Test yourself
docs.text:
Twelve questions drawn at random from the findings above. Pick an answer, see why, and learn. Replayable, and your best score is remembered on this device.

  1. Delpino FM, et al. (2022) Nutrition 103-104:111791. Meta of 35 RCTs / 1,192 people: lean mass +1.10 kg with resistance training, +0.03 kg (NS) without. DOI 10.1016/j.nut.2022.111791 · PMID 35986981. ↩↩↩↩↩↩

  2. Chilibeck PD, et al. (2017) Open Access J Sports Med 8:213-226. Meta of 22 RCTs / 721 older adults: +1.37 kg lean mass with resistance training. DOI 10.2147/OAJSM.S123529 · PMID 29138605. Authors declare no COI. ↩↩↩

  3. Devries MC, Phillips SM (2014) Med Sci Sports Exerc 46(6):1194-1203. Meta, 357 older adults: greater lean-mass/strength gains with creatine + RT. DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000000220 · PMID 24576864. ↩

  4. Lanhers C, et al. (2015) Sports Med 45(9):1285-1294. Meta-analysis: creatine increases lower-limb strength. DOI 10.1007/s40279-015-0337-4 · PMID 25946994. ↩

  5. Lanhers C, et al. (2017) Sports Med 47(1):163-173. Meta-analysis: creatine increases upper-limb strength. DOI 10.1007/s40279-016-0571-4 · PMID 27328852. ↩

  6. Rawson ES, Volek JS (2003) J Strength Cond Res 17(4):822-831. Review of 22 RCTs: ~8% greater strength and ~14% greater weightlifting-performance vs RT alone. PMID 14636102. ↩

  7. Branch JD (2003) Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 13(2):198-226. Meta-analysis (~100 effect sizes): small-to-moderate effect on body composition and high-intensity performance. DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.13.2.198 · PMID 12945830. ↩

  8. Volek JS, et al. (1999) Med Sci Sports Exerc 31(8):1147-1156. RCT + biopsies: increased Type I/IIa/IIx fiber cross-sectional area beyond placebo. PMID 10449017. ↩

  9. Burke DG, et al. (2003) Med Sci Sports Exerc 35(11):1946-1955. RCT in vegetarians vs omnivores: vegetarians (lower baseline) gained more muscle creatine and lean mass. PMID 14600563. ↩↩↩

  10. Olsen S, et al. (2006) J Physiol 573(Pt 2):525-534. RCT + biopsies: augmented satellite-cell and myonuclei accretion — true remodeling. PMID 16581862. ↩

  11. Safdar A, et al. (2008) Physiol Genomics 32(2):219-228. Human gene-expression: creatine upregulated cytoskeletal/glycogen/protein-synthesis genes. PMID 17957000. ↩

  12. Powers ME, et al. (2003) J Athl Train 38(1):44-50. Creatine raised total body water but preserved the intracellular:extracellular ratio — the water is intracellular, not bloat. PMID 12937471. ↩↩↩↩
