  13. Desai I, et al. (2025) Nutrients 17(6):1081. RCT, N=63, with wash-in: the +0.51 kg early gain was largely water; no lean-mass benefit beyond RT thereafter. DOI 10.3390/nu17061081 · PMID 40292479. ↩↩

  14. de Souza e Silva A, et al. (2019) J Ren Nutr 29(6):480-489. Meta-analysis: creatine mildly raises serum creatinine (the artifact) but "does not induce renal damage." DOI 10.1053/j.jrn.2019.05.004 · PMID 31375416. ↩↩↩↩↩

  15. Antonio J, et al. (2021) J Int Soc Sports Nutr 18(1):13. "Common questions and misconceptions": rebuts kidney/hair/dehydration myths; explains the creatinine artifact. DOI 10.1186/s12970-021-00412-w · PMID 33557850. ISSN. ↩

docs.title: Magnesium: What It Actually Does vs What People Think
docs.text:
An essential mineral with a genuinely real dietary gap — where almost every benefit turns out to be deficiency-correction, the strongest evidence is for a use nobody buys a supplement for, and the popular claims mostly don't survive.

Independent research, 14 August 2026. 151 cited sources (147 PubMed-verified — every PMID title-matched against PubMed). Not medical advice.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Bottom line

Magnesium is an essential mineral with a genuinely real dietary gap — but almost every benefit is deficiency-correction, not "boosting." Its strongest evidence is intravenous hospital medicine (the opposite of what supplements are sold for), and the popular claims you actually buy it for — cramps, the "sleep form," testosterone — are weak or refuted. Status predicts health; a pill mostly helps if you're low.

Myths vs. reality

The claim you've heard What the evidence actually shows "Everyone is magnesium deficient" Half of adults under-eat it (a real gap), but only ~2–15% are clinically deficient — the scary figure conflates the two "Magnesium stops muscle cramps" Refuted for adult leg cramps (Cochrane + independent trials null); the one positive trial was manufacturer-funded "Magnesium glycinate is the sleep form" Zero head-to-head evidence any form beats another for sleep; the clean bisglycinate trial was barely significant "It boosts testosterone" One flawed 2011 trial with no real placebo; ZMA is a clean null; no regulator recognizes the claim "Rub on magnesium oil / soak in Epsom salts" The one skin-cream trial missed significance; the Epsom claim was never peer-reviewed "Take it for your heart" Its strongest evidence is IV magnesium in the hospital (eclampsia, torsades); oral heart benefit is small and deficiency-gated "Magnesium oxide is useless" Poorly absorbed (~4%), but a genuine, guideline-recommended constipation laxative

What you actually learn

  • The best magnesium evidence is intravenous, in a hospital — halving eclampsia seizures, protecting preterm babies' brains, stopping a lethal heart rhythm — not a daily capsule.
  • The dietary gap is real (unlike vitamin D's cutoff artifact): ~half of adults under-eat magnesium, and blood tests genuinely miss tissue depletion.
  • Almost every oral benefit is deficiency-correction — blood pressure, blood sugar and mortality signals all concentrate in the deficient or diseased, and "more is better" is false (risk is U-shaped).
  • The consumer claims mostly fail: cramps refuted, "glycinate for sleep" unproven, L-threonate is rodent + industry data, testosterone and transdermal are myths.
  • One under-sold real use: magnesium oxide is a legitimate constipation laxative.

What this means for you

  • Eat magnesium before you supplement it — leafy greens, pumpkin seeds, almonds, legumes, whole grains and dark chocolate close most of the gap.
  • Supplement only for a real reason: a plausible intake gap, or a depleting condition (type 2 diabetes, heavy alcohol, long-term acid-blockers or diuretics, heavy sweating).
  • If you do: a modest dose (~200 mg), citrate or glycinate, with food, split if it loosens your stool — don't pay for exotic forms.
  • Don't take it for cramps, testosterone, "detox," or because a particular form is marketed as a sleep drug.
  • Check with a clinician first if you have kidney disease or take regular medication.

TL;DR

Magnesium is essential, and unlike vitamin D the dietary shortfall is real — roughly half of adults fall below the intake reference8. But the discipline is the same: almost every benefit is deficiency-correction, not "boosting." The strongest, cleanest evidence in the whole field is intravenous magnesium as hospital medicine — halving eclampsia seizures3, protecting preterm babies' brains at the highest grade of evidence7, stopping a lethal heart rhythm5 — the exact opposite of what supplements are sold for. Real but deficiency-gated oral wins: blood pressure (only in the hypomagnesemic, ~null in normotensives)27, type 2 diabetes (from dietary intake, not pills)28, constipation (magnesium oxide is a guideline-recommended laxative)21, and modest migraine prevention37. Refuted or unproven: leg cramps12, "magnesium glycinate is the sleep form"45, L-threonate for the brain46, testosterone55, ZMA57, transdermal "magnesium oil"59 and Epsom-salt "detox." Your magnesium status strongly predicts health; a pill mostly helps you if you're actually low.

The picture, ranked by how strongly the evidence agrees

Tier 1 (settled): IV magnesium is real emergency medicine · the dietary gap is real but "everyone is clinically deficient" is not · leg cramps refuted · magnesium oxide is a genuine laxative · safety is a kidney question. Tier 2 (real but deficiency-gated): blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, migraine, depression, depletion from PPIs/diuretics — all concentrated in the deficient or diseased. Tier 3 (weak/unproven): sleep, the "glycinate" form, L-threonate cognition, anxiety, bone, athletic performance, PMS, ADHD. Tier 4 (myths): testosterone boost, ZMA, transdermal oil, Epsom "detox," "your food has no magnesium anymore."

docs.title: What this review covered
docs.text: Magnesium is one of the most claim-laden supplements on the shelf: "everyone's deficient," "glycinate is the sleep form," "it stops cramps," "it boosts testosterone," "spray it on your skin," "soak in an Epsom bath." Two structured evidence sweeps (a broad core pass and a deepen pass for the newest 2024–26 trials and industry-independent replications) tested each claim against the peer-reviewed literature — meta-analyses, randomized trials, Mendelian-randomization studies and large cohorts. Every one of the 147 PubMed citations was title-matched against PubMed before use. The result is a genuinely different shape from the vitamin D story, and it's worth being precise about how it differs.

docs.title: Tier 1 — The strongest evidence
docs.text:
Magnesium is genuinely essential, and blood tests hide most of it. It's a cofactor for over 600 enzymes, and ATP only works as Mg-ATP1. About 99% of your magnesium is inside cells and bone; only ~1% is in the blood, where it's tightly defended — so a "normal" serum magnesium can't rule out tissue depletion2. That measurement gap is why intake and status keep looking more important than supplement trials do.

The best magnesium evidence is intravenous, in a hospital — not a pill. IV magnesium sulfate more than halves eclampsia seizures in pregnancy (the 10,141-woman MAGPIE trial, RR 0.42)3 and beats the standard anti-seizure drugs for recurrence4; it's first-line for torsades de pointes, a dangerous heart rhythm, even when blood magnesium is normal5; and it's a proven add-on in severe asthma attacks6. The single highest-certainty magnesium indication anywhere is antenatal magnesium to protect preterm babies' brains — the updated Cochrane review grades it HIGH: cerebral palsy down 29%, severe brain hemorrhage down 24%7. None of this is a daily capsule. The irony is worth saying plainly: magnesium's best evidence is for uses almost nobody buys a supplement for.

The dietary gap is real — which is the key difference from vitamin D. About 68% of US adults consume less than the magnesium reference intake89. Unlike vitamin D's "everyone is deficient" scare (which was mostly a moved goalpost), this is a genuine dietary shortfall.

But "everyone is clinically deficient" still overstates it. Actual measured low blood magnesium is only ~2–15% of the general population10 — higher in type 2 diabetes (~32%)11, intensive care, and people on certain drugs. The scary figure conflates "not eating the recommended amount" with "clinically deficient."

Leg cramps — the flagship reason people take it — is refuted. The Cochrane review (11 trials) found magnesium "unlikely to provide clinically meaningful" cramp relief12, an independent trial in a major journal was null13, and so was an independent 2026 trial (compression stockings worked; magnesium didn't)14. The one clearly positive cramp trial was funded by the product's manufacturer15. It survives only for pregnancy cramps.

Safety is a kidney story, not a poison story. The famous 350 mg/day ceiling is the diarrhea threshold for supplements, not a toxic dose, and food magnesium has no limit — healthy kidneys just excrete the excess16. Genuinely dangerous magnesium build-up happens almost only with impaired kidneys plus magnesium-containing laxatives or antacids1718.

One oral use marketing under-sells: constipation. Magnesium oxide (~1.5 g/day) roughly tripled the response rate over placebo and matched a stimulant laxative in double-blind trials1920, and it's now conditionally recommended in the 2023 gastroenterology guideline21. This is a plumbing (osmotic) effect in the gut that works whether or not you're deficient.

Forms matter less than folklore says. Magnesium oxide is poorly absorbed (~4%)22 — inefficient, but not "useless," since it's ~60% elemental magnesium. Citrate and chelated forms absorb better than oxide23, yet the differences between forms shrink at steady state when you take them with food24 — and "premium" liposomal magnesium showed no absorption advantage even in its own maker's trial25.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Real but bounded (all deficiency-gated)
docs.text:
Blood pressure: a small drop, and only where there's a deficit. Supplements lower blood pressure ~2 mmHg on average26, and the 2025 meta-analysis pinned it down: up to −7.7 mmHg in medicated hypertensives and −6 in the magnesium-deficient, but essentially nothing in normotensive, replete adults, and bigger at ≥400 mg/day27.

Type 2 diabetes: the food, not the pill. Higher dietary magnesium robustly predicts lower diabetes risk (−14% per 100 mg/day)28, but supplements barely move glucose (fasting glucose −0.58 mmol/L, HbA1c ~−0.16%)29, and the largest 2026 insulin-resistance meta-analysis was actually null, with the effect depending on your baseline30.

The cardiovascular story is genuinely contested. Mendelian randomization once supported a causal effect on ischemic stroke31, but composite cardiovascular disease is null in dose-response meta-analysis32, and — the tell — dietary magnesium tracks lower mortality while supplemental magnesium shows nothing33, the classic signature of a nutrient that marks a healthier overall diet. In 1.28 million diabetic veterans, benefit was deficiency-gated and risk was U-shaped (both low and high were harmful; replacement helped only the low)34. Meanwhile a magnesium-depletion score predicts ~2.5–2.9× mortality across many cohorts35 — a powerful marker that, as with omega-3, doesn't prove pills fix the outcome.

Migraine and depression: modest, and bounded. Oral magnesium has guideline-level (but dated) support for migraine prevention3637, though the definitive Cochrane review isn't finished38; depression shows a fragile pooled signal in diagnosed patients only, built on small trials — the most-cited of which was unblinded3940.

Depletion is real — and one drug reverses it. Long-term acid-blocking PPIs are linked to low magnesium41, as are diuretics, metformin and heavy drinking. Usefully, the newer SGLT2-inhibitor diabetes drugs do the opposite — they raise magnesium42.

docs.title: Tier 3 — Weak, unproven, or over-sold
docs.text:
Sleep — a small, deficiency-gated signal, and no "special form." The only meta-analysis found magnesium shortens time to fall asleep by ~17 minutes in older insomniacs but does not increase total sleep time, at low certainty4344. And the popular belief that magnesium glycinate is the sleep form has zero head-to-head evidence — the single clean bisglycinate trial was barely significant (p=0.049, tiny effect), and its responders were the people with low dietary magnesium45. The "glycinate for sleep" reputation borrows glycine's own separate story.

L-threonate for the brain — rodent data and manufacturer-funded trials. The brain-magnesium boost behind L-threonate is shown only in rats46; every positive human cognition or sleep trial is small and run or funded by the compound's commercial owner474849, and no independent human trial exists.

The rest of the Tier 3 list. Anxiety benefit appears only in already-anxious groups, at poor quality50. Higher magnesium tracks slightly better bone density but not fewer fractures51. No performance boost in athletes who aren't deficient52. PMS mood relief is unproven53, and Mendelian randomization is null for ADHD54.

docs.title: Tier 4 — Myths & marketing
docs.text:
"Boosts testosterone." The whole idea rests on one small 2011 trial with no real placebo, where testosterone rose even in the exercise-only group55; the proposed hormone mechanism was shown only in a test tube56. No regulator recognizes a testosterone claim.

ZMA. The best-designed trial found no effect on testosterone, body composition or strength57, replicated by independent 2024 crossovers58. The only positive study is non-indexed and co-authored by the ZMA patent-holder.

Transdermal "magnesium oil" and Epsom-salt "detox." The one human skin-cream trial missed significance on its main result59, and a review judged skin absorption unsupported60; the Epsom-bath claim was never peer-reviewed. Oral is the evidenced route.

"Your food has no magnesium anymore." The most-cited "declining nutrients" study never actually measured magnesium61, and the best critical review blames apparent declines on changed lab methods and crop breeding, not depleted soil62.

And the causal caveat that ties it together: the impressive observational links keep dissolving under Mendelian randomization — later, larger analyses find no causal magnesium effect on diabetes, heart disease, heart failure or atrial fibrillation63, against one earlier positive study64. Magnesium status is a great marker of health; supplementing it is mostly correcting a deficiency.

docs.title: Who actually benefits
docs.text:
• You probably don't need a pill if you eat leafy greens, nuts, seeds, legumes and whole grains — that closes most of the gap (magnesium is the atom at the center of chlorophyll).
  • Topping up is genuinely justified if you have a plausible intake gap, or a depleting condition: type 2 diabetes, heavy alcohol use, long-term PPI or diuretic use, or heavy sweating.
  • If you supplement: a modest dose (~200 mg elemental), citrate or glycinate, with food, split if it loosens your stool. Don't pay up for exotic forms.
  • Skip it for: cramps, testosterone, "detox," and the belief that a particular form is a sleep drug.

docs.title: The bottom line
docs.text:
Magnesium is a real mineral with a real dietary gap and a real place — just not the one the supplement aisle sells. Its best evidence is intravenous hospital medicine; its oral benefits are modest and concentrated in people who are actually low; and its headline consumer claims (cramps, the "sleep form," testosterone, transdermal) are weak or refuted. Eat the greens and nuts. If you have a plausible gap, a cheap citrate or glycinate with food is a sensible, low-risk top-up — for the gap, not the marketing.

Not medical advice. If you have kidney disease or take a PPI, diuretic or other regular medication, check with a clinician before supplementing.

docs.title: The full findings — all 35
docs.text:
Every conclusion this review reached, grouped by how strongly the evidence backs it. Each finding is distilled from the fully-cited evidence above.

Tier 1 — Settled: strongest, cleanest evidence (9 findings)

1. Magnesium is genuinely essential, and serum testing hides most of it.

Magnesium is a cofactor for over 600 enzymes and ATP is biologically active only as Mg-ATP. About 99% of body magnesium is intracellular (bone ~60%, soft tissue ~39%) and only ~1% is extracellular, with serum holding ~0.3% of the total — the anatomical reason a "normal" serum magnesium can't rule out tissue depletion.

2. The single strongest evidence in the whole field is IV magnesium as emergency medicine, not the supplement.

Intravenous magnesium sulfate more than halves eclampsia seizures (MAGPIE, N=10,141, RR 0.42), beats diazepam and phenytoin for recurrent eclamptic convulsions, is first-line for torsades de pointes even when serum magnesium is normal, and is a proven add-on in acute severe asthma. This is pharmacologic IV dosing under monitoring — the opposite end of the spectrum from a daily oral pill.

3. Antenatal magnesium for fetal neuroprotection is the highest-certainty magnesium indication on record.

The updated 2024 Cochrane review found antenatal magnesium sulfate cuts cerebral palsy (RR 0.71, HIGH grade) and severe intraventricular hemorrhage (RR 0.76) in babies at risk of preterm birth, reconfirmed by an independent 2025 meta-analysis.

4. Leg cramps — the flagship consumer claim — is refuted.

The Cochrane review (11 RCTs, N=735) found oral magnesium "unlikely to provide clinically meaningful" cramp prophylaxis, an independent JAMA Internal Medicine RCT was null, and so was an independent 2026 three-arm RCT (compression stockings worked; magnesium did not). The one clearly positive nocturnal-cramp trial was funded by the product's manufacturer. The effect survives only for pregnancy cramps, and even there trials split.

5. The dietary shortfall is real — which makes magnesium different from vitamin D.

Roughly half of Western adults consume less than the magnesium reference intake (in NHANES, 68% of US adults below the RDA, 19% below half). Unlike the vitamin-D "everyone is deficient" panic — which was mostly a cutoff artifact — the magnesium intake gap is a genuine dietary shortfall.

6. But "everyone is clinically deficient" still overstates it.

Measured hypomagnesemia (serum <0.75 mmol/L) is only ~2–15% of the general population — higher in type 2 diabetes (~32%), ICU, and PPI/diuretic users. The scary "everyone" figure conflates dietary-intake inadequacy with clinical deficiency, and no alternative status marker (RBC, ionized, the loading test) has a validated standardized cutoff.

7. Safety is a kidney story: the 350 mg ceiling is the diarrhea threshold, not a poison dose.

The 350 mg/day upper limit applies only to supplemental elemental magnesium and is set by the osmotic-diarrhea threshold, not systemic toxicity; food magnesium has no upper limit because healthy kidneys excrete the excess. Diarrhea is the dose-limiter. Dangerous hypermagnesemia is essentially a renal-impairment event — reduced kidney function plus magnesium-containing laxatives or antacids.

8. Magnesium oxide is a genuine, guideline-recommended laxative — a real oral use marketing under-sells.

Two double-blind RCTs found magnesium oxide (~1.5 g/day) roughly tripled the constipation-response rate over placebo and matched the stimulant laxative senna, and the 2023 AGA–ACG guideline conditionally recommends it for chronic idiopathic constipation. This is a lumen-level osmotic effect that works regardless of magnesium status — not deficiency correction.

9. Oxide is inefficiently absorbed but not "useless," and exotic forms matter less than folklore says.

Magnesium oxide's fractional absorption is only ~4%, far below soluble salts, but at ~60% elemental magnesium by weight it still delivers a usable amount. Citrate, chloride and chelates are better absorbed than oxide, yet a systematic review shows inter-form differences shrink at steady state when taken with food. "Premium" delivery forms don't reliably beat cheap salts — liposomal magnesium showed no absorption advantage even in its own maker's trial.

Tier 2 — Real but modest, and deficiency-gated (10 findings)

10. Blood pressure: a small drop, cleanly concentrated in deficiency and hypertension.

Magnesium supplements lower blood pressure only modestly (~2 mmHg average), and the 2025 Hypertension meta-analysis (38 RCTs) localized the effect sharply: SBP up to −7.7 mmHg in medicated hypertensives and −6 in the hypomagnesemic, but ~null in normotensive replete adults, and larger at ≥400 mg/day. (One 2024 meta found some effect in normotensives too, so this isn't unanimous.)

11. Higher dietary magnesium tracks lower type 2 diabetes — but supplements barely move glucose.

Dietary magnesium intake is consistently and dose-dependently associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk (RR 0.86 per 100 mg/day). Supplements produce small glycemic gains in diabetics (fasting glucose −0.58 mmol/L, HbA1c ~−0.16%), and the largest 2026 insulin-resistance meta-analysis was actually null, with the effect gated by baseline status.

12. The causal cardiovascular story is genuinely contested.

Mendelian randomization once supported a causal protective effect on ischemic (especially cardioembolic) stroke and coronary disease, but every later, larger MR analysis found no causal link to type 2 diabetes, coronary disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, or cardiac structure, leaving only a weak metabolic-syndrome signal. Composite CVD is null in dose-response meta-analysis.

13. Dietary magnesium lowers mortality; supplemental magnesium doesn't — the healthy-diet-marker tell.

In a 19-cohort dose-response meta-analysis (1.17M people), dietary magnesium tracked lower all-cause (0.87) and cancer (0.80) mortality, but supplemental and total magnesium showed no mortality benefit — the classic signature of a nutrient that partly marks a healthier overall diet rather than causing the benefit itself.

14. Benefit is deficiency-correction, not dose-response — and "more is better" is false.

In 1.28M diabetic US Veterans, magnesium–cardiovascular risk was U-shaped (both low AND high serum magnesium were harmful), and propensity-matched oral magnesium replacement cut cardiovascular events only in the hypomagnesemic (HR 0.89), not the normomagnesemic (HR 1.07).

15. Magnesium depletion status strongly predicts mortality — the biomarker-vs-supplement paradox.

A higher Magnesium Depletion Score (a kidney-reabsorption index, not a serum level) predicts roughly 2.5–2.9× all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, reproducibly across 10+ cohorts of older adults, cancer survivors, fatty-liver, diabetes and stroke. As with omega-3, status is a powerful predictor — which does not prove that supplements fix the outcome.

16. Migraine prophylaxis: guideline-level but modest, and the definitive review isn't in yet.

Oral magnesium (~600 mg/day, which exceeds the supplemental upper limit and causes diarrhea in some) has guideline-level support for migraine prevention (an American Academy of Neurology Level-B rating, since formally retired) and a 2025 dose-response signal. IV magnesium does not reliably abort an acute attack, and the definitive Cochrane review is still only a registered protocol.

17. Depression: a fragile signal in the already-diagnosed only.

Magnesium's antidepressant evidence is a statistically significant but fragile pooled effect in diagnosed depressed adults, built on few small, heterogeneous trials — the most-cited of which (Tarleton) was unblinded with no placebo. Independent meta-analyses give at most a tiny effect (SMD 0.16), and it is null for perinatal depression.

18. Real depletion drivers: PPIs, diuretics, metformin, alcohol.

Long-term proton-pump-inhibitor use is associated with hypomagnesemia (pooled OR ~1.43) via impaired intestinal uptake, strongest with concurrent diuretics, and PPI-induced hypomagnesemia still causes seizures and neurological syndromes. Loop/thiazide diuretics waste magnesium, metformin is an under-recognized driver, and alcohol depletion concentrates in drinkers with liver fibrosis or kidney impairment.

19. SGLT2 inhibitors raise magnesium — a genuinely new, direction-reversing drug fact.

Unlike PPIs, SGLT2-inhibitor diabetes drugs increase serum magnesium by ~0.07 mmol/L as a class effect, can correct hypomagnesemia even in non-diabetics and transplant patients, and have been used to treat refractory hypomagnesemia.

Tier 3 — Weak or unproven: marketing outruns the data (8 findings)

20. Sleep: a small, low-certainty signal for falling asleep faster in older insomniacs — and no more.

The only meta-analysis (3 RCTs, N=151 older adults) found magnesium cut sleep-onset latency ~17 minutes but did NOT change total sleep time, at low-to-very-low certainty. The foundational trial used poorly-absorbed oxide in 43 elderly insomniacs and showed no change in objective sleep time.

21. "Magnesium glycinate is special for sleep" has zero head-to-head evidence.

The single clean bisglycinate sleep RCT (N=155) was only marginally significant (ISI p=0.049, effect size d≈0.2, subjective-only), and its responders were the low-dietary-magnesium subgroup. No trial shows glycinate beats any other form for sleep — the "glycinate" reputation borrows glycine's own separate sleep story.

22. L-threonate cognition and sleep: rodent brain data, and every human trial is manufacturer-linked.

The brain-magnesium elevation behind L-threonate is shown only in rats — no human study has measured raised brain or CSF magnesium. Every positive human trial (MMFS-01 cognition, Magtein cognition, the threonate sleep RCT) is small and run or funded by the compound's commercial owner; there is still no independent human RCT, and threonate delivers little elemental magnesium per capsule.

23. Anxiety, cortisol and stress: suggestive only in vulnerable groups, unproven in healthy people.

Magnesium's anxiety benefit appears only in already-anxiety-vulnerable samples and the evidence quality is poor; no well-powered RCT shows it blunts the cortisol/stress response in replete, healthy adults, and the most-cited stress trial was industry-funded with no placebo.

24. Bone: higher intake tracks modestly higher density but not fewer fractures.

Higher magnesium intake is associated with slightly higher bone mineral density in observational cohorts (~3% in the WHI top-intake group) but NOT with lower fracture risk in that cohort or in meta-analysis; one cohort dissents, no RCT proves benefit, and Mendelian randomization even suggested lower lumbar bone density.

25. No ergogenic effect in already-replete athletes.

Any performance signal is confined to magnesium-deficient, older or untrained people; there is no good evidence of a supra-physiologic strength or endurance boost in replete athletes.

26. PMS mood is unproven; the menstrual signal is for period pain, not premenstrual mood.

Serum magnesium is not reliably lower in PMS, and a 2025 systematic review found insufficient evidence that magnesium relieves psychological PMS symptoms (the supporting evidence is one small 1991 trial). The better signal is for dysmenorrhea (period-cramp) pain.

27. ADHD: unproven, and Mendelian randomization is null.

Magnesium's ADHD evidence is low-quality and usually confounded by co-administered vitamin B6, and a 2025 Mendelian-randomization study found no causal magnesium effect on ADHD (it flagged a novel, watch-list magnesium–autism signal instead).

Tier 4 — Myths and refuted claims (4 findings)

28. "Magnesium boosts testosterone" rests on a single flawed trial.

The entire claim comes from one small 2011 trial with no true placebo arm and unreported baseline magnesium status, in which testosterone rose even in the exercise-only group — so exercise, not magnesium, plausibly drove it. The proposed SHBG-binding mechanism was shown only in a test tube, the human link is cross-sectional, and no regulator recognizes a testosterone claim. Only deficiency-correction is plausible.

29. ZMA is a clean null, replicated three times.

The best-designed ZMA (zinc-magnesium aspartate) trial found no effect on testosterone, body composition or strength, and two independent 2024 crossovers found no sleep or performance benefit either. The only positive ZMA study is non-indexed and co-authored by the ZMA patent-holder.

30. Transdermal "magnesium oil" and Epsom-salt "detox" are unproven.

The only human transdermal-cream pilot missed significance on its primary serum endpoint (p=0.29), reaching it only in a subgroup, and a topical-magnesium review judged skin absorption unsupported. The flagship Epsom-salt absorption claim was never peer-reviewed or indexed, and "detox" has no defined mechanism or endpoint. Oral remains the evidenced route.

31. "Your food has no magnesium anymore" (soil depletion) is mostly a mis-citation.

The most-cited "declining nutrients" study never actually measured magnesium, and the most rigorous review attributes apparent historical mineral declines mainly to changed analytical methods and high-yield-crop "dilution," not depleted soil. Some datasets show declines, but the confident claim outruns the data.

Practical — what to actually do (4 findings)

32. Food first — and it's easy to see where magnesium lives.

Magnesium is the central atom of chlorophyll, so leafy greens are rich, along with pumpkin seeds, almonds, legumes, whole grains and dark chocolate; refining strips ~80% of a grain's magnesium. A whole-food diet closes most of the intake gap.

33. If you supplement: citrate or glycinate, split-dosed, with food — don't chase exotic forms.

Aim for a modest elemental dose (~200 mg), take it with food and split it to blunt the laxative effect; citrate and bisglycinate are sensible, well-absorbed, well-tolerated picks, and form differences shrink at steady state. Oxide is fine only for cheap bulk dosing or when you actually want the laxative effect.

34. The real reason to top up is a plausible gap or a depleting condition — not the marketing claims.

Benefits cluster in people who are magnesium-insufficient or already symptomatic. A genuine intake gap (few greens/nuts/legumes), heavy sweating, or a depleting drug/condition (type 2 diabetes, alcohol, long-term PPI or diuretic use) is the evidence-based reason to supplement — not sleep, testosterone, or cramp marketing.

35. Stack cautions: spacing, kidneys, and drug interactions.

Space magnesium several hours from tetracycline/fluoroquinolone antibiotics and bisphosphonates (it chelates them); avoid magnesium-containing laxatives/antacids in kidney impairment (hypermagnesemia risk); expect more depletion on a PPI or diuretic — and note an SGLT2-inhibitor diabetes drug raises magnesium instead.

docs.title: Melatonin: What It Actually Does vs What People Think
docs.text:
A clock-shifting darkness signal that has been mis-sold as a sleeping pill. Almost every consumer error about melatonin, the dose, the timing and the disappointment, follows from that single category mistake.

Independent research, 9 September 2026. 139 cited sources; 223 PMIDs resolved and 193 title-matched claim/citation pairs verified against PubMed, 0 wrong. Not medical advice.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Bottom line

*Melatonin is a clock-shifting darkness signal, not a sleeping pill. As a sleep aid it buys you about 4 to 7 minutes, which is why sleep doctors formally recommend against it for insomnia; as a tool for a timing problem such as jet lag or a delayed sleep phase it genuinely works. Timing matters far more than milligrams, mistimed melatonin shifts your clock the wrong way, and the usual 3 to 10 mg dose is 10 to 100 times more than your body ever makes at night.*

Myths vs. reality

The claim you've heard What the evidence actually shows "Melatonin is a natural sleeping pill" It is a timing signal. The measured hypnotic effect is 4 to 7 minutes off sleep latency, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends clinicians NOT use it for chronic insomnia "Take more for a stronger effect" 0.5 mg equals 3.0 mg when each is given at its own optimal time; the clock responds to timing, not dose. One blind patient entrained on 0.5 mg and failed on 10 and 20 mg "Take it 30 minutes before bed" Bedtime is the phase-shifting dead zone. For a real clock shift the dose belongs hours earlier, and morning melatonin actively shifts your clock the wrong way "It stops your body making its own" Refuted by every study that measured it. Half a milligram for a week, and even 50 mg a day for 37 days, left natural production unchanged. It moves your rhythm, it does not switch off your pineal gland "Your melatonin collapses as you age, so replace it" In healthy older adults, melatonin was indistinguishable from young adults on every measure. What shifts with age is the timing of the peak, not the amount "I'm low in melatonin, so I should supplement" In the largest trial to test it, low melatonin did not predict who responded. Age did "It's natural, so it's harmless" The FDA's own survey found products at 0 to 667 percent of their label, and melatonin measurably impairs glucose tolerance in carriers of a common gene variant "Melatonin is an antioxidant that fights cancer and ageing" No human longevity trial exists. That literature is preclinical and unusually retraction-prone, and the famous cancer-survival result came from unblinded trials at a single hospital "Blue-blocking glasses fix your sleep" Evening light really does suppress melatonin, but the blue-blocker trials are null, and Cochrane found no trial evidence at all linking these lenses to melatonin levels "It's banned across Europe" Prescription-only in the UK, Australia and Switzerland, but legally sold as a low-dose supplement in Spain, Italy, France, Poland, Portugal and Belgium

What you actually learn

  • The category error is the whole story. Melatonin was studied as a clock-shifter and sold as a sedative. Once you see that, the dose confusion, the timing confusion and the disappointment all follow.
  • Timing beats dose, and it is not close. The size of the clock shift tracks when you take it at r-squared 0.94, while doubling or sextupling the dose changes almost nothing.
  • Mistimed melatonin is worse than none. Morning dosing pushes your clock later, and the Cochrane jet-lag review warns it delays adaptation.
  • The best uses are narrow and real: jet lag, a genuinely delayed sleep phase, and non-24-hour rhythm in blind people, where it is the single strongest treatment available.
  • The scary claims and the real risk are different things. "It stops your own production" and "it delays puberty" do not hold up in humans. What does hold up is a measurable hit to glucose tolerance, and a product where half the bottles miss their label, usually by containing too much.
  • The strongest sleep lever in this whole topic is free: ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99 percent of people tested.

What this means for you

  • If you sleep badly in general, melatonin is the wrong tool. The guideline-backed answer for chronic insomnia is cognitive behavioural therapy, and melatonin is specifically recommended against.
  • If you are crossing time zones or your body clock genuinely runs late, it is the right tool - and it works at a small dose.
  • Use 0.3 to 1 mg, not 5 or 10. Higher doses mostly extend the signal into your morning, which is the opposite of what you want.
  • Take it hours before your target bedtime for a clock shift, not minutes before, and never in the morning.
  • Buy only a USP Verified or NSF-certified product. Half of surveyed products miss their label and the usual error is too much, not too little.
  • Do not take it right before eating. Melatonin impairs glucose handling, sharply so if you carry the common MTNR1B variant.
  • Get the light right first. Dimming the room in the evening moves your own melatonin more reliably than a tablet does.

TL;DR

Melatonin is a timing signal, not a sedative12. As a sleeping pill its effect is real but trivial: 4 to 7 minutes off sleep-onset latency78, which is why the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends clinicians not use it for chronic insomnia11 and why three independent network meta-analyses rank it below the prescription hypnotics121314. As a chronobiotic it genuinely works: jet lag with a number needed to treat of 222, delayed sleep-wake phase disorder34, and non-24-hour rhythm in totally blind people36. The mechanism is timing - the melatonin phase-response curve runs about 12 hours out of phase with the light curve17, the phase advance tracks administration time at r-squared 0.9419, and mistimed melatonin shifts the clock the wrong way1822. Three popular claims are refuted: it does not suppress your own production7879, melatonin does not decline with healthy ageing80, and being "low in melatonin" did not predict who responds48. The real risks are not where people look: the FDA's own survey found products at 0% to 667% of label27, and melatonin measurably impairs glucose tolerance, concentrated in carriers of a common genetic variant5354.

The picture, ranked by how strongly the evidence agrees

  • Settled: weak hypnotic (4-7 min), real chronobiotic, timing dominates dose, retail doses are supraphysiological, product labels are unreliable.
  • Well supported: jet lag, delayed sleep phase, blind non-24, larger effects in children but at very low certainty.
  • Contested: the glucose effect's long-term meaning, and every "no tolerance, no withdrawal" claim, which rests almost entirely on manufacturer-authored studies.
  • Refuted or preclinical: endogenous suppression, age-related decline, "low melatonin" predicting response, antioxidant and anti-cancer and longevity claims, and blue-blocking glasses fixing sleep.

docs.title: What this review covered
docs.text: Seven parallel evidence sweeps: foundations and pharmacology; sleep efficacy in insomnia and healthy sleepers; circadian uses (jet lag, shift work, delayed sleep phase, blindness); dose, timing, tolerance and dependence; safety, hormones and children; product quality and regulation; and the beyond-sleep claims. Every PubMed-indexed citation was then independently title-matched against the PubMed summary API before publication.

docs.title: Tier 1 - The strongest, settled evidence
docs.text:
Melatonin is a darkness signal with two separable actions. A chronobiotic action that shifts and entrains the body clock, which is overwhelmingly timing-dependent, and a much weaker hypnotic action producing mild sleepiness and a small drop in core temperature12. Its production is gated by darkness under control of the body clock34, and its onset in dim light is the accepted marker of circadian phase5. Both actions run through the same two high-affinity receptors, MT1 and MT26. Marketing sells the second action while borrowing the credibility of the first.

As a sleeping pill, the number is 4 to 7 minutes. Two independent meta-analyses agree: -4.0 minutes and -7.06 minutes of sleep-onset latency78. Total sleep time gains 8 to 13 minutes, with lower confidence bounds under 3 minutes87. Sleep efficiency moves about 2%, and one umbrella review found it not significant at all9. One independently funded meta-analysis shows the whole story inside a single dataset: -7.2 minutes for insomnia, but -38.8 minutes for delayed sleep phase syndrome10. The authors of the most-cited meta-analysis describe their own result as modest.

The professional guideline recommends against it, and the head-to-head evidence agrees. The AASM suggests clinicians not use melatonin for sleep-onset or sleep-maintenance insomnia in adults, placing it alongside valerian and diphenhydramine11. The largest network meta-analysis, covering 154 trials and 44,089 participants and publicly funded, found melatonin "did not show overall material benefits"12, and two further independent network meta-analyses reach the same ranking1314. An age-stratified meta-analysis found it not significantly effective in adults at all15. Even the closest comparator drug, ramelteon, moves latency only 4.3 minutes16.

Timing is the mechanism; dose is the wrong lever. The melatonin phase-response curve runs roughly 12 hours out of phase with the light curve17. For 3 mg, maximum clock advance comes about 5 hours before dim-light melatonin onset and maximum delay about 11 hours after it, with a dead zone across the first half of habitual sleep18. The size of the phase advance correlates with administration time at r-squared 0.94 while 0.3 mg and 3.0 mg do not separate19; in children, circadian timing predicted the effect and dose did not20; and 0.5 mg equals 3.0 mg when each is given at its own optimal time21.

Mistimed melatonin makes things worse, so the worst case is not "nothing happens". Morning dosing falls in the delay region of the curve18, and the Cochrane review warns explicitly that early-day dosing causes sleepiness and delays adaptation22.

Retail doses are supraphysiological by one to two orders of magnitude. Only 0.1-0.3 mg produces peaks inside the normal nocturnal range23, oral bioavailability is about 15% with a 45-minute half-life2425, and pharmacological doses measurably degrade vigilance while circulating26.

The product is unreliable, and the dominant error is overdosing. The FDA's own laboratory survey of 110 products marketed to children found content spanning 0% to 667% of label, half outside an acceptable range, and doses reaching 50 mg per serving27. In US gummies, 88% were inaccurately labelled at 74-347% of label28. The original Canadian survey found -83% to +478% of label with up to 465% lot-to-lot variation inside a single product29.

Evening light suppresses melatonin more easily than most people assume. Roughly half the suppressing effect of 9,000 lux bright light is reached at about 100 lux30, and ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99.0% of 116 people31.

docs.title: Tier 2 - Real, with limits
docs.text:
Jet lag is the best-replicated use, with a number needed to treat of 222, confirmed by a newer meta-analysis showing similar benefit eastbound and westbound32 - so the folk rule that it only helps flying east is wrong, even though jet lag itself is worse eastward because the human clock runs at 24.18 hours33.

Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder moves the clock about an hour while total sleep time does not change34 - the chronobiotic signature in one sentence. The largest single trial found a smaller effect and no between-group circadian shift35.

Non-24-hour rhythm in totally blind people is the strongest indication of all: six of seven free-running subjects entrained36, at doses as low as 300 micrograms37. The prescription receptor agonist in this indication works but entrains only a minority, and its evidence is entirely manufacturer-funded38.

Shift work is the weakest circadian use: about 24 extra minutes of daytime sleep, graded low quality, with no meaningful reduction in sleepiness39.

Guidelines encode timing, not dose4041, and the same body that recommends against melatonin for insomnia endorses it, weakly, for circadian disorders1140.

Children show larger effects at much lower certainty. Total sleep time +30 minutes and latency -18 minutes42 - three to four times the adult effect43 - but the independently funded panel graded certainty very low, found non-serious adverse events tripled, and concluded melatonin "should never be the first choice"42. An independent trial found children gained little additional sleep because they woke earlier too44. In autism the pooled effects are large but heterogeneity reaches 94%45, and in ADHD melatonin shifts sleep timing without improving behaviour, cognition or quality of life46.

The regulator that approved it recorded a small effect: prolonged-release melatonin is licensed only for the over-55s, short-term, up to 13 weeks, and the manufacturer's own trials show a net benefit of about 11 minutes4748, with the independent meta finding even less49. Dose-response for sleep peaks near 4 mg and roughly 3 hours before bed may beat 30 minutes505152.

docs.title: Tier 3 - Contested, or resting on the manufacturer
docs.text:
The glucose effect is the under-appreciated real risk. 5 mg taken before a glucose load raised the incremental glucose AUC by 186% in the morning53; the cleanest double-blind test localises this to carriers of the common MTNR1B diabetes-risk variant, in whom first-phase insulin secretion fell 40%54, and the variant magnifies the effect roughly sixfold55. The same physiology explains why late dinners harm carriers56. Two honest limits: every study is an acute challenge in about 20 people, and no trial has followed chronic users to a diabetes endpoint. The actionable variable is proximity to food.

"No tolerance, no rebound, no withdrawal" is probably true and almost entirely manufacturer-authored4857. What does happen is relapse: stopping delayed sleep onset again in 92% of children and only 9% could stop entirely58 - the underlying problem returning, not a rebound above baseline59. No independent purpose-designed discontinuation trial exists60.

Two drug interactions matter. Fluvoxamine raised melatonin exposure roughly 17-fold61, and in patients on nifedipine melatonin raised 24-hour blood pressure62.

Adverse events are mild but poorly measured. Daytime sleepiness runs 1.66% across 37 RCTs63; at 10 mg or more minor events rise, though 37% of those trials reported no adverse-event data at all64, and roughly half of controlled studies report at least one significant adverse event65.

Blood-pressure lowering does not survive independent re-analysis: the positive meta was manufacturer-co-authored66 and the independent version crosses zero, with no trial ever reporting a cardiovascular outcome67.

Migraine prophylaxis is the best-supported non-sleep use, beating placebo and matching amitriptyline with better tolerability6869.

Delirium splits by setting, and the split is a bias story. Post-operatively the receptor agonists help70, but in the ICU the definitive 847-patient blinded trial was flatly null71 and a bias-restricted meta gives a null result72.

Paediatric ingestions rose 530% in a decade - but across 260,435 cases there were 5 ventilations and 2 deaths73, tracking availability and gummy formatting rather than a change in toxicity. Adult use roughly quintupled over two decades74. Prolonged-release tablets must not be crushed or quartered75.

A 2026 cohort reporting more dementia among melatonin users should not be read as causal - its own authors say so, and melatonin is preferentially prescribed for REM-sleep behaviour disorder and circadian disruption, both prodromes of dementia and Parkinson's76. Classic reverse causation.

Pregnancy data are thin rather than reassuring: no RCT has tested melatonin for sleep in pregnancy at all77.

docs.title: Tier 4 - Refuted, or preclinical only
docs.text:
"It stops your body making its own" is refuted by every study that measured it. 0.5 mg for 7 days, and even 50 mg/day for 37 days, left endogenous amplitude unchanged78; 2 mg for 3-4 weeks phase-advanced secretion without suppressing it, and changed no measured hormone including testosterone79; and after 6-12 months of nightly use there was no suppression of endogenous production57. It moves your rhythm; it does not switch off your pineal gland.

"Melatonin collapses with age" is refuted. In healthy drug-free 65-81-year-olds versus young adults, there was no difference on any measure80. What changes is the timing of the peak, not the amount. Relatedly, being "low in melatonin" did not predict who responds - age did48, and older normal sleepers with low melatonin gained nothing at any dose81.

"More is better" fails for the clock, though the sleep picture is genuinely messier. A blind subject entrained on 0.5 mg and failed on 10 and 20 mg82, and 0.3 mg outperformed 3.0 mg on carryover8183. But the largest meta-regression found higher doses associated with larger sleep effects8, so there is no clean inverted-U for falling asleep - the real high-dose problems are carryover, hypothermia and failed entrainment.

"It delays puberty" is not supported in humans at supplement doses. Up to 104 weeks left Tanner staging and growth within normal ranges59. The human LH-suppression study everyone cites used 300 mg/day, roughly 100 times a supplement dose84. One retrospective self-report survey hints at delay85 - a reason to keep watching, not a demonstrated harm.

"Blue-blocking glasses fix your sleep" does not follow from the real physiology. Evening light genuinely suppresses melatonin3031, but a meta-analysis of double-blind crossover trials found latency and total sleep time both non-significant86, and Cochrane found no RCT evidence at all relating these lenses to serum melatonin87.

The antioxidant, anti-cancer and longevity claims are preclinical, and that literature is unusually retraction-prone. No human longevity trial was found; the mechanism corpus is rodent and cell-line88, and PubMed flags 89 retracted melatonin-titled papers, including one retracted human RCT89. In humans melatonin moves inflammatory biomarkers and no clinical outcome90. The famous cancer-survival result comes from ten unblinded trials at a single hospital network91, and the one independent double-blind oncology trial was stopped for futility92. The IARC classification applies to shift work, not supplements93, and the prospective evidence across 1.4 million women is null94, though a premenopausal signal survives in retrospective data95. Melatonin did not reduce COVID-19 mortality96. The honest summary of the whole field is an umbrella review: 195 reviews, mostly low quality, only 7 meta-analyses significant at P<0.00197.

Tart cherry is inconsistent: it raised urinary melatonin and helped in one 20-person crossover98, but the largest trial found no effect on sleep at all99.

The regulatory picture is more nuanced than "banned in Europe". Melatonin is prescription-only in the UK, Australia and Switzerland, but legally sold as a low-dose supplement in Spain, Italy, France, Poland, Portugal and Belgium, and not permitted in Denmark, Germany, Sweden, Slovenia or Czechia100.

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text: Weak hypnotic, real chronobiotic, badly labelled product. If melatonin is used, the evidence-aligned pattern is narrow: a low dose (0.3-1 mg, not 5-10), correctly timed (hours ahead for a phase shift, not minutes before bed), for a timing problem (jet lag, a genuinely delayed sleep phase) rather than ordinary insomnia, from a USP Verified or NSF product, and not immediately before eating. For ordinary adult insomnia the guideline-backed answer is cognitive behavioural therapy, and melatonin is specifically recommended against11.

docs.title: The full findings — all 44
docs.text:
Every conclusion this review reached, grouped by how strongly the evidence backs it. Each finding is distilled from the fully-cited evidence above.

Tier 1 - Settled, multi-study consensus (11 findings)

1. Melatonin is a darkness signal, not a sedative, and that single distinction explains almost everything else.

It has two separable actions: a chronobiotic action that shifts and entrains the body clock, which is timing-dependent, and a much weaker hypnotic action that produces mild sleepiness and a temperature drop. Nearly every consumer disappointment, dosing error and mistimed dose follows from treating the second as if it were the first.

2. As a sleeping pill the measured effect is 4 to 7 minutes of sleep-onset latency.

Two independent meta-analyses agree: -4.0 min (95% CI 2.5-5.4) and -7.06 min (95% CI 4.37-9.75). Total sleep time gains 8 to 13 minutes, with lower confidence bounds of 1.7 and 2.9 minutes. The effect is statistically real and clinically marginal, well below the ~20-minute threshold usually treated as meaningful in insomnia trials.

3. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends AGAINST melatonin for chronic insomnia in adults.

The guideline suggests clinicians not use it for sleep-onset or sleep-maintenance insomnia, grouping it with valerian, tryptophan and diphenhydramine, while ramelteon (a melatonin receptor agonist) received a weak recommendation for.

4. Three independent network meta-analyses rank melatonin below the prescription hypnotics.

The largest, covering 154 trials and 44,089 participants and publicly funded, concluded that "melatonin, ramelteon, and non-licensed drugs did not show overall material benefits", with benzodiazepines, eszopiclone, zolpidem and zopiclone more efficacious (SMD 0.27-0.71); two further independent network meta-analyses reach the same ranking. Three independent syntheses agreeing is as close to settled as this literature gets.

5. Melatonin's genuine strength is circadian, not insomnia, and the same professional body says so in both directions.

The AASM recommends against it for chronic insomnia while positively (if weakly) endorsing strategically timed melatonin for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, non-24-hour rhythm in blind adults, and irregular rhythm in children with neurological disorders. This is not a contradiction - it is the chronobiotic/hypnotic distinction expressed as clinical policy.

6. Timing is the mechanism, and the melatonin phase-response curve runs roughly 12 hours out of phase with the light phase-response curve.

For 3 mg, maximum clock advance occurs about 5 hours before dim-light melatonin onset and maximum delay about 11 hours after it, just after habitual wake, with a dead zone across the first half of habitual sleep.

7. Mistimed melatonin shifts the clock the wrong way - the worst case is not "nothing happens".

Morning administration falls squarely in the delay region of the phase-response curve, and the Cochrane jet-lag review warns explicitly that melatonin taken early in the day causes sleepiness and delays adaptation. For someone whose sleep is already delayed, morning melatonin should be expected to make it worse.

8. Oral melatonin has low and highly variable bioavailability - about 15%, ranging 9-33% - with a half-life near 45 minutes.

A 100 mg oral dose produced a peak of 101,163 pg/mL against 72.1 pg/mL from 0.02 mg intravenously. This is why a large tablet does not reproduce the nocturnal signal: it overshoots it enormously and then clears.

9. Retail doses of 3 to 10 mg are supraphysiological by roughly one to two orders of magnitude.

Only 0.1-0.3 mg oral produces peak serum levels inside the normal nocturnal range; even 0.3 mg produced peaks around 220 pg/mL.

10. Ordinary evening light suppresses melatonin far more easily than most people assume.

Roughly half the melatonin-suppressing effect of ~9,000 lux bright light is reached at about 100 lux, and ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99.0% of 116 people and shortened melatonin duration by about 90 minutes. The behavioural lever here is real and free.

11. Product content does not reliably match the label, and the dominant error is overdosing.

The FDA's own laboratory survey of 110 products marketed to children found content spanning 0% to 667% of label, with half outside an acceptable range - 35 above label versus 20 below - and doses reaching 50 mg per serving. In US gummies, 22 of 25 (88%) were inaccurately labelled at 74-347% of label, with one product containing no detectable melatonin at all. The original Canadian survey found -83% to +478% of label and up to 465% lot-to-lot variation within a single product.

Tier 2 - Well supported, with real limits (10 findings)

12. Jet lag is melatonin's best-replicated indication, with a number needed to treat of 2.

Nine of ten trials found benefit crossing five or more time zones, and the newest quantitative synthesis confirms it eastbound (SMD -0.76, 95% CI -1.06 to -0.45) and westbound (-0.66, -1.07 to -0.26). The honest caveat: the Cochrane review dates from 2002 and a 2008 updating search found no new trials.

13. The popular "it only works flying east" rule is not supported.

Jet lag is worse eastward, because the human clock runs at an intrinsic 24.18 hours and therefore drifts naturally later, but the meta-analysed melatonin benefit is similar in both directions.

14. In delayed sleep-wake phase disorder melatonin moves the clock without adding sleep.

It advanced endogenous melatonin onset by 1.18 h (95% CI 0.89-1.48) and sleep-onset clock time by 0.67 h, cutting sleep-onset latency by 23.27 min - while wake time and total sleep time did not change significantly. That pattern is the chronobiotic signature.

15. Non-24-hour rhythm disorder in totally blind people is the single strongest indication.

Six of seven free-running blind subjects entrained to 24.0 h (P<0.001) from a baseline mean period of 24.5 h, and entrainment works at genuinely physiological doses as low as 300 micrograms.

16. Timing dominates dose, and this is measured, not asserted.

In delayed sleep phase syndrome the size of the phase advance correlated with time of administration at r-squared 0.94 (P<0.0001) while 0.3 mg and 3.0 mg did not separate; in children, circadian time of administration predicted the effect and dose did not; and in matched phase-response curves, 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg produced similarly sized shifts when each was given at its own optimal time.

17. For the sleep effect, dose-response peaks around 4 mg per day and taking it earlier probably beats taking it later.

A dose-response meta-analysis of 26 RCTs found the effect peaking near 4 mg and timing significantly predicting sleep-onset latency, suggesting roughly 3 hours before desired bedtime rather than the conventional 30 minutes; for jet lag, doses above 5 mg were no more effective than 0.5-5 mg.

18. The effect is larger in children than adults, but the certainty is graded very low and the panel that produced the numbers said not to reach for it first.

Total sleep time +30.33 min and sleep-onset latency -18.03 min, both with zero heterogeneity - three to four times the adult effect. The same independently funded review graded certainty very low, noted the outcomes were sleep-diary rather than objective, found non-serious adverse events tripled (RR 3.44, 95% CI 1.25-9.42), and concluded melatonin "should never be the first choice". Two further reviews independently reproduce the children-over-adults pattern.

19. In adults with chronic insomnia specifically, one good age-stratified meta-analysis found melatonin not significantly effective at all

for sleep-onset latency, total sleep time or sleep efficiency.

20. The regulator that approved melatonin recorded that its effect is small.

Prolonged-release melatonin is authorised in the EU only for primary insomnia in patients aged 55 and over, short-term, up to 13 weeks - and the CHMP stated it "has only been shown to have a small effect in a relatively small number of patients": 32% responders versus 19% on placebo [R1]. Approval documented the small effect rather than contradicting it.

21. Objective and subjective measurements agree, so this is not a case of "feels better, measures worse".

Prolonged-release melatonin gave subjective sleep-onset latency -6.30 min alongside objective -5.05 min. The effect is small on both.

Tier 3 - Contested, single-source, or industry-dependent (9 findings)

22. Melatonin measurably impairs glucose tolerance, and this is the most under-appreciated real risk.

A 5 mg dose taken 15 minutes before a glucose load raised the incremental glucose AUC by 186% in the morning and 54% in the evening. The cleanest test - a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover - localises the effect to carriers of the common MTNR1B diabetes risk variant, in whom glucose tolerance worsened 11.7% and first-phase beta-cell responsivity fell 40%; the variant magnifies the effect roughly sixfold and explains about 26% of between-person variance. The same physiology explains why late dinners harm carriers. Honest limits: every human study is an acute challenge in about 20 people, and no trial has followed chronic nightly users to a diabetes endpoint.

23. The actionable variable is melatonin's proximity to food, not the dose alone

  • the trial authors' own conclusion. No trial has yet tested whether separating melatonin from eating prevents the effect.

24. At 10 mg and above, minor adverse events rise measurably while serious ones do not.

RR 1.40 (p<0.001) for drowsiness, headache and dizziness across 79 studies and 3,861 participants - but only 4 studies were at low risk of bias and 37% reported no adverse-event data at all. Roughly half of controlled studies report at least one significant adverse event, most often fatigue, mood change and psychomotor impairment.

25. The entire "no tolerance, no rebound, no withdrawal" evidence base is manufacturer-authored.

Six-month, 6-12 month, 52-week and 104-week studies all report no efficacy loss and no withdrawal syndrome, and every one was authored by staff of the company making the prolonged-release product, with three of four open-label and lacking a placebo arm. Independent corroboration exists but is indirect: a meta-regression found longer trials showed larger effects, and academic follow-up cohorts agree in direction. No independent purpose-designed placebo-controlled discontinuation trial exists.

26. Relapse on stopping is real and is not the same thing as dependence.

In children followed a mean 3.7 years, 65% were still using daily, temporary discontinuation delayed sleep onset again in 92%, and only 9% could stop entirely. But after two years of treatment, sleep during a blinded two-week withdrawal was still better than pre-treatment baseline - the underlying problem returning, not a rebound above baseline.

27. There is one genuinely serious drug interaction, and one counterintuitive cardiovascular one.

Fluvoxamine raised oral melatonin AUC roughly 17-fold via CYP1A2 inhibition, an effect specific enough that citalopram does not share it. Separately, in hypertensive patients well controlled on nifedipine, melatonin raised 24-hour blood pressure by 6.5/4.9 mmHg - the opposite of its usual direction.

28. Blood-pressure lowering does not survive independent re-analysis.

The positive meta-analysis was co-authored by manufacturer staff and found the all-trials pool non-significant, with only a controlled-release subgroup positive. The independent re-analysis found asleep systolic -3.57 mmHg with a confidence interval crossing zero, from four trials of which one was at low risk of bias, at low-to-very-low certainty, and no trial has ever reported a cardiovascular outcome.

29. Migraine prophylaxis is melatonin's best-supported non-sleep use.

A 196-patient three-arm RCT found melatonin 3 mg cut headache days by 2.7 versus 2.2 for amitriptyline and 1.1 for placebo (P=0.009 versus placebo), with better tolerability than amitriptyline; a nine-RCT meta-analysis agrees (-1.54 headache days, responder RR 1.38).

30. Delirium prevention splits cleanly by setting, and the split is a bias story.

Post-operatively, melatonin receptor agonists gave OR 0.54 across 158 trials and 41,084 participants, though rated moderate-to-very-low quality and behind dexmedetomidine. In the ICU, the definitive 847-patient blinded trial was flatly null on delirium, mortality and sleep, and a meta restricted to low-risk-of-bias trials gives RR 0.89 (0.73-1.09). Benefit appears when high-risk-of-bias trials are included and disappears when they are excluded.

Tier 4 - Refuted, or preclinical-only (9 findings)

31. "Taking melatonin stops your body making its own" is refuted by every study that has actually measured it.

0.5 mg nightly for 7 days left the amplitude of endogenous secretion unchanged, and 50 mg/day for 37 days produced no change in the endogenous profile; 2 mg for 3-4 weeks phase-advanced endogenous secretion by 1-3 hours without suppressing it; and urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin after 6-12 months of nightly use showed no suppression. It moves your rhythm; it does not switch off your pineal gland. Honest limit, stated plainly: the direct evidence is roughly 34 subjects across two studies, and nobody has tested nightly 10 mg for years.

32. "Melatonin collapses with age, so older people should replace it" is refuted.

In healthy drug-free adults aged 65-81 versus healthy young adults under constant-routine conditions, there was no difference on any measure: 24-hour mean 70 versus 73 pmol/L (P=0.97), nocturnal peak 162 versus 161 pmol/L (P=0.63), integrated area 85,800 versus 86,700 (P=0.66). What changes with age is the timing of the peak, not the amount.

33. "I'm low in melatonin so I should supplement" is refuted by the one large trial that tested it.

In 791 patients, those with low endogenous melatonin did not respond better than placebo; age predicted response, melatonin level did not. Older normal sleepers with low melatonin gained nothing at any dose.

34. "More is better" is refuted for the clock, but the picture for sleep is genuinely messier and the honest version matters.

For entrainment, a blind subject entrained on 0.5 mg and failed on 10 mg and 20 mg, the authors' interpretation being that excess melatonin spills onto the wrong zone of the phase-response curve. For sleep, 0.3 mg restored sleep efficiency while 3.0 mg caused hypothermia and left melatonin elevated into daylight - but the largest meta-regression found higher doses associated with larger sleep effects. So there is no clean inverted-U for falling asleep; the real high-dose problems are carryover, thermoregulation and failed entrainment.

35. "It delays puberty in children" is not supported in humans at supplement doses.

Up to 104 weeks of prolonged-release melatonin in 80 children aged 2-17.5 left Tanner staging, height, weight and BMI within normal ranges. The fear is extrapolated from seasonal-breeding animals where melatonin gates reproduction. The one human study showing LH suppression used 300 mg/day, roughly 100 times a supplement dose, in a contraceptive-development programme - citing it as a risk of a 3 mg gummy is a dose-level category error. The honest counterweight: one retrospective self-report survey after a mean 7.1 years suggested a tendency toward delayed puberty, which is a reason to keep watching, not a demonstrated harm.

36. "Blue-blocking glasses fix your sleep" does not follow from the real physiology.

Evening light genuinely suppresses melatonin, but a meta-analysis of the double-blind crossover trials found sleep-onset latency -4.86 min (95% CI -20.23 to 10.52, p=0.54) and total sleep time +8.75 min (-35.31 to 52.82, p=0.70), both non-significant. Cochrane found sleep-quality effects indeterminate and no RCT evidence at all relating these lenses to serum melatonin; the famous positive trial had 14 participants.

37. The antioxidant, anti-cancer and longevity claim families are preclinical - and that preclinical corpus carries an unusual integrity burden.

No human trial of melatonin for longevity or healthspan was found. PubMed flags 89 papers with "melatonin" in the title as Retracted Publication and 21 with an Expression of Concern, with J Pineal Res alone carrying 22 retractions and 16 EoCs, almost entirely preclinical antioxidant, mitochondrial and anti-cancer mechanism papers. One human melatonin oxidative-stress RCT was retracted in 2025, and the meta-analysis pooling that literature was co-authored by the same advocacy group and found no TNF-alpha effect while concluding favourably. In humans melatonin moves inflammatory biomarkers and no clinical outcome.

38. The cancer-survival claim does not survive scrutiny.

The famous 34% one-year mortality reduction comes from ten unblinded trials conducted at a single hospital network - the authors say so verbatim - with implausibly perfect homogeneity. The one independent double-blind placebo-controlled melatonin oncology trial was stopped for futility. Separately, IARC's Group 2A classification applies to shift work, not supplements, and the prospective evidence on night work and breast cancer is null across 1.4 million women (RR 0.99), though a premenopausal signal survives in retrospective data.

39. Melatonin did not reduce COVID-19 mortality in the most rigorous synthesis

(RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.47-1.11, I-squared 82%, low certainty), with recovery and every inflammatory marker non-significant; the dramatic positive result came from an advocacy-co-authored meta-analysis.

Practical — what to actually do (5 findings)

40. If melatonin is used, use a low dose: roughly 0.3-1 mg, not 5-10 mg.

Only 0.1-0.3 mg produces peaks inside the normal nocturnal range, and in the cleanest head-to-head 0.3 mg restored sleep efficiency while 3.0 mg caused hypothermia and left melatonin elevated into the daylight hours. Guidance for older adults is 0.3-2 mg immediate-release. Higher doses do not buy a bigger clock shift.

41. Take it hours before target bedtime for a phase shift, not minutes before.

Bedtime dosing sits in the phase-shifting dead zone, the dose-response analysis suggests roughly 3 hours before desired bedtime rather than the conventional 30 minutes, and mistimed melatonin actively shifts the clock the wrong way. Never take it in the morning.

42. Use it for a timing problem, not for ordinary insomnia.

Jet lag, a genuinely delayed sleep phase and non-24 in blind people are where melatonin earns its place; for chronic adult insomnia the AASM recommends against it and the guideline-backed alternative is cognitive behavioural therapy.

43. Buy only a USP Verified or NSF-certified product.

Content variability did not correlate with manufacturer or product type, the FDA's own survey found half of 110 children's products out of specification with doses to 50 mg, and 88% of gummies were mislabelled. Third-party certification is the only buyer-side lever. Prolonged-release tablets must not be crushed or quartered.

44. Do not take it immediately before eating, and fix the light first.

Melatonin measurably impairs glucose tolerance, concentrated in MTNR1B carriers, so proximity to food is the actionable variable. And the largest free lever in this whole topic is light: ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99.0% of 116 people and shortened its duration by ~90 minutes.

docs.title: Test yourself
docs.text:
Twelve questions drawn at random from the findings above. Pick an answer, see why, and learn. Replayable, and your best score is remembered on this device.

  1. Arendt J 2005, Sleep Med Rev. PMID 15649736. The chronobiotic framing of melatonin's action. ↩↩

  2. Cruz-Sanabria F 2023, Curr Neuropharmacol. PMID 35176989. The clearest modern statement that melatonin has a chronobiotic action and a separable, weaker sleep-promoting one. ↩↩

  3. Klein DC 2007, J Biol Chem. PMID 17164235. AANAT, 'the Timezyme', as the rhythm-controlling enzyme of nightly melatonin synthesis. ↩

  4. Lewy AJ 1980, Science. PMID 7434030. The foundational demonstration that light suppresses human melatonin secretion. ↩

  5. Lewy AJ 1989, Chronobiol Int. PMID 2706705. Defines dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), the gold-standard marker of circadian phase. ↩

  6. Dubocovich ML 2010, Pharmacol Rev. PMID 20605968. IUPHAR nomenclature for the MT1 and MT2 receptors. ↩

  7. Brzezinski A 2005, Sleep Med Rev. PMID 15649737. Independent meta: sleep-onset latency -4.0 min (95% CI 2.5-5.4), sleep efficiency +2.2%, total sleep time +12.8 min, from only 284 subjects. ↩↩↩

  8. Ferracioli-Oda E 2013, PLoS One. PMID 23691095. Sleep-onset latency -7.06 min (95% CI 4.37-9.75), total sleep time +8.25 min; the authors call the effects modest. Its meta-regression found higher doses associated with LARGER effects. ↩↩↩↩

  9. Lim S 2022, Pharmacol Res. PMID 34999224. Umbrella review: sleep-onset latency SMD 0.33, but sleep efficiency not significant. ↩

  10. Buscemi N 2005, J Gen Intern Med. PMID 16423108. AHRQ-funded meta: -11.7 min overall, only -7.2 min in insomnia, but -38.8 min in delayed sleep phase syndrome. ↩

  11. Sateia MJ 2017, J Clin Sleep Med. PMID 27998379. The AASM guideline recommending clinicians NOT use melatonin for sleep-onset or sleep-maintenance insomnia in adults. ↩↩↩↩

  12. De Crescenzo F 2022, Lancet. PMID 35843245. The largest network meta-analysis, 154 trials and 44,089 participants: melatonin 'did not show overall material benefits'. ↩↩

  13. Pan B 2023, Drugs. PMID 36947394. Independent second network meta-analysis of 153 RCTs, same ranking. ↩↩

  14. Yue JL 2023, Sleep Med Rev. PMID 36701954. Independent third network meta-analysis, same direction. ↩↩

  15. Choi K 2022, Sleep Med Rev. PMID 36179487. Age-stratified meta of 24 RCTs: not significantly effective in adults; significant only in children and adolescents. ↩

  16. Kuriyama A 2014, Sleep Med. PMID 24656909. Ramelteon meta of 13 trials: subjective sleep latency -4.30 min; the authors conclude the clinical impact is small. ↩

  17. Lewy AJ 1998, Chronobiol Int. PMID 9493716. The melatonin phase-response curve runs ~12 hours out of phase with the light curve. ↩↩

  18. Burgess HJ 2008, J Physiol. PMID 18006583. The modern phase-response curve for 3 mg, including the dead zone across the first half of habitual sleep. ↩↩↩

  19. Mundey K 2005, Sleep. PMID 16295212. Phase advance correlated with time of administration at r-squared 0.94, while 0.3 mg and 3.0 mg did not separate. ↩↩

  20. van Geijlswijk IM 2010, Psychopharmacology (Berl). PMID 20668840. No dose-response across a threefold range in 72 children; circadian timing predicted the effect, dose did not. ↩

  21. Burgess HJ 2010, J Clin Endocrinol Metab. PMID 20410229. Matched phase-response curves: 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg give similarly sized shifts when each is at its own optimal time. ↩

  22. Herxheimer A 2002, Cochrane Database Syst Rev. PMID 12076414. The anchor jet-lag review: number needed to treat 2; doses above 5 mg no better; warns that wrong-time dosing DELAYS adaptation. ↩↩↩↩

  23. Dollins AB 1994, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. PMID 8127888. Only 0.1-0.3 mg oral produced peak serum levels inside the normal nocturnal range. ↩

  24. Harpsøe NG 2015, Eur J Clin Pharmacol. PMID 26008214. Core pharmacokinetics: oral bioavailability ~15% (range 9-33%), half-life ~45 min; 100 mg oral gave a peak of 101,163 pg/mL versus 72.1 pg/mL from 0.02 mg intravenously. ↩

  25. Lane EA 1985, J Clin Endocrinol Metab. PMID 4055987. The original demonstration of extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism. ↩

  26. Dollins AB 1993, Psychopharmacology (Berl). PMID 7871062. Pharmacological daytime doses of 10-80 mg all cut vigilance accuracy and raised fatigue. ↩

  27. Pawar RS 2025, Drug Test Anal. PMID 39482109. The FDA's own survey of 110 children's products: 0% to 667% of label, half out of specification, doses to 50 mg - and no serotonin detected in any product. ↩↩

  28. Cohen PA 2023, JAMA. PMID 37097362. US gummies: 88% inaccurately labelled, 74-347% of label, one product with no detectable melatonin. Maximum measured was 13.1 mg. ↩

  29. Erland LA 2017, J Clin Sleep Med. PMID 27855744. Content -83% to +478% of label, up to 465% lot-to-lot variation, serotonin in 26% of a Canadian sample. ↩

  30. Zeitzer JM 2000, J Physiol. PMID 10922269. Light dose-response: roughly half the melatonin suppression of ~9,000 lux is reached near 100 lux. ↩↩

  31. Gooley JJ 2011, J Clin Endocrinol Metab. PMID 21193540. Room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99.0% of 116 people and shortened its duration by ~90 minutes. ↩↩

  32. Chan V 2021, Nutrients. PMID 33809656. Newest jet-lag synthesis: eastbound SMD -0.76, westbound -0.66 - similar in both directions. ↩

  33. Czeisler CA 1999, Science. PMID 10381883. Human intrinsic circadian period averages 24.18 h - why eastward travel is harder. ↩

  34. van Geijlswijk IM 2010, Sleep. PMID 21120122. Delayed sleep phase: clock advanced 1.18 h and latency -23.27 min, while wake time and total sleep time did NOT change. ↩↩

  35. Sletten TL 2018, PLoS Med. PMID 29912983. The largest DSWPD RCT: sleep onset only 34 min earlier, and post-treatment DLMO did not differ between groups. ↩

  36. Sack RL 2000, N Engl J Med. PMID 11027741. Six of seven free-running blind subjects entrained to 24.0 h. ↩↩

  37. Lewy AJ 2005, Chronobiol Int. PMID 16393710. Entrainment in blind people works at physiological doses as low as 300 micrograms. ↩

  38. Lockley SW 2015, Lancet. PMID 26466871. Tasimelteon phase-3 trials: entrainment 20% vs 3% placebo, entirely manufacturer-funded. ↩

  39. Liira J 2014, Cochrane Database Syst Rev. PMID 25113164. Shift work, melatonin's weakest indication: +24 min daytime sleep, graded low quality, no meaningful sleepiness reduction. ↩

  40. Auger RR 2015, J Clin Sleep Med. PMID 26414986. The AASM circadian guideline: every melatonin recommendation is weak-for, and the only strong recommendation is AGAINST sleep-promoting medication in demented elderly. ↩↩

  41. Morgenthaler TI 2007, Sleep. PMID 18041479. The AASM practice parameters that remain its most recent formal word on jet lag and shift-work disorder. ↩

  42. Edemann-Callesen H 2023, EClinicalMedicine. PMID 37457117. Independently funded paediatric meta: total sleep time +30.33 min, latency -18.03 min - but certainty very low, adverse events tripled, and 'melatonin should never be the first choice'. ↩↩

  43. Salanitro M 2022, Neurosci Biobehav Rev. PMID 35691474. One criteria set across ages: significant in children with neurodevelopmental disorders; in adults only in delayed sleep phase disorder. ↩

  44. Gringras P 2012, BMJ. PMID 23129488. Independent trial: children gained little additional sleep because they also woke 29.9 minutes earlier. ↩

  45. Nogueira HA 2023, Prog Neuropsychopharmacol Biol Psychiatry. PMID 36584862. Autism meta: large pooled effects but with I-squared of 91-94%. ↩

  46. Van der Heijden KB 2007, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry. PMID 17242627. ADHD: sleep timing advanced, but no significant effect on behaviour, cognition or quality of life. ↩

  47. Wade AG 2007, Curr Med Res Opin. PMID 17875243. Manufacturer trial in 55-80s: a net 11.4-minute latency benefit, responders 26% vs 15%. ↩

  48. Wade AG 2010, BMC Med. PMID 20712869. 6-month RCT, 791 randomised. Critically, patients with LOW endogenous melatonin did not respond better than placebo - age predicted response. ↩↩↩↩

  49. Maruani J 2023, J Sleep Res. PMID 37434463. Prolonged-release melatonin: subjective sleep-onset latency -6.30 min alongside objective -5.05 min. ↩

  50. Cruz-Sanabria F 2024, J Pineal Res. PMID 38888087. Dose-response meta of 26 RCTs: the effect peaks near 4 mg/day, and timing predicted sleep-onset latency, suggesting ~3 hours before bed. ↩

  51. Vural EM 2014, Drugs Aging. PMID 24802882. In older adults, higher doses kept levels supraphysiological longer; recommends the lowest immediate-release dose, 0.3-2 mg. ↩

  52. Suhner A 1998, Chronobiol Int. PMID 9844753. Largest dose-comparison field trial: 0.5 mg was almost as effective as 5 mg. ↩

  53. Rubio-Sastre P 2014, Sleep. PMID 25197811. 5 mg before a glucose load raised the incremental glucose AUC by 186% in the morning and 54% in the evening. ↩↩

  54. Qian J 2026, Diabetes Care. PMID 42346809. Double-blind crossover: in MTNR1B risk carriers only, first-phase beta-cell responsivity fell 40% and insulin feedback was blunted. ↩↩

  55. Garaulet M 2015, Metabolism. PMID 26440713. The MTNR1B variant magnifies the glucose effect roughly sixfold and explains ~26% of between-person variance. ↩
